It would also be better if conditions such as whether it is better to use the same series of LLMs as the subsequent LLMs or whether models of the best possible quality should be used are discussed.
469.llm_review: Explanation, Model: The paper’s explanation for why uniform weight averaging of 12 text-reading encoders with a base CLIP preserves general vision capabilities while boosting text-centric understanding remains mostly empirical. There is limited analysis of failure modes or representation changes introduced by the soup (e.g., attention to fonts/layout vs. natural-object features), and the trade-off where general-image performance lags the CLIP-L baseline (C6) is only briefly acknowledged. More diagnostic analyses (feature visualizations, probing, or per-category error breakdowns) would clarify when and why the ELVA-encoder underperforms on entity recognition and general visual tasks.

470.human_review: W2. The largest improvement in Figure 1 is achieved by adding the open-source training dataset, but detailed discussion, such as data sampling strategy and the process that led to that recipe, is limited.
470.llm_review: Data, Discussion, Improvement: While the data curation is extensive, the new resources raise questions. Parsing-Bench appears small (≈30 images for key sources), limiting statistical confidence; CORD-Instruct relies on GPT-3.5 for instruction synthesis, but the paper provides limited discussion on quality control, bias, leakage, and licensing breadth across the many datasets. The discussion of limitations (e.g., entity knowledge gaps, OCR latency) is appreciated but could be strengthened with concrete improvement plans and additional evaluations on larger, standardized document suites (e.g., broader ID/receipt/passport corpora, multi-language settings) and more comparisons to the latest high-res LVLMs under matched token budgets.

471.human_review: The method section describes the proposed method and its components in detail. Especially, each component is explained thoroughly and supported by appropriate citations.
471.llm_review: The paper clearly motivates and explains the method: starting from the empirical observation that compositional attributes in prompts improve CLIP alignment, it designs a prompt-tuning framework that explicitly learns attribute-level inductive biases alongside class tokens. The training objective is well laid out (classification loss plus attribute alignment and prompt regularization), and the rationale for learning an attribute embedding at training time (since class labels and off-the-shelf captioners are unavailable at inference) is clearly articulated with intuitive figures and a step-by-step description.

472.human_review: Utilizing BLIP-2 model for attribute generation is an interesting idea. This external knowledge may offer information not easily captured with only a few-shot examples.
472.llm_review: The model is thoughtfully constructed and modular: a lightweight attribute extractor (two-layer MLP) predicts a 512-d embedding aligned to CLIP’s text space; instance-conditioned prompts are formed via a multi-head attention mechanism that uses learnable context tokens as queries; and visual prompting augments the ViT with learnable tokens at deeper layers to enrich the image representation for attribute prediction. A regularization term anchors prompts to a diverse pool of attribute-aware textual templates. Crucially, CLIP encoders remain frozen, preserving pretraining priors while adding interpretable, attribute-aware components.

473.human_review: Both base-to-novel generalization and domain generalization experiments are conducted.
473.llm_review: Experiments are broad and targeted to generalization: base-to-novel class generalization across 10 datasets in a 16-shot regime shows consistent improvements in HM (80.75 vs. 79.48 for LFA and +7.5 over CoOp on average), with stronger gains on attribute-rich datasets (e.g., OxfordPets, Flowers102). Domain generalization from ImageNet to four challenging variants yields the best or tied-best average (60.71), and the paper also reports 4-shot results (Appendix) indicating similar trends. The evaluation protocols follow established setups, and ablations probe key design choices.

474.human_review: There is no need to limit the BLIP-2 model to generate in “one-word” because the answers from BLIP-2 will be encoded to a single embedding vector and used as a target for the Attribute Extractor. This raises the question about the necessity of ‘single-word prediction’ (which seems to be the key contribution).
474.llm_review: The contribution feels incremental. Leveraging attributes to guide prompts, instance conditioning, visual prompting, and prompt regularization are all known directions; the novelty lies mainly in combining them and using a learned attribute embedding trained from BLIP-2–derived labels. The interpretability claim is largely inferential (attributes embedded in prompts) without human studies, systematic probing, or task-level interpretability evaluation, which limits the perceived conceptual contribution.

475.human_review: The demonstration of cosine similarity (Figure 3) alone is not sufficient to show that the attribute extractor effectively extracts information predicted from BLIP-2. The performance of the ‘oracle’ setting, using BLIP-2 embeddings (i.e., the target of L_attr loss) instead of predicted ones, should be presented. Also, a direct comparison between estimated and BLIP-2 embeddings is necessary.
475.llm_review: Comparisons and embedding details leave gaps. Some baseline numbers (e.g., PLOT’s very low domain generalization) suggest possible reimplementation or tuning issues; parameter counts and compute overhead are not matched, despite adding visual tokens and extra modules. The instance conditioning is said to attend over "various points" of the image, yet the text describes attention over a single global CLIP embedding, raising questions about what is actually being attended and whether spatial/patch features are used. Performance-wise, base accuracy sometimes drops (e.g., ImageNet base vs. strong baselines), indicating potential trade-offs not fully analyzed.

476.human_review: Based on the ablation results (Table 3), adding attribute information does not appear to be a critical factor for performance improvement. In other words, visual prompting, instance conditioning, and regularization contribute significantly more.
476.llm_review: Ablations do not isolate all components. While Table 3 examines visual prompting depth and conditioning type, the paper does not ablate the individual contributions of the attribute loss vs. the regularization loss, the number/choice of attributes, or the attribute vocabulary. Robustness to noisy attributes is only shown via a label-swap stress test; finer-grained noise sensitivity is missing. Reported gains over the strongest baseline are modest on average (~1.3 HM), vary by dataset, and lack statistical significance tests, making it hard to assess the reliability of the improvements.

477.human_review: Novel approach using semantic representations to improve AVQA. It uses source-wise learnable tokens to extract semantic features from audio and visual inputs and employs a source-aware semantic representation block to align audio-visual features. In addition, it also applies multi-modal spatial and temporal attention to focus on relevant regions, with integrated features using a fusion network for final answer prediction.
477.llm_review: Approach and Novelty: The paper proposes a source-aware architecture that injects semantics directly into multimodal fusion via Source-wise Learnable Tokens (SLT) and a Source-aware Semantic Representation (SaSR) block. The design couples token–feature cross-attention with auxiliary objectives (source-presence BCE and category-regularizing CE) and a matched/mismatched contrastive-style loss, offering a principled way to bind audio sources and visual objects to question-relevant concepts. This token-centric, source-aware formulation goes beyond generic cross-modal attention used in prior A/VQA work (e.g., A-VST, PSTP-Net) and is a compelling idea for object/sound disambiguation.

478.human_review: Comprehensive experiments and comparisons with existing methods. It outperforms existing AVQA methods on the Music-AVQA dataset, especially for complex question types. It also achieves 89.9% accuracy on the AVQA-Yang dataset, surpassing previous methods. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed components.
478.llm_review: Accuracy, Comparison, Data, Experiment: On MUSIC-AVQA, the model reports the best overall accuracy (74.21%) among compared methods, surpassing strong A/V baselines such as PSTP-Net (73.52%) and TJSTG (73.04%). The approach also transfers well to AVQA-Yang (89.9% vs 89.0% for the best listed baseline). The comparisons span audio-only, visual-only, and audio-visual question types on public datasets, and the ablations are informative: adding SLT and SaSR yields a +3.90% absolute gain over the base model; the spatial and temporal attention modules further contribute. Together, these results demonstrate empirical benefits attributable to the proposed source-aware components.

479.key_points: Strength: Attention, Figure, Interpretation, Model, Result
479.human_review: Visualization of model attention helps interpret results.
479.llm_review: Attention, Figure, Interpretation, Model, Result: The spatial attention heatmaps and temporal attention visualizations illustrate where the model localizes sounding objects and when it attends to relevant segments, improving interpretability of the attention mechanisms. The architecture figure clarifies how SLT and SaSR interact with SA/TA blocks, helping readers connect the model design to observed gains in localization-, comparison-, and temporal-related question types. These qualitative results complement the quantitative improvements and make the model’s reasoning behavior more transparent.

480.human_review: The authors focused on Source-wise Learnable Tokens to extract semantically compact features from videos and employ Source-aware Semantic Representation to align these with visual and audio features. Visualizing and comparing the features in latent space would be helpful to demonstrate SaSR-Net as a better representation method.
480.llm_review: Comparison, Figure, Method: Some method details and figures are underspecified or inconsistent. The loss definitions and notation contain ambiguities (e.g., the matched/mismatched loss appears to reuse the same variable for both positive and negative terms; references to which embeddings are used in Lsource are unclear), and there are typos and formatting issues that hinder precise understanding. The comparative scope could be strengthened by including more recent/strong AVQA baselines (e.g., LA-VISH) and MUSIC-AVQA v2.0 results. Figure captions are brief and could better explain settings and failure cases to substantiate the claimed mechanisms.

481.human_review: From Table 1, SaSR-Net seems to perform poorly on single-modality questions. I would like to see further elaborations on potential reasons.
481.llm_review: Performance: While overall accuracy improves, the margin over the strongest baselines on MUSIC-AVQA is modest (~0.7% absolute), and the method appears to underperform some baselines on certain subtasks (e.g., audio-only QA compared to TJSTG). The reliance on fixed category tokens may constrain performance in open-vocabulary or out-of-domain settings, potentially limiting gains beyond instrument-centric datasets.

482.human_review: Computational costs should be discussed and compared for multi-modal experiments.
482.llm_review: Comparison, Experiment: The experimental protocol lacks some details needed to assess fairness and generality: backbone parity with baselines is not fully justified; category token count and supervision for AVQA-Yang are not clearly described; negative-pair sampling strategy is under-specified; and no significance testing is reported. Additional experiments—robustness to noise/overlap, sensitivity to frame/audio rates, cross-dataset generalization beyond two benchmarks, and analysis on MUSIC-AVQA v2.0—would provide a stronger comparative picture.

483.human_review: The paper introduces a unique approach to TKG reasoning by addressing the asynchronous evolution of events, which has not been adequately considered in previous works.
483.llm_review: Approach and novelty are well-motivated: the paper introduces a natural division of history into explicit and implicit patches based on target-entity occurrence and combines a dual-level aggregation scheme (relation-aware intra-patch encoding plus inter-patch attention). This directly targets asynchronous event evolution and long-range dependencies, a gap in prior GCN/GRU-based temporal models. The mechanism is conceptually clear, technically plausible, and distinct from prior query- or candidate-centric encoders that treat all snapshots uniformly.

484.human_review: The proposed dual-level aggregation framework is well-designed and effectively captures both local and global temporal dependencies, improving the accuracy of entity representations.
484.llm_review: The framework delivers strong accuracy: across six benchmarks, the method consistently achieves state-of-the-art MRR and Hits gains, with notable margins on ICEWS datasets and robustness under limited training data. The architecture is coherent and modular (patch construction, intra-patch encoder, inter-patch attention, dual decoder), and ablations indicate each module contributes materially to the final performance.

485.human_review: Extensive experiments on six datasets show that NEDA significantly outperforms existing methods, providing strong empirical evidence for its effectiveness.
485.llm_review: Data and experimental effectiveness are compelling: results are reported on four standard datasets plus two newly curated ICEWS22/23 sets, using time-aware filtered MRR and Hits with averages over five runs. The study includes ablations, sensitivity analyses (e.g., L and n), and a low-data regime evaluation, all pointing to stable effectiveness. The addition of ICEWS22/23 expands temporal coverage and supports external validity, and code availability further strengthens reproducibility.

486.human_review: The framework's complexity might lead to scalability issues when applied to very large TKGs. The paper could benefit from a discussion on the computational efficiency and possible optimizations.
486.llm_review: Complexity and efficiency concerns within the framework are insufficiently addressed. The per-query patch construction, k-hop subgraph extraction, and dual-level aggregation can introduce notable time and memory overhead versus snapshot-level methods. No asymptotic analysis, runtime, or memory benchmarks are provided, and scalability to high-degree graphs or long histories is unclear. The smaller gains on GDELT suggest potential efficiency and scalability limits in dense patches. Reporting throughput, adding batching/caching, lightweight patch pruning, and sparse inter-patch attention would improve the framework’s efficiency story.

487.human_review: The proposed method is evaluated only on TKG reasoning tasks. It would be interesting to see its applicability and performance on related tasks, such as temporal link prediction or temporal knowledge graph completion.
487.llm_review: Application and evaluation scope are narrow in places. The paper focuses on extrapolative entity prediction; relation prediction—described in the setup—is not evaluated. Generalization beyond news/event-centric TKGs (e.g., Wikidata/YAGO, domain-specific TKGs) is not demonstrated. Several baselines are missing on the new ICEWS22/23 datasets, weakening comparative breadth, and there is no statistical significance testing or runtime comparison. More detail on ICEWS22/23 construction choices and potential biases would strengthen the evaluation.

488.human_review: The natural division strategy for patch selection is not deeply analyzed. Further discussion on its limitations and potential improvements could strengthen the paper.
488.llm_review: Analysis, discussion, and improvement avenues could be deeper. The paper does not inspect inter-patch attention weights, provide error analyses, or qualitative case studies to substantiate the asynchronous-evolution claim. The inter-patch attention uses a single learnable query vector rather than conditioning on the specific query (s, r, t), potentially limiting adaptivity. As acknowledged, only dominant topics per patch are modeled. Improvements could include query-conditioned inter-patch attention, multi-topic modeling within patches, learning patch boundaries instead of a fixed rule, and richer interpretability and failure-mode analyses.

489.human_review: The proposed method effectively combines the content-based filtering capability of LLMs with collaborative filtering. It outperforms both LLM-based baselines and collaborative filtering baselines.
489.llm_review: Method, Performance: The paper introduces a clear, training-free pipeline that combines content-based and collaborative filtering within an LLM prompting framework. The preference generator distills likes/dislikes from user histories, while clustering and iterative bootstrapping bring in similar-user signals; convergence is measured via cosine similarity on summary embeddings. Empirically, the approach delivers strong AUC/Logloss gains over both traditional DLRMs and prior prompt-based systems on two Amazon datasets, indicating the method’s practical effectiveness.

490.human_review: The proposed method is tuning-free, which saves the expensive cost of fine-tuning LLMs.
490.llm_review: Fine-tuning, Method: A notable contribution is achieving collaborative-filtering benefits without any fine-tuning or alignment of the LLM. By leveraging fixed LLMs with progressive prompt enhancement, the method avoids expensive instruction tuning while still capturing cross-user preferences via clustering and iterative aggregation. This design choice lowers engineering overhead and improves portability across domains and models, especially compared to instruction-tuned baselines like TALLRec and ReLLA.

491.human_review: The proposed method provides better explainability to the recommendation results.
491.llm_review: Explanation, Method, Result: The preference generator yields concise, human-readable rationales (e.g., favored attributes, disfavored brands/categories), and the iterative enhancement surfaces additional, cohort-derived evidence. Case studies show how added signals from similar users shift predictions in sensible ways and highlight relevant attributes (e.g., appliance parts, skincare). This explains why recommendations change across iterations and ties directly to measured performance improvements in the results.

492.human_review: The authors conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method and the necessity of each component.
492.llm_review: Effectiveness, Experiment: The ablations are informative and well-aligned with the design: incorporating dislikes helps over positives-only; the preference generator adds value; adding similar-user histories improves further; and iterative bootstrapping yields the best results. Hyperparameter analysis suggests reasonable robustness (few clusters/users suffice) and underscores LLM choice sensitivity. The case studies concretely illustrate the mechanism’s effectiveness and how iterative enrichment improves predictions.

493.human_review: PepRec requires a significant amount of LLM calls to predict a user's preference on one item. This is computationally inefficient and can incur a high latency. Although this is an inherent limitation of LLM-based recommendation and the authors also note this in the Limitations Section, the iterative prompt enhancement (each iteration requires two LLM calls) in PepRec makes it worse.
493.llm_review: Efficiency: The approach can be expensive and slow at inference due to multiple LLM calls per user–item pair during bootstrapping, plus token-heavy prompts summarizing histories. There is no quantitative cost/latency analysis, throughput study, or budgeted variant (e.g., early-stopping heuristics, token pruning, caching strategies). Clustering/encoding adds preprocessing overhead, and the iterative loop risks variable latency, which could hinder deployment in high-QPS settings.

494.human_review: PepRec can only capture users' recent preference given the context-length limitation of LLMs.
494.llm_review: Model: Several modeling choices are potentially brittle or under-justified: (i) representing users by averaged sentence-transformer embeddings and clustering via K-Means may not capture nuanced, multi-faceted preferences; (ii) convergence based on cosine similarity between short textual summaries could be noisy and sensitive to phrasing; (iii) the LLM-generated preference summaries may hallucinate or overfit to recent histories; and (iv) reliance on GPT-4 raises reproducibility concerns and masks how well the method works with smaller/open models. Robustness checks (multiple LLMs, different encoders/clustering schemes, significance testing) and stronger CF baselines would strengthen the modeling claims.

495.human_review: This paper is well-written and motivated, accompanied by many nicely drawn figures and tables illustrating the major information of the paper.
495.llm_review: Clear motivation and presentation: the paper convincingly argues that binary answer accuracy obscures why LMMs fail on multimodal math, motivating process-level evaluation and fine-grained categorization. Figures (e.g., the overview in Figure 1 and the error-type illustration in Figure 3) effectively communicate the pipeline, error taxonomy, and dataset structure, helping readers quickly grasp the problem framing and design choices.

496.human_review: Fully open-ended problem evaluation instead of other formats like multiple-choice, avoiding LMM to guess an answer, which has been a serious problem in other current evaluation benchmarks.
496.llm_review: Benchmark and evaluation novelty: MM-MATH contributes an open-ended, middle-school multimodal math benchmark with both outcome and process evaluation, filling a gap left by prior benchmarks that are predominantly multiple-choice or outcome-only. The evaluation protocols are thoughtfully designed (boxed-answer extraction, tolerance for numeric answers, symbolic simplification for expressions), and the comparison across difficulty, grade, and knowledge points provides multi-dimensional diagnostic power.

497.human_review: Fine-grained meta-information annotation, including difficulty, grade level, and problem type. This information can help LMM developers better understand their model’s weaknesses.
497.llm_review: Annotation and model coverage: Each problem includes a human-checked, step-by-step solution and multi-dimensional metadata (difficulty calibrated by student scoring rates, grade levels, and a teacher-defined knowledge taxonomy). The process-evaluation labeling uses GPT-4V to identify first-error types, with a reported manual spot-check of the outcome pipeline. The experimental suite spans 10 models (open- and closed-source) and both text-only and multimodal settings, enabling broad, model-agnostic insights.

498.human_review: Process evaluation with error identification helps people know better about model’s error categories, clearly shown in Figure 4.
498.llm_review: Evaluation depth and informative figures: The study evaluates both final accuracy and error processes, revealing that diagram misinterpretation dominates, and that visual input yields limited gains over text-only. Figures 4–6 distill error distributions and counts across models, making the diagnostic findings easy to interpret and compare.

499.human_review: Comprehensive experiments on the most powerful and popular LMMs demonstrate they need help with MM-Math.
499.llm_review: Thorough experiments: The paper reports results across difficulty tiers, grades, and knowledge categories, plus a text-only vs. multimodal ablation. Practical evaluation details (numeric tolerance, unit handling, symbolic equivalence) make the outcome scoring robust. The breadth of models and consistent prompting ensure the findings are comprehensive and reproducible in spirit.

500.human_review: Great insights with detailed examples of LMMs’ errors on the MM-Math. Example figures are clearly drawn and give reader a better deeper view of model’s behavior on the benchmark
500.llm_review: Benchmark clarity, figures, and model insights: The benchmark is well-scoped (open-ended computational problems with diagrams), clearly illustrated by figures that show the end-to-end evaluation pipeline. Model-level analyses translate into concrete takeaways (e.g., limited visual grounding and theorem-use issues), which should guide both model and training-data design.

501.human_review: The process evaluation still requires GPT4-o in the loop. Considering the size of the benchmark (5929), running GPT4-V on all the examples of the benchmark for process evaluation can be quite expensive.
501.llm_review: Benchmark and evaluation limitations: Process evaluation relies on a single closed-source LMM-as-a-judge (GPT-4V) and a first-error heuristic, which can misattribute root causes and introduces potential bias (the authors note ≈9% misidentification). There is no inter-annotator agreement or multi-judge aggregation, and the human validation for process evaluation appears limited. Statistical significance testing of model differences is not reported, and the use of a proprietary judge challenges strict reproducibility. Calibrations (e.g., numeric tolerance, expression equivalence) are reasonable but could be stress-tested more extensively (e.g., adversarial formats, unit handling edge cases).

502.human_review: The category of the problems in the MM-Math might be homogeneous, though Figure 2 clearly shows the detailed category. About 78% of the problems are shape-related (Properties of Shapes, Shape Transformation), thus making the tested ability in the benchmark easy to be optimize by incorporating more domain-related data.
502.llm_review: Benchmark and data concerns: The dataset is restricted to Chinese middle-school computational problems from a single academic year and excludes proofs/drawing tasks, limiting coverage of multimodal math reasoning. Transforming multiple-choice and composite items into open-ended format via rephrasing may change difficulty and introduce artifacts; translation to English with GPT-4 risks subtle semantic shifts. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement for knowledge-point tagging or grade labels, nor detailed quality-control metrics for the LaTeX/MathML conversion and de-duplication. Potential overlaps with public training corpora are not discussed, which could confound performance interpretation.

503.human_review: The paper analyzes biases in sign language understanding models, covering various demographic and lexical features.
503.llm_review: Comprehensive analysis tied to concrete model behavior: the paper examines biases across participant-, sign-, and video-level factors using two standard ISLR models (I3D and ST-GCN). The use of per-sign normalization (z-scores), mutual information, and rank correlations provides a clear bridge between model outputs and interpretable sources of variance, yielding a nuanced picture of where the models succeed and fail.

504.human_review: It implements and evaluates multiple bias mitigation strategies, such as training on single-gender subsets, label shift approaches, and weighted resampling.
504.llm_review: Careful evaluation and training design: the study reuses released baselines with consistent splits, reports Top-1/5/10 and parity metrics, and implements multiple mitigation strategies with clear procedural details (e.g., label-shift via reduction-to-binary, weighted resampling based on standard deviations from per-sign means, and a female-only resampling variant). Training set-ups (e.g., epoch counts) are specified, making the implementation reproducible and the evaluation fair.

505.human_review: The empirical evaluation utilizes established models (I3D and ST-GCN) and performs detailed statistical analyses to understand the impact of various features on model performance.
505.llm_review: Strong linkage between analysis and performance outcomes across models: the paper quantifies disparities (gender, skin tone, age) and shows, via both I3D and ST-GCN, that video-level features (quality/BRISQUE, length deviation, signing speed deviation, pose dissimilarity) are the most predictive of performance. The evaluation demonstrates that targeted resampling yields small but consistent accuracy gains and improved gender parity, validating the analysis-to-intervention pipeline.

506.human_review: The analysis of how various features (demographic, lexical, video-level) impact model performance enhances the understanding of model interpretability.
506.llm_review: Thoughtful interpretation of results grounded in model behavior: the authors acknowledge confounds (lighting, participant-level idiosyncrasies, small test set) and interpret performance gaps through plausible mechanisms tied to the models (e.g., pose-based sensitivity to right-hand dissimilarity, degradation with lower image quality or atypical speed/length). This careful interpretation avoids over-claiming while offering concrete, model-relevant insights.

507.human_review: The paper does not discuss the potential trade-offs between accuracy and fairness.
507.llm_review: Accuracy remains modest and gaps persist: even after mitigation, overall Top-1 accuracy stays around the mid-50s to low-60s and the female-to-male parity remains low (approximately 0.7). The absolute gains from resampling are small (~1–2 points), and single-gender training yields very low accuracy, limiting the practical impact on end users.

508.human_review: Why is RQ1 (How is the ASL citizen data distributed demographically and linguistically) important? This essentially reflects the data characteristics collected by the Microsoft Research Team and may not be considered a strong contribution to the work. The analysis, however, is important, but I feel it should be in a ‘Data’ section and not individually represented as a research question that the authors investigate.
508.llm_review: Data limitations reduce importance and generalizability: the analysis is confined to a single dataset with 52 participants and only 11 in the test set, with demographic skews and no self-reported race/ethnicity. The use of a skin-tone classifier as a proxy is sensitive to lighting and yields inconsistent readings, weakening conclusions about fairness across racialized groups and reducing broader impact.

509.human_review: The findings related to participant-level differences are interesting; however, the work basically uses existing models and runs them to compare scores between ASL demographics (Similarly, existing bias mitigation strategies have been used and compared) if I frame it in a simplified view, and thus it is unclear to me from the current text how or why this is new or important.
509.llm_review: Findings are largely correlational with small effect sizes and limited modeling breadth: many reported associations are statistically significant but tiny (|rho| < 0.07), some counterintuitive results (e.g., higher sign frequency correlating with lower accuracy) are not fully explained, and the label-shift debiasing underperforms the baseline. With only two baseline models and no multivariate or causal analyses, attribution of bias sources remains uncertain.

510.human_review: A novel method named TWIST is proposed to achieve robust and scalable text style transfer in low-resource scenario.
510.llm_review: Method: TWIST introduces a principled mechanism to reuse LoRA weight increments for new styles via a multi-key memory retriever and SVD-truncated merging. The SVD step directly targets parameter interference during weight interpolation—an issue known to harm generation—and the ablations and q-sensitivity analyses provide empirical support that each component (adaptive retrieval, multi-key design, SVD truncation) contributes to the gains.

511.human_review: A multi-key memory network and an adaptive retrieval mechanism are designed to capture task- and instance-level information in weight increments.
511.llm_review: Task: The paper focuses on low-resource text style transfer, a setting of clear practical importance, and evaluates across diverse style families (sentiment, formality, literary style, and character-specific dialogue). The few-shot regimes (1–10%) and the unseen-style protocol (rotating holdouts) are well aligned with the intended use case, showing robust cross-style generalization under constrained supervision.

512.human_review: A clustering-based weight pool is constructed to identify similarities between source tasks for more effective style knowledge transfer.
512.llm_review: Method: Using LoRA as the transferable unit keeps the backbone depth unchanged while enabling informative initialization for unseen styles, thereby reducing data dependence. The dual-level retrieval (task-level and instance-level) is well motivated for generation tasks where instance nuances matter, and the approach is shown to be model-agnostic by working across encoder–decoder (T5) and decoder-only (LLaMA-2) backbones.

513.human_review: There are some unclear and imprecise parts in the Method section. (1) How should we understand the similarity and its calculation in the Multi-Keys Optimization section? q is a semantic feature, while k is a weight. Why can cosine similarity be used to measure the similarity between them? (2) How is q^{task} obtained? Why is its dimensionality c? (3)  The calculations in equation 5 are imprecise or wrong.
513.llm_review: Method: Important training details are under-specified. It is unclear how the task-level query vector and key embeddings are learned/updated (what objective, where gradients flow), how the retriever is trained jointly with the generator, and how initialization interacts with subsequent fine-tuning. The reliance on a frozen BERT encoder for instance-level queries introduces an extra component whose effect and alternatives are not analyzed.

514.human_review: The related work is not comprehensive. More PEFT algorithms should be discussed because the core of this paper is reusing weight increments.
514.llm_review: Algorithm, Related Work: The algorithmic core—retrieval and merging of PEFT modules/adapters—overlaps with prior work on parameter interpolation/model soups, task arithmetic, and attention-weighted adapter fusion. The paper does not clearly differentiate its contributions from these lines or benchmark against the most closely related merging methods for generation, and the related work omits several recent weight-merging techniques.

515.human_review: The comparison algorithms are insufficient and outdated (considering T5-Large as the backbone network).
515.llm_review: Algorithm, Comparison: Empirical comparisons are not fully compelling. T5-Large is mainly contrasted with older, smaller baselines rather than strong contemporary TST systems (e.g., recent transformer/diffusion-based approaches), and PEFT baselines beyond QLoRA (such as adapters/prompts or other merging/fusion strategies) are missing. Statistical significance, variance across seeds, and explicit main-text quantification of retrieval/merging overhead are limited.

516.human_review: The hyperparameter settings are not described. Moreover, what is the impact of the parameter r in the LoRA model? And what is the impact of different combinations of r and q?
516.llm_review: Model, Parameter: The approach adds nontrivial compute/memory overhead by storing many LoRA increments and keys, running a frozen BERT for queries, and performing per-layer SVD and retrieval. Storage scales with the number of source styles and layers, and performance appears sensitive to rank r and truncation q; yet prescriptive guidance for selecting these hyperparameters across backbones and data regimes is limited.

517.human_review: The presentation needs further improvement. There are many very long sentences that affect readability. What is the 'source key'?
517.llm_review: Clarity, Presentation: The exposition has typos and notation inconsistencies, and some algorithmic details (e.g., the precise training of keys/queries, Algorithm 1) are missing or hard to follow. Figures/equations are occasionally difficult to parse, and essential elements are deferred to appendices, which hinders reproducibility and reader understanding.

518.human_review: The proposal of Incompleteness to KGQA is novel, well motivated and seems very reasonable in real-world tasks. Previous methods thoroughly tested in incompleteness setting, great ablation is performed with varying the degree of incompleteness.
518.llm_review: Ablation analyses directly target the proposed components and support the paper’s novelty claim. In particular, the study varies the number of BM25-selected related triples and shows a clear performance curve (initial gains then noise-induced decline), and it toggles the Generate action to quantify its contribution across completeness levels. These controlled ablations substantiate the central idea of treating the LLM as a triple generator on top of graph exploration, demonstrating that both the generation and subgraph-selection mechanisms materially contribute to the gains.

519.human_review: Despite proposed method being constructed from previously used Ideas, it is indeed novel and effective. The use of Think-Search-Generate, akin to ReACT is a powerful technique to elicit reasoning abilities of LLM, resulting in best performance across multiple settings and datasets.
519.llm_review: The method is a training-free Thinking–Searching–Generating framework that treats the LLM as both an agent and a knowledge source, and it proves effective: across CWQ and WebQSP, it consistently outperforms prompt-based baselines under both complete and incomplete KGs, with notable gains under incompleteness (e.g., around 5 points on CWQ with GPT-3.5 at IKG-40%). The approach scales across different backbones (GPT-3.5/4, Qwen-1.5-72B, Llama-3-70B), and with GPT-4 it reaches or surpasses strong baselines under complete KGs while remaining robust when knowledge is missing, highlighting tangible performance and methodological novelty in integrating internal (LLM) and external (KG) knowledge.

520.human_review: The method and motivation of paper is well described, figures help understand the paper and code is open sourced. The method is also well ablated
520.llm_review: Figures clearly motivate the problem and method: Fig. 1 contrasts standard LLM QA, KGQA, and the proposed incomplete-KG QA setting, making the motivation concrete; Fig. 2 situates the approach within existing paradigms; and Fig. 3 walks through the method’s steps with a running example, clarifying the Thinking–Searching–Generating loop. These visuals effectively anchor the methodological design in the stated motivation and help readers follow how the agent alternates between graph exploration and triple generation.

521.human_review: IKGQA is presented as a novel task with no "datasets readily available". However, there  exist multiple papers solving the IKGQA task (without LLMs), however, they do not formulate the task "officially". Moreover, they also generate datasets based on WebQSP, however, I do not find the citations and comparison of the datasets or dataset creation process
521.llm_review: The IKGQA data is synthetically created by randomly dropping crucial triples along gold paths on only 1,000 samples per dataset, which may not reflect real-world incompleteness patterns (e.g., type-specific sparsity, relation skew, bursty missingness). This limits the novelty and external validity of the benchmark and makes it difficult to assess generalization beyond these controlled dropouts. A larger, more realistic IKG setting or a human/audit study of missingness patterns would strengthen claims.

522.llm_review: The related work discussion underrepresents prior lines on KG completion/augmentation for QA under missing facts (e.g., KGE-augmented QA, rule mining, graph completion before QA) and broader literature on LLM-based fact verification/calibration. A deeper treatment of these areas would better situate the contribution among methods that fill or reason over missing KG edges.

523.llm_review: While GAG-like approaches are mentioned, the paper does not provide an in-depth comparison or empirical evaluation against closely related LLM-as-KG/graph-generation frameworks. Similarly, comparisons to multi-hop agent frameworks and hybrid text+KG retrieval methods are thin. This leaves unclear how much the gains derive from the specific design versus general benefits of agentic LLMs with on-the-fly triple generation.

524.human_review: According to ablation method heavily depends on the LLM.
524.llm_review: Methodological ablations are incomplete: there is no dedicated analysis of the verification module (LLM-only verification vs alternatives), entity-linking accuracy and its impact, the maximum number of Generate iterations, or sensitivity to prompt parameters and temperature. Cost/latency and failure-mode analyses are also missing. These gaps make it harder to assess robustness and practical trade-offs.

525.human_review: Is it not clear whether the fine-tuned approaches for comparison were run by the authors themselves or the numbers were taken from previous papers (for CKG)
525.llm_review: The approach relies on proprietary LLMs for top results and compares against a mix of fine-tuned and prompt-based baselines, but fairness and breadth of comparisons could be improved. For instance, there is no fine-tuned IKG baseline adapted to the incomplete setting, no hybrid pipeline baseline (e.g., SP with an LLM fallback), and the reported deviation from ToG’s evaluation protocol complicates apples-to-apples comparison. A discussion of training-based variants or stronger fine-tuned baselines under IKG would clarify the competitive landscape.

526.key_points: Strength: Baseline, Comparison, Method, Related Work
526.human_review: The paper is well written and clearly explains the methodology used with comparisons to popular baselines such as DPO. It effectively addresses the shortcomings of earlier methods and builds on existing literature to mitigate them.
526.llm_review: Strong baseline coverage and fair comparisons. The method is instantiated on three representative DAP losses (DPO, IPO, SLiC) and compared in both offline and online settings under an equal annotation budget, using multiple seeds and aggregate statistics. The core methodological change (anchoring the trust region to the behavior model) is simple and broadly applicable across losses, and the paper positions the idea in the context of online DAP and trust-region literature, clarifying how it differs from prior static-reference approaches.

527.human_review: The dynamic adjustment of the trust region during training is a significant contribution.
527.llm_review: Clear and focused contribution around training-time trust region design. Framing the KL constraint around the behavior LLM directly addresses the distribution shift inherent in online preference collection, leading to a practical training recipe that integrates seamlessly with existing DAP objectives. The training pipeline is well specified (behavior updates every K steps, fixed beta, LoRA adapters), and the proposed LoRA-ensemble stabilization is pragmatic and incurs no inference overhead.

528.key_points: Strength: Ablation, Analysis, Comparison, Method, Model, Training
528.human_review: The authors conduct a thorough ablation of their proposed method. The analysis with variable time step intervals and comparison with a gold model provide very interesting insights. The use of ensemble LoRA to stabilise training was particularly noteworthy.
528.llm_review: Thorough ablations and analysis tied to method, model, and training choices. The study varies data collection frequency to simulate realistic online regimes, performs head-to-head output comparisons, and uses robust aggregate statistics. The ablation on the reference model (πgold) convincingly shows gains come from proximity to the behavior policy rather than a stronger static reference. Stability analyses (number of LoRA adapters, EMA variants) isolate the cause of instability and justify the chosen fix. Results are consistent across three tasks and three DAP losses on the Gemma-2B base with controlled training hyperparameters.

529.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Method, Novelty, Related Work
529.human_review: Although the paper claims this to be a novel methodology using a dynamic reference policy, there has been some related work [1] that uses DPO iteratively. It would be beneficial to compare their methodology and include a citation for this work.
529.llm_review: Novelty is incremental and some comparisons are missing. While setting the trust region around the behavior policy is intuitive and consistent with behavior-regularized RL, the paper could more directly compare against dynamic-reference DAP variants (e.g., TR-DPO adapted to the online case) and stronger on-policy baselines. The method lacks theoretical justification for why πbeta should dominate over other dynamic references beyond empirical evidence, leaving the contribution primarily methodological and empirical.

530.human_review: There is a missing citation for the use of LoRA ensembling. Additionally, it would be helpful to have a discussion on why the authors chose to use 5 LoRA weights.
530.llm_review: Limited discussion of failure modes and connections to broader literature. The paper does not deeply analyze when a behavior-anchored trust region might be harmful (e.g., if πbeta produces low-quality or biased data) or how to trade off exploration versus conservatism. A richer discussion linking to off-policy correction and behavior-regularized RL (e.g., BRAC/AWAC-style analyses), and acknowledging counter-arguments or negative cases, would strengthen the positioning.

531.human_review: The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion on the computational cost of the proposed BPO method in comparison to existing techniques. This would provide a clearer understanding of its practical applicability.
531.llm_review: External validity and application breadth are limited. All annotation and evaluation rely on a single reward model whose training data overlaps the tasks studied, raising concerns about in-domain bias and generalization. Results are shown only for a 2B-parameter model on three benchmarks, with no human evaluation, multi-turn dialogue, or larger-scale deployments. Practical aspects (compute/training cost, impact of LoRA ensembles on training scalability, real human-in-the-loop workflows) are under-discussed.

532.human_review:
Since this strategy uses on-policy learning, it would be very difficult to incorporate humans in the loop for preference annotation. This could limit the applicability of the method in scenarios where human feedback is essential.

References
[1] Self-Rewarding Language Models. Yuan et al.
532.llm_review: Annotation and evaluation are both driven by the same preference simulator, which risks circularity and reward overfitting. There is no cross-reward or human validation, no analysis of annotator disagreement, and no sanity checks to detect reward hacking. This undermines claims about alignment to human preferences and makes it hard to assess real-world gains.

533.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
533.llm_review: The paper introduces a well-scoped benchmark (AR-Bench) that isolates four retrieval-timing criteria (intent-, knowledge-, time-, and self-awareness) as balanced binary tasks (8k samples each) and reports no overlap with training data. The data pipeline is clearly described: time sensitivity from TAQA, static facts from TriviaQA, non-knowledge tasks from Self-RAG, and synthetic intent signals via Self-Instruct. Methodologically, UAR is cleanly unified: per-criterion plug-and-play MLP heads over frozen LLM last-layer representations plus a deterministic decision policy (UAR-Criteria), yielding a simple, reproducible procedure that avoids full-model finetuning and minimizes inference overhead.

534.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
534.llm_review: The paper motivates multifaceted active retrieval convincingly by showing that single-criterion baselines underperform when the instruction mix spans diverse scenarios. Empirically, UAR substantially outperforms FLARE, SKR, and Self-RAG on AR-Bench overall accuracy (e.g., 86.33 vs. 57–63 on 13B) and yields the best overall downstream score across six datasets and two model sizes. Training is efficient and pragmatic: lightweight heads trained on hidden states, shared tokenization/encoding with generation, and ablations indicating full-model finetuning offers only marginal gains for the self-aware classifier, supporting the choice of value heads.

535.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
535.llm_review: Performance is consistently strong on the diagnostic benchmark and competitive or best overall on downstream tasks: on AR-Bench, UAR leads across all criteria and both model sizes; on downstream evaluations, UAR achieves the highest overall scores while using fewer retrieval calls than always-retrieve and avoiding degradation on non-knowledge tasks, and it nearly perfectly triggers retrieval on time-sensitive datasets.

536.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
536.llm_review: Despite covering four scenarios, AR-Bench’s construction may not fully reflect real-world distributions: it is balanced 50/50 per class, uses synthetic intent signals (via Self-Instruct) that may introduce stylistic artifacts, and defines time sensitivity and static knowledge using specific datasets (TAQA, TriviaQA), potentially narrowing domain coverage. Methodologically, the decision policy imposes a fixed priority order whose rationale is not empirically validated, and the single-layer MLP over last-token hidden states may be underpowered for self-awareness, which the paper itself identifies as a bottleneck.

537.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
537.llm_review: The claim of negligible overhead is plausible but not quantified end-to-end, and no latency/throughput measurements are reported with all four classifiers enabled. Performance justifications sometimes rely on re-implemented baselines with different architectures (e.g., SKR’s BERT classifier versus Llama-based heads) and ChatGPT-based grading for long answers, without significance testing, leaving uncertainty about robustness of the improvements. Training labels for self-awareness are derived from sampling multiple generations and marking an item as known if all are correct, which risks label noise and calibration bias; generalization to other base models requires retraining per-model heads but training cost and data needs are not analyzed.

538.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
538.llm_review: Gains are not uniform across tasks: UAR underperforms never-retrieval on DROP with 7B (52.55 vs. 57.67) and underperforms always-retrieval on FreshQA with 13B (55.45 vs. 62.05). The integrated UAR accuracy can lag single-criterion classifiers on their own scenarios, reflecting a self-aware bottleneck that can propagate through the decision policy. These inconsistencies suggest headroom in reliability across diverse workloads.

539.human_review: The experiments are well-organized and reasonably comprehensive, effectively supporting the insights and conclusions drawn in the paper. It is particularly intriguing for this reviewer to observe the efficacy of granularity expansion in achieving these positive results.
539.llm_review: The experimental study is broad and careful. The paper evaluates on the AGGRE FACT benchmark with diverse baselines spanning QA-based, NLI-based, parsing-based, and LLM-based methods, and reports balanced accuracy with validation-set thresholding consistent with prior work. It includes per-split and single-threshold evaluations with confidence intervals, and demonstrates average state-of-the-art performance. The ablations are informative: removing granularity expansion or atomic facts, varying document granularity, and quantifying the effect of coreference resolution all illuminate where gains come from. The analysis of which LLMs work best for atomic fact generation and a concrete failure-case study further strengthen the experimental narrative and interpretability claims.

540.human_review: Although the task performance results would depend on the quality of the generated atomic facts, its impact on the task performance is not discussed.
540.llm_review: Performance and Task: The headline gains over strong NLI-based baselines are modest on average and not uniform across splits; in some cases, the variant without atomic facts outperforms the full system, which weakens the performance claim for the proposed decomposition. The method is only validated on news-style summarization within AGGRE FACT, leaving its effectiveness on other summarization tasks (e.g., dialogue, biomedical) untested. The computational overhead also raises concerns about practical performance for real-time or large-scale task settings.

541.human_review: Similarly, the performance outcomes could also vary with an NLI model utilized. Nevertheless, almost no discussions are presented that makes comparisons with models other than SUMMAC and/or substantiate the adoption of SUMMAC.
541.llm_review: Comparison, Discussion, Model, Performance: While the comparisons are extensive, fairness is partly confounded by threshold tuning that benefits some baselines but not others (e.g., ChatGPT-based metrics), and statistical significance against the strongest competitors is not established across the full benchmark. The discussion articulates a failure case but does not provide a deeper error taxonomy or human assessment of interpretability. At the model level, the pipeline relies on a large coreference model and an NLI classifier; the contribution of each module is not fully disentangled, especially given instances where removing atomic facts helps. The choice of a minimum-over-atomic-facts aggregator is brittle and likely to depress performance due to single-fact errors; alternative aggregation or calibration strategies are not explored.

542.human_review: The criterion for expanding the context, namely that max(e_k, c_k, n_k) ≠ e_k, may seem intuitive, but it might be overly simplistic. This hypothesis should be experimentally validated.
542.llm_review: Experiment, Hypothesis, Validation: The central hypotheses are that atomic fact decomposition and adaptive context expansion improve factual inconsistency detection and interpretability. The ablations partially support these claims, especially for granularity expansion and coreference resolution, but key validations are missing: there is no human study to verify interpretability benefits, no measurement of the correctness of generated atomic facts or of the filtering step, and no robustness analysis to different prompts, seeds, or LLMs beyond token-length correlations. The experiments are confined to one domain and language, and rely on tuned thresholds; additional validation via threshold-free metrics (e.g., AUROC), cross-domain tests, and controlled studies isolating each component would better substantiate the hypotheses.

543.human_review: While query expansion and entity retrieval are standard techniques to enhance RAG system ability, combining these is non-trivial. MiRAG uses the K*M combinations of retrieved passages to jointly train the answer generator, passage retrieval and entity retriever.
543.llm_review: Method/Technique: The paper introduces a clear and effective multi-level RAG pipeline that first performs cross-modal entity retrieval and then uses query entity expansion to guide fine-grained passage retrieval, with answer generation conditioned on both levels. The joint training objective explicitly couples entity and passage retrievers with the generator, enabling gradients to flow end-to-end and mitigating the usual retriever–reader mismatch. The design is pragmatic—CLIP for entity retrieval, DPR-style encoders for passages, and a standard encoder–decoder generator—yet the integration via a unified RAG loss is novel for KB-VQA and technically sound.

544.human_review: Comparisons w/ existing VQA RAG baselines are fair and complete, and MiRAG achieves consistent and obvious performance improvements on ViQuAE KVQAE benchmarks. Qualitative examples in the appendix show that MiRAG is able to refer to relevant entities and generate correct answers conditioned on the augmented passage.
544.llm_review: Baseline/Benchmark/Comparison/Performance: The comparisons are thorough and fair, covering strong literature baselines (ECA, ILF, DPR v+t, PaLM) and well-constructed internal baselines (standard RAG and a multimodal score-fusion RAG). Retrieval budgets are kept comparable, and both T5-large and BLIP-2 generators are evaluated. The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on ViQuAE (e.g., EM 36.6 / F1 41.2 with BLIP-2), with consistent gains over fusion-based multimodal RAG and text-only RAG, demonstrating that entity-level signals materially improve final answer quality.

545.human_review: Ablation studies in Tables 1, 4, and Section 5.5 validate the effectiveness of enabling gradient flow (a.k.a end-to-end training) in RAG joint training, bringing significant performance gain. Multi-modal retrieval proves to be better than using the uni-modal retrieval method.
545.llm_review: Ablation/Performance/Training/Validation: The paper provides informative ablations and validations: (i) analysis of K_train and M_train showing the computation–performance trade-off and identifying K×M≈15 as a good operating point; (ii) freezing vs training the entity encoder, demonstrating that end-to-end gradients improve answer EM even if pseudo-retrieval metrics fluctuate; (iii) retrieval metrics (MRR@100, P@1/P@20) across DPR/CLIP/fusion and with entity expansion (EExp-DPR), clarifying why pseudo-relevance does not fully predict answer quality. These studies substantiate the training choices and validate the contribution of entity-driven query expansion.

546.human_review: Training Efficiency: in Section 3.5, the authors mentioned that answer generation loss has to be backward for all K$\times$M combinations, leading to the concern of training efficacy. In Appendix A, the authors do not report training GPU hours.
546.llm_review: Efficiency/Training: The multi-level retrieval and joint training introduce notable computational and memory overhead. Retrieving K entities and M passages per entity multiplies indexing and scoring costs, and the generator consumes concatenated top-N passages (M_test restricted by GPU memory), which can inflate training/inference latency. The approach also requires pretraining and maintaining a large FAISS index for millions of entities plus DPR passage indexing. While the paper discusses a K×M trade-off, it does not quantify wall-clock time, memory usage, or scalability to larger KBs, nor does it explore efficiency optimizations (e.g., dynamic K/M selection, lightweight reranking, or distillation).

547.human_review: Focuses on highly understudied topic in RAG research i.e. the importance how information is structured is also critical
547.llm_review: Importance: The paper tackles a well-motivated and timely problem in RAG—the lost-in-the-middle effect and difficulty of synthesizing scattered evidence across retrieved chunks—by restructuring content post-retrieval. Focusing on the post-retrieval stage is impactful for multi-hop QA and complements extensive pre-/in-retrieval work, making the contribution relevant to both research and practical deployments of RAG systems.

548.human_review: Introduces a training dataset which will be released for future research to enhance RAG models
548.llm_review: Data, Model, Training: The multi-teacher knowledge distillation pipeline is thoughtfully designed: teacher outputs are parsed, filtered for verbatimness against source chunks, and majority-voted to curate high-quality supervision for a student 7B decoder-only model. Training details (LoRA, SFT, progressive curriculum) are reported, and the model learns to adaptively keep necessary local context while enforcing a structured, sectioned output. This end-to-end setup is sensible, compute-aware, and aligns training signals with the desired behavior in deployment.

549.human_review: Token reduction / compression rates of Refiner upto 89% which is beneficial for reducing real-world costs
549.llm_review: The method is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, making it easy to integrate into diverse RAG stacks and to pair with various downstream LLMs. It achieves substantial token reduction while preserving or improving answer quality, which is attractive for production settings with cost and latency constraints.

550.human_review: The reduction and refinement into structured content also adds a notion of explainability
550.llm_review: Explanation: The explicit, hierarchical sections with document titles make the support structure more transparent and easier to audit, aiding interpretability and facilitating citation or retrospection. The analysis of verbatimness (87–97%) and qualitative case studies further help readers understand how the structured outputs guide downstream models.

551.human_review: Ablation showing resilience to adding extra content, where Refiner is still able to maintain performance partly mitigating "lost-in-the-middle" problem
551.llm_review: Ablation, Performance, Robustness: Strong empirical evidence supports the design choices. Removing the structural sections degrades performance, especially under longer contexts (top-10 retriever setting), indicating that sectioning improves information disentanglement. Refiner consistently boosts multi-hop accuracy over strong baselines while achieving high compression (~89%), and shows robustness to added noisy/irrelevant chunks and across multiple downstream LLMs, with low in-task variance.

552.human_review: New STOA results for multi-hop QA datasets including: HotpotQA and 2Wiki with comparable results on single-hop datasets; its worth highlighting that the gains are significantly pronounced when compared to baseline ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo for multi-hop datasets
552.llm_review: Comparison, Data, Result: The evaluation spans five public QA datasets (PopQA, TriviaQA, ARC-Challenge, HotpotQA, 2Wiki) and compares against advanced RAG methods (Self-RAG, RQ-RAG) and strong compressors (RECOMP, LongLLMLingua). The experiments control for retriever and downstream LMs for fair comparisons. Results show notable gains on multi-hop tasks (e.g., +6–7% over the next best) and competitive single-hop performance with far fewer tokens, substantiating the claimed benefits.

553.human_review: The organization of paper is such that it becomes difficult to understand the methodology that is introduced by the work, e.g. sections 4.1 and 4.2 in less than a page mentions the main contribution of the paper i.e. multiple teacher KD-based dataset curations
553.llm_review: Contribution, Data, Method: While useful, the methodological novelty is incremental: the core is extraction plus grouping into sections, learned via instruction-like prompts and distillation. The grouping criterion (semantic relatedness) is largely delegated to teacher LMs without a clear algorithmic formulation or guarantees. The reliance on teacher-generated supervision risks propagating their biases and may entangle the contribution with prompt engineering rather than a principled new method.

554.human_review: Pertaining to above, plenty of effort went into analysis where Table 3 and 4 are too redundant in terms of reporting all numbers for +5 and +10 documents across all datasets to derive a conclusion for a given ablation study
554.llm_review: Ablation, Analysis, Data: The ablations stop short of fully isolating design choices. For example, there is no systematic study of section granularity, ordering strategies, or the adaptive context window size; no comparison of different voting thresholds or teacher sets; limited sensitivity to retriever choices beyond top-k; and no statistical significance testing. The main metric is exact-match/regex accuracy, which may not reflect semantic answer quality; complementary metrics or human evaluation would strengthen claims.

555.human_review: Figure 4 in appendix gives detail about the training dataset construction and even it lacks several details like what is "ParseGeneratedContent" and what is "V"? similary there is a "Counter" and an "assignSection" not very clear
555.llm_review: Clarity, Data, Figure, Training: The paper has noticeable formatting/typo issues (e.g., broken numbers/spacing), and some tables/figures are hard to parse. Training data statistics (Table 7) appear inconsistent/unclear after cleaning, making dataset scale ambiguous. Important implementation details (regex matching rules, section restoration, edge-case handling when teachers disagree) could be elaborated. These clarity gaps hinder reproducibility despite the provided prompts and high-level pipeline.

556.human_review: Based on these, it is difficult to assess the contribution of this work as the core contribution seems to be introducing this additional training data which is thin for a full paper
556.llm_review: Contribution, Data, Training: Generalization is not demonstrated beyond open-domain text passages; the method may not directly extend to tables, code, or domain-specific corpora, which the authors also acknowledge. The model’s temptation to answer or extract from the query and the non-negligible non-verbatim rate raise fidelity concerns for high-stakes settings. The training relies on curated teacher outputs for a limited set of datasets; broader or domain-specific training/evaluation and human verification of structured output faithfulness would strengthen the contribution.

557.human_review: The proposed method is effective on in- and out-of-domain unanswerable questions when training sets include unanswerable questions while degrading scores for answerable questions. The improvement in out-of-domain unanswerable questions is significant.
557.llm_review: Method and improvement: The paper introduces a simple, model-agnostic training modification that jointly (i) replaces the [CLS]-span convention with a loss that treats unanswerable cases as having no span and (ii) breaks the single-answer shortcut by adding a second synthetic span to a subset of answerable questions. This yields substantial robustness gains without sacrificing in-domain SQuAD 2.0 performance, with consistent improvements across BERT, RoBERTa, and SpanBERT and averaging over five seeds. The overall F1 lift (~5.7 across all test sets) and large OOD gains on information-seeking unanswerables (e.g., +18.4 F1 on SQuAD AGent) demonstrate clear methodological impact.

558.human_review: The authors show that the proposed method improves the robustness to two types of adversarial attacks.
558.llm_review: Adversarial, method, and robustness: The study evaluates robustness under two adversarial attacks (AddOneSent and Negation) and shows the proposed training reduces average performance drop by about two-thirds (from 40.7 to 13.2 F1 when trained on SQuAD 2.0). The analysis further disentangles components, showing synthetic multi-span augmentation is critical to adversarial robustness, and the effect persists when training on both adversarial (SQuAD 2.0) and information-seeking (SQuAD AGent) settings. This links the method design directly to improved adversarial robustness.

559.human_review: It is simple yet reasonable to use 1/n as labels for unanswerable questions, and synthetic answers to avoid overfitting to one answer.
559.llm_review: The experimental setup is careful and transparent: results are averaged over five random initializations, multiple encoder backbones are tested, both distribution shift and adversarial robustness are measured, and training dynamics are analyzed to contextualize robustness trends. The approach is easy to implement in existing EQA systems and has practical implications for dataset design (multi-span answers).

560.human_review: No ablation study is conducted, so it is unclear from the experiments which component of the proposed method (QA loss, sequence tagging loss, synthetic answers, and inference pipeline) has an effect on the improved robustness.
560.llm_review: Ablation, experiment, method, and robustness: While there is a helpful “no synthetic” ablation, the ablation suite is limited. Missing are sensitivity analyses over the proportion and construction of synthetic spans, weight selection for the two loss terms (lambda values), comparisons to standard label smoothing or alternative no-answer formulations, and calibration/threshold studies. Since adversarial robustness largely disappears without synthetic spans, the method’s robustness story would be stronger with broader ablations isolating the loss vs. augmentation contributions and testing on multi-span evaluation benchmarks.

561.human_review: The motivation to use sequence tagging loss instead of the cross entropy loss is unclear to me.
561.llm_review: Motivation: The paper posits two key causes of brittleness (the [CLS]-span convention and the single-answer assumption). Although plausible, the causal link to robustness is only partially substantiated. In particular, the claim that the single-answer assumption drives adversarial failures could be bolstered by targeted diagnostics (e.g., stress tests varying answer multiplicity, counterfactual training without multi-span but with other regularizers, or controlled calibration experiments) to rule out alternative explanations such as confidence miscalibration or lexical overlap heuristics.

562.human_review: The details about synthetic answers are omitted from the main part. I think it should be described in the main part if it is a part of the proposed method.
562.llm_review: Detail and method: Important implementation details are underspecified. The QA loss assigns uniform labels (1/n) for unanswerables within a softmax—this is effectively soft-labeling; more clarity is needed on stability, rationale versus standard label smoothing, and how this interacts with the token-level BCE loss. The inference rule that predicts "empty" when max span score is negative requires justification and discussion of calibration. The synthetic span generation procedure needs clearer criteria (selection, non-overlap, semantic validity, quality control), along with reproducibility details and error analyses.

563.human_review: This paper may need justification for using only BERT families in the era of decoder-only large language models such as llama.
563.llm_review: Justification and model: The empirical scope is confined to base encoder models (BERT, RoBERTa, SpanBERT). There is limited justification for omitting larger or more recent architectures (e.g., DeBERTa, Longformer for long contexts) or retrieval-augmented QA settings where unanswerability is common. This raises questions about generality, and whether the gains persist at larger scales or in more realistic open-domain scenarios.

564.human_review: The experiments seem to lack baseline methods. The proposed method is compared against only a default method.
564.llm_review: Comparison, experiment, and method: The paper does not compare against several strong and relevant baselines: (i) alternative no-answer handling (separate null logits, threshold tuning, confidence-based abstention), (ii) adversarial training/data augmentation (e.g., AddSent/AdversarialQA), (iii) broader OOD MRQA-style benchmarks. Without these comparisons, it is difficult to attribute gains uniquely to the proposed loss/augmentation rather than known techniques. Statistical significance reporting for key improvements is also missing.

565.human_review: Improving efficiency in long document tasks is an important research problem.
565.llm_review: The paper foregrounds efficiency trade-offs by benchmarking KV cache quantization, token dropping, prompt compression, and linear-time/hybrid architectures under aligned compression ratios. It explicitly analyzes constant versus linear memory regimes, prefill versus decoding compression, and system-level support, giving practitioners actionable guidance. The observations about keeping prefill uncompressed and FlashAttention compatibility provide concrete, efficiency-relevant insights for real deployments.

566.human_review: While I am not an expert in this field, it seems that the authors have surveyed, organized and implemented a comprehensive set of methods to reduce memory usage in long sequence modeling. These were applied to several LLMs (where possible) and the results seem to agree.
566.llm_review: The authors provide a minimalistic, open-source workbench and adhere to official or endorsed implementations, improving reproducibility and comparability. The method taxonomy is clear and spans major families (quantization, token dropping, prompt compression, linear-time and hybrids), with practical implementation details such as dynamic kept-token settings and system support annotations. Coverage across representative backbones (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, LongChat-7B, Mamba, RWKV, RecurrentGemma) enables method-model interaction analyses.

567.human_review: The methods were evaluated on a large set of 16 long document tasks. As the compression ratios are given, the trade off between compression and performance becomes visible.
567.llm_review: Evaluation is broad and method-aware: 10+ approaches are tested across seven long-context task categories (LongBench) plus a needle-in-a-haystack suite, yielding 65 settings. The study isolates method-level behaviors, showing quantization’s robust cross-task retention, token dropping’s strength on code, hybrids’ benefits over pure linear models, and the degradation from prefill-time compression in long-input short-output scenarios. Performance is reported by task category with clear observations that are consistent with the methods’ design premises.

568.human_review: The experimental results can be useful to researchers and practitioners working with these and related methods.
568.llm_review: Experiments span multiple compression ratios per approach and replicate trends across different backbones, strengthening the credibility of the results. The inclusion of ablations across ratios, category-level summaries, and targeted visualizations (radar plots, needle depth curves, per-model H2O comparisons) makes the empirical story coherent. The results surface non-obvious phenomena and provide concrete recommendations for future method design.

569.human_review: The analysis mostly remains on the surface.
569.llm_review: The analysis stops at high-level observations without deeper causal investigation or statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, significance testing, or sensitivity analyses, and limited error analysis at the dataset/subtask level. Important design factors (e.g., effect of sliding windows in quantization or token-selection heuristics) are not ablated, making it hard to attribute performance differences to specific mechanisms.

570.human_review: For example, an interesting result from Figure 2 is that coding tasks seems to suffer less from compression methods than other tasks (noted in L456ff), but there is no attempt to explain this. Figure 2 itself is mentioned only once in the main text.
570.llm_review: Some figures are hard to parse: radar plots compress many dimensions without uncertainty cues, axis ranges and legends are not always self-explanatory, and the needle depth plots need clearer narration of how depth is computed and interpreted. Dense tables mix models and methods with minimal visual guidance, and a few typographical issues reduce readability. More descriptive captions, consistent units, and per-figure takeaways would improve explanation.

571.human_review: While Table 2 shows results split into 7 task types, only two of them (Code and Needle) are mentioned in the main text. It would be interesting if there are other task- or instance specific phenomena that can be observed.
571.llm_review: Results are confined largely to long-input short-output tasks, limiting conclusions for long-generation scenarios such as multi-turn dialogue, long code synthesis, or creative writing. The task suite is predominantly English and does not explore multilingual or domain-shifted settings, reducing generalizability. As a result, the claims about method performance may not transfer to broader long-context tasks and usage patterns.

572.human_review:
Do the results agree between the different LLMs tested?

(The authors have added analyses to their author response)
572.llm_review: Cross-model comparisons are confounded by heterogeneous pretraining corpora, scales, and recipes, particularly when contrasting linear-time models with transformer baselines. Without aligned training (e.g., same data and size) or controlled fine-tuning, conclusions about architectural advantages can be overstated. Reporting normalized results or adding experiments on fully aligned open families (e.g., Pythia-style) would strengthen model-level analysis and causal interpretation.
