573.human_review: PER-PCS significantly reduces computational and storage requirements, achieving 7x faster computation and 38x less storage compared to training individual PEFTs.
573.llm_review: Efficiency and Training: The framework is notably efficient in both compute and storage. The assembly stage for target users is training-free and only stores per-layer indices and composition weights, while sharer-side gate training is light (tens of steps) and keeps all other parameters frozen. Empirically, the method reports about 7x lower computation and 38x lower storage than training per-user PEFT (e.g., OPPU), making it practical for large user populations. The one-time task adaptation of the base model and the minimal post-hoc gate updates further reduce training overhead.

574.human_review: PER-PCS maintains model ownership and fine-grained personalization for target users. It also shows robustness in terms of the number of sharers, sharer selection strategy, and the number of PEFT parameters shared.
574.llm_review: Model, Parameter, Robustness: The piece-wise parameterization (per-layer LoRA pieces with trainable gates) is a clean, modular design that enables fine-grained reuse and composition across users. The auto-regressive layer-by-layer selection with normalized weights provides a principled aggregation of parameters. The approach is compatible with multiple PEFT families (LoRA, Adapters, IA3, prefix), and experiments indicate robustness to the number of sharers, sharer selection strategies, and partial sharing ratios (down to 20%) without large performance drops, demonstrating model and parameter-level resilience to real-world variability.

575.human_review: Extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency. The experiments demonstrate that PER-PCS outperforms non-personalized baselines and PEFT retrieval methods across 6 personalization tasks, with performance comparable to training individual PEFTs (OPPU) but much lower computational and storage costs.
575.llm_review: Effectiveness, Efficiency, Experiment, Performance: Across six LaMP tasks, the method consistently improves over non-personalized and PEFT retrieval baselines, while matching or very nearly matching OPPU performance with substantially less compute and storage. The experimental suite includes ablations on sharer count, selection strategy, and sharing ratio, plus time/space complexity analyses, supporting both effectiveness and efficiency claims. The method achieves roughly 99% of OPPU’s accuracy on average despite the resource savings and shows clear gains in classification and generation metrics over alternative compositions.

576.human_review: Overall, the manuscript is well-organized and well-written.
576.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is generally well-structured with a clear problem setup, a concise description of the pipeline (selection, gating, assembly), and helpful figures illustrating the workflow and complexity advantages. The related work is well-organized, positioning the contribution within model/PEFT/piece-level composition and personalization. The experimental section offers a readable set of tables and plots with sensible baselines and metrics, aiding comprehension.

577.human_review: From Figure 3, it seems that increasing the number of users who consent to share their personal PEFT will not help improve performance. I would like to see a more detailed explanation of why.
577.llm_review: Explanation, Figure, Performance: Some methodological details need clearer exposition. The objective for gate training is only briefly described, and the rationale for the cosine-scoring/top-k selection and the softmax scaling by 1/sqrt(n) is not theoretically motivated. Notation around the piece-level scoring (e.g., token range aggregation) can be hard to follow. Figures would benefit from more precise axis labels and clearer captions (e.g., better readability of weight heatmaps and explicit units), and performance tables lack confidence intervals/significance tests. On a few tasks, gains over strong baselines are small, so statistical backing would help substantiate performance claims.

578.human_review: In several tasks like LaMP-1, PER-PCS+RAG seems not to contribute and even causes a performance drop (compared with PER-PCS Base). I am curious about the potential reasons behind this.
578.llm_review: Performance: The evaluation is limited to the LaMP benchmark with Llama-2-7B and a relatively small test cohort per task, leaving questions about scalability to larger user bases, different foundation models, and real-world heterogeneity. Performance under cold-start or sparse-history conditions is not reported, and some improvements on generation tasks are modest. The absence of stronger personalization baselines (e.g., mixture-of-experts personalization or multi-PEFT fusion with stronger retrieval) makes it harder to fully contextualize performance at the high end.

579.human_review: In the method section, why are the PEFT pieces selected in an autoregressive way? Can we directly weigh the average/merge all the left parameters with the gating score you have learned?
579.llm_review: Method, Parameter: The method’s privacy claim rests on partial parameter sharing but lacks a formal privacy analysis; even small fractions of PEFT or gate vectors might leak user information. The linear combination of multiple PEFT pieces per layer may introduce interference, and there is limited discussion of stability when piece ranks or magnitudes differ. Key parameterization choices (e.g., LoRA ranks, per-layer k, pool size scaling) are not systematically tied to resource budgets, and the impact of these hyperparameters on accuracy–efficiency trade-offs is underexplored.

580.human_review: MINT offers a diverse set of IR tasks, covering a wide range of domains and document types. This ensures a representative and challenging evaluation of instruction-following abilities across various scenarios.
580.llm_review: Evaluation and Task: The benchmark targets instructed retrieval directly, spanning 100 heterogeneous IR tasks across six domains with diverse query/document types and relevance criteria. The evaluation is carefully designed to probe instruction-following via two settings (no instruction vs. +instruction), reports both overall and per-domain nDCG@10, and includes diagnostic analyses: (a) task correlation based on model performance to evidence heterogeneity; (b) a sampling effectiveness study showing >0.95 Pearson correlation at 100 queries/task with the full test, supporting efficiency without sacrificing fidelity. This breadth and rigor make the tasks and their evaluation well-suited to stress generalization and alignment to instructions.

581.human_review: The manual annotation of 776 detailed instructions provides a clear and specific guidance for each task. This allows for a more nuanced assessment of models’ ability to understand and execute complex retrieval instructions.
581.llm_review: Annotation and Task: The paper contributes 776 expert-authored instructions that specify query types, document types, and relevance criteria, with query-level instructions for tasks that require them. Instructions are reviewed and include domain-specific nuances (e.g., entity types in biomedical tasks), yielding realistic, fine-grained guidance that mirrors real user intents. This annotation quality, coupled with the wide task coverage, enables a faithful assessment of whether retrieval models can accurately interpret and follow varied instructions.

582.human_review: The paper benchmarks a variety of retrieval models, including both traditional and state-of-the-art LLM-based approaches. This allows for a comprehensive comparison of different methods and highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each.
582.llm_review: Benchmark, Comparison, Method, Model: The study benchmarks a diverse suite of methods—sparse (BM25), single-task dense, multi-task dense, instruction-tuned embedders, cross-encoder re-rankers, and LLM-based re-rankers—under consistent protocols, with and without instructions. Comparative results are substantive and actionable: instruction-tuned models benefit most from instructions (e.g., e5-mistral-7b-instruct, NV-Embed-v1), while non-instruction-tuned models often regress when instructions are added. Cross-benchmark comparison with MTEB highlights differences in generalization, offering insight into model robustness on long-tail, unseen tasks. The methodology provides a clear, reproducible yardstick for future models.

583.human_review: The paper acknowledges the importance of prompt sensitivity in LLMs but does not extensively explore this aspect. Investigating the impact of different prompts on model performance would provide valuable insights for improving instruction understanding.
583.llm_review: Model and Prompt: Prompting and instruction design are under-explored experimentally. LLM-based re-ranking is evaluated only with GPT-3.5 and a single zero-shot prompting approach, without prompt template ablations (instruction phrasing, structure, length), few-shot exemplars, or formatting studies. Likewise, the degradation observed in non-instruction-tuned embedders when instructions are added is not probed with prompt variants tailored to those models. A systematic prompt-sensitivity analysis would clarify whether performance gaps are due to model limitations or prompt design.

584.human_review: MINT primarily focuses on text retrieval tasks. Expanding the benchmark to include other retrieval types, such as image or code retrieval, would provide a more holistic evaluation of LLM capabilities.
584.llm_review: Benchmark, Evaluation, Model: While the sampling study supports reliability, the pipeline introduces potential confounds: (a) merging corpora for small tasks and random negative sampling may alter original distributions and difficulty; (b) all re-rankers depend on a single first-stage retriever, conflating re-ranker quality with upstream recall; (c) only nDCG@10 is reported, with no significance testing or robustness intervals; and (d) English-only, text-only scope limits broader applicability. Adding multiple first-stage retrievers, additional metrics (e.g., Recall@k, MAP), statistical tests, and multilingual/structured modalities would strengthen claims about generality and model comparisons.

585.human_review: TGB significantly improves the temporal grounding capabilities of MLLMs, allowing for more accurate interpretation of long-form videos by efficiently extracting and preserving relevant temporal features.
585.llm_review: Accuracy, Improvement, Interpretation: The method yields clear accuracy gains across diverse video-language tasks while making the temporal reasoning process more interpretable via multi-span grounding. On AGQA 2.0, TGB-BLIP2 improves overall accuracy from 54.00 to 61.45 (+7.45). On NExT-QA, it raises accuracy from 69.6 (BLIP2) to 72.1, and on EgoSchema (zero-shot) it achieves 41.2 vs. 40.2 (Video-LLaVA) and 25.7 (SeViLA) using far fewer training frames. For temporal question grounding (NExT-GQA), TGB reaches mIoU 19.9, outperforming prior methods (e.g., IGV mIoU 14.0). The multi-span selection explicitly surfaces the key temporal segments tied to a query, improving interpretability of which moments drive the model’s answer, and the preservation of low-dim motion features helps explain improvements on relation/action and sequencing categories.

586.human_review: The framework’s ability to handle sequences up to 16 times longer than initially trained without sacrificing performance highlights its scalability and effectiveness in real-world applications.
586.llm_review: Framework, Performance: The Temporal Grounding Bridge is a practical, pluggable module that pairs low-dimensional motion features with language-guided multi-span selection and extrapolative positional encoding, enabling temporal length extrapolation and efficient integration with existing MLLMs. The framework consistently boosts performance across encoder, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only stacks, showing favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs (e.g., near-BLIP2 compute with higher accuracy on NExT-QA, and strong results on long-form EgoSchema with only 4 training frames). The bootstrapped training pipeline avoids costly manual temporal annotations yet delivers strong gains, demonstrating a compelling blend of performance and deployability.

587.human_review: TGB’s bootstrapping framework eliminates the need for explicit temporal grounding annotations, reducing the reliance on costly manual annotations and leveraging existing MLLMs for improved performance.
587.llm_review: Framework: The design is modular and general: (i) the bridge is lightweight and MLLM-agnostic, (ii) the flow-based temporal feature is swappable for other low-dim motion features, (iii) joint optimization via Gumbel-Softmax aligns the bridge with any pluggable MLLM, and (iv) the bootstrapping scheme provides pseudo temporal labels for both close- and open-ended tasks without human annotation. The authors validate generality across five MLLMs and two LLMs, and show that TGB-grounded frames alone can enhance multiple base models, supporting the claim that the framework is broadly applicable.

588.human_review: Could the authors provide ablation studies on the different strategies of multi-span selection that are discussed in Section D of the Appendix?
588.llm_review: Ablation: While Table 6 ablates several key components (optical flow, fixed bridge, uniform sampling, zero-shot), important sensitivities remain underexplored: (1) the impact of the number of predicted spans k and span-union strategy on accuracy and grounding quality; (2) the contribution of extrapolative positional encoding versus standard positional schemes; (3) robustness to motion feature quality (e.g., different flow estimators, noisy flow, or learned motion tokens) and to the number/quality of keyframes; (4) the effect of the Gumbel-Softmax temperature and sampling count on stability and gradients; (5) training context length sensitivity (e.g., 4 vs. 8 frames) and how it interacts with extrapolation; (6) detailed error analyses per question type when adding/removing motion features. These ablations would clarify which design choices are most critical and how reliable the gains are across settings.

589.human_review: It is interesting to see how the number of layers of Transformer in TGB influences the tradeoff between the efficiency and performance on downstream tasks.
589.llm_review: Efficiency, Performance, Task, Transformer: (1) Efficiency: The method relies on optical flow (RAFT) precomputation and an extra bridge, which may add nontrivial runtime/memory overhead on very long videos; when swapping in heavy offline vision features, FLOPs increase substantially (Table 7), tempering the efficiency narrative. A full end-to-end wall-clock analysis (with flow) on long videos would strengthen claims. (2) Performance: Despite gains, temporal grounding remains low in absolute terms (mIoU < 0.20 on NExT-GQA), and some temporal categories such as duration comparison remain challenging. (3) Task coverage: Evidence is strongest for long-form QA and temporal grounding; it is unclear how well the approach transfers to other long-video tasks (dense captioning, event detection, moment retrieval at scale) where fine-grained localization and recall may be stricter. (4) Transformer module: The 6-layer bridge may be underpowered for fine-grained or multiple overlapping events, and cross-attention still scales with input length; the demonstrated length extrapolation is promising but validated up to 16×—robustness beyond that is unknown.

590.human_review: Could the performance be further improved when the size of the backbone LLMs grows larger than 7B?
590.llm_review: Improvement, Model: (1) Some gains are modest on certain benchmarks (e.g., +0.6 on NExT-QA over SeViLA) and vary by base MLLM, suggesting the improvement magnitude depends on the underlying model and task. (2) The method underperforms specialized retrieval models on specific AGQA categories (e.g., duration-related queries), indicating that model design and output format (generative vs. discriminative) still limit improvements. (3) Bootstrapped pseudo labels inherit biases/errors of the teacher MLLM, risking confirmation bias; more diagnostics or teacher-agnostic signals would help. (4) Comparisons to recent token-compression/retrieval memory approaches are limited, making it hard to isolate the incremental benefit of the proposed bridge versus alternative long-context strategies.

591.human_review: The article introduces a new self-evaluation method that leverages the model's own features, avoiding dependence on external APIs and concerns about privacy leakage.
591.llm_review: Clear, model-aware methodology: the paper systematically explores glass-box features available from the evaluated model itself (softmax entropy/variance, ensemble-based uncertainty, attention-entropy) and frames them as an evaluation signal. The method is lightweight, requires only logits/attention from the same Transformer model being judged, and avoids external evaluators. Demonstrations on two popular 7B chat models (LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B) show that the approach is broadly model-compatible without additional training.

592.key_points: Strength: Accuracy, Evaluation, Experiment, Result, Validation
592.human_review: The experimental results show that the self-evaluation method based on softmax distribution achieves higher accuracy than some existing evaluation methods, validating the feasibility of this approach.
592.llm_review: Empirical validation shows that softmax-based features correlate well with reference judgments. On MT-Bench and Vicuna-Bench, softmax entropy/variance (and their simple combination) achieve strong Pearson correlations, often surpassing Auto-J and being competitive with GPT-3.5 in several settings (e.g., LLaMA2-7B-Chat on MT-Bench: Softmax-combo Pearson 0.588 vs. GPT-3.5 0.434; Vicuna-7B on MT-Bench: 0.536 vs. 0.481). The reference-informed calibration and in-context illustration further improve accuracy in multiple cases, supporting the paper’s central claim that softmax-derived confidence is a useful self-evaluation signal.

593.human_review: This method is not only applicable to existing smaller models (e.g., 7B parameter models) but also holds potential for larger-scale models.
593.llm_review: Practical applicability: the approach enables privacy-preserving, on-device self-evaluation by leveraging only the model’s own glass-box signals, which is attractive when API use is restricted or reproducibility is a concern. The technique can readily support downstream applications like self-reflection triggers and reward modeling data selection without training a separate evaluator.

594.human_review: Simple Variants: The new metrics proposed (such as entropy and variance of the softmax distribution) are merely simple variants of existing signals, lacking in-depth analysis and explanation of their benefits and drawbacks. These variants do not demonstrate unique advantages in practical applications.
594.llm_review: Metrics and reporting choices limit interpretability. The paper primarily emphasizes Pearson correlation to GPT-4 labels, with Spearman/Kendall provided but downplayed (and described as "not fair"), and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported. The inclusion of an additional coarse "Average" score bucket (e.g., 0.6, 0.5) is not a standard evaluation metric and can be misleading. Calibration quality (e.g., ECE) is not assessed despite claims about confidence signals, and sensitivity to output length/frequency effects is not quantified.

595.human_review: Lack of Comprehensiveness: The article does not provide sufficient experimental evidence to support its conclusions. The experiments mainly focus on smaller-scale models and do not consider a wider range of models and larger datasets, which is not good for the confidence of the conclusions.
595.llm_review: Evidence base is narrow. Experiments cover only two 7B models and two 80-question benchmarks, all judged by GPT-4 without any human evaluation to cross-check biases. The uncertainty ensemble uses only 10 forward passes, making the negative result hard to interpret, and key ablations (e.g., effect of response length, decoding temperature/top-k, prompt variants, or domain/task diversity) are missing. Reference-based evaluation is insufficiently evidenced for settings where no canonical references exist, reducing the generality of the experimental support.

596.human_review: Practical Issues: Although the self-evaluation method theoretically has certain advantages, there are still practical issues, i.e., can higher glass-box metric performance provide strong evidence that one model is better than the other on a given task. How can these general evaluations results finally affect the model development remains an issue.
596.llm_review: Evaluation vs. baselines and performance consistency are not fully convincing across models/benchmarks. While softmax features often outperform Auto-J, they are only competitive with GPT-3.5 in some cases and clearly trail it in others (e.g., Vicuna-Bench with LLaMA2-7B-Chat: GPT-3.5 Pearson 0.670 vs. Softmax-Var 0.651; Vicuna-7B: GPT-3.5 0.695 vs. Softmax-combo 0.686). Claims of surpassing proprietary evaluators are therefore overstated. The method’s performance appears model- and benchmark-dependent, and the absence of significance testing makes it hard to judge the robustness of these differences.

597.human_review: The entry point of this paper (i.e., knowledge inconsistencies) is very novel as well as important. Meanwhile, the introduction of KCA offers a systematic and highly applicable method to reduce knowledge inconsistencies in LLMs.
597.llm_review: The paper introduces a novel data-curricular perspective on hallucination mitigation by explicitly verifying alignment data against the foundation models latent knowledge. The exam-style knowledge verification plus three targeted calibration strategies (open-book, discard, refusal) is a fresh idea that generalizes beyond binary QA tasks and enables attribution to specific knowledge snippets, addressing key limitations of prior inconsistency-detection approaches.

598.key_points: Strength: Benchmark, Experiment, Model, Result, Validation
598.human_review: The paper provides extensive experimental results across six benchmarks, utilizing different foundation LLMs to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
598.llm_review: The experimental validation is broad and convincing: multiple backbones and scales (Pythia 7B, Llama-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B) are tested across six benchmarks spanning LLM-as-judge hallucination settings and metric-based evaluations. Results consistently show reduced hallucination rates and improved ROUGE on MS MARCO/ACI-Bench, with additional analyses (correlation between inconsistency and hallucination; refusal-targeted instances being more hallucinatory) that reinforce the main claims. The comparison of the three strategies clarifies trade-offs (refusal reduces hallucinations most; open-book preserves helpfulness; discard balances both), strengthening empirical credibility.

599.human_review: The paper meticulously describes the steps involved in KCA, from knowledge requirement classification to the implementation of different tuning strategies, providing clear guidance for replication.
599.llm_review: The method is well described and implementable: the four-stage detection pipeline (knowledge requirement classification, reference knowledge generation, exam formulation, completion) is clearly specified, including prompts (appendix), question counts, thresholding, and scoring. Training and inference settings, hardware, and hyperparameters are provided, and the authors commit to releasing code, data, and weights, which supports reproducibility and adoption.

600.human_review: The reference knowledge for an instruction is generated by a well-aligned LLM G, but G may also hallucinate and generate wrong knowledge. Hence KCA typically relies on a stronger LLM which stores broader knowledge than the foundation model M (ChatGPT-3.5 v.s. open-sourced LLMs in this paper), which restricts the scalability and makes self-improvement difficult.
600.llm_review: The approach relies heavily on an external, proprietary LLM (GPT-3.5) to classify knowledge requirements, generate reference knowledge, and author the exams, which introduces potential bias, cost, and reproducibility concerns. Using only three multiple-choice questions per snippet with a fixed threshold may yield noisy decisions, and the calibration strategies are relatively coarse (e.g., wholesale refusal), which demonstrably depresses helpfulness. The pipeline may also inherit inaccuracies from G (e.g., imperfect or outdated knowledge), leading to misclassification of a models knowledge state.

601.human_review: When evaluating the hallucination rate, the refusal response is not considered in the calculation, so the comparison between refusal tuning and other methods may not be an apple-to-apple comparison. A comparison of different methods on the instructions with non-refusal responses should be provided.
601.llm_review: Head-to-head comparisons with the most relevant alternatives are missing. The paper does not benchmark against prior data-curation inconsistency methods (e.g., uncertainty/appended disclaimers) or strong decoding/training baselines (e.g., DoLA, CoVe, Fact-RLHF, retrieval-augmented alignment). Evaluation relies largely on LLM-as-judge without complementary human assessment, and there are limited ablations on key design choices (choice of G, number/quality of exam questions, threshold sensitivity), making it hard to position KCAs gains relative to established baselines.

602.human_review: The analysis of over 1.2 million posts allows for robust statistical insights and the development of a well-informed model.
602.llm_review: Strong end-to-end pipeline spanning data, analysis, and modeling. The authors curate a large-scale dataset (1.51M posts) from non-drug-related subreddits to target public/directed stigma, then use a two-stage LLM filter (GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 validation) to isolate 16,277 drug-related posts and 3,207 stigmatizing instances. They operationalize Link & Phelan’s stigma framework in both detection (with an explanation layer) and generation, and propose an Informed + Stylistic LLM that couples stigma-aware instructions with emotion/syntax/lexical style preservation. The mixed-methods analysis (entity/subject–verb patterns, BERTopic, LIWC) yields interpretable insights about substance-specific and interpersonal stigma, while human evaluation shows the informed+stylized GPT-4 model best balances de-stigmatization and faithfulness. The planned release of labeled data and de-stigmatized pairs will be a useful resource.

603.human_review: The use of Informed and Stylized LLMs to transform stigmatizing language into empathetic expressions is innovative and addresses a significant social issue.
603.llm_review: Timely, socially impactful problem framing with clear motivation and thoughtful ethical considerations. The work is practical for moderation and supportive communication tooling and is likely to interest both NLP and social computing audiences.

604.human_review: The study is limited to Reddit, which may not generalize to other social media platforms where user demographics and discussion dynamics differ.
604.llm_review: Limited generalization. The study focuses on English Reddit, and only four subreddits, which may not reflect broader platform norms or cultural/linguistic contexts. The de-stigmatization approach is evaluated primarily on directed stigma about SUD; it is unclear how well the method transfers to self/structural stigma, other health conditions, other marginalized groups, or non-English settings. The reliance on GPT-4 throughout the pipeline (filtering/validation, labeling, generation) also raises questions about portability to lower-resource or open-source deployments.

605.human_review: The manual annotation process could introduce biases, particularly in subjective interpretations of what constitutes stigmatizing language.
605.llm_review: Annotation pipeline depends heavily on LLM-generated labels after a relatively small human seed. The reported perfect agreement (100%) on an initial 200-post relevance sample is atypically high, and the stigma annotation achieves only moderate agreement (k=0.67) before scaling to GPT-4 labeling. There is no systematic audit of LLM labeling errors, no multi-annotator adjudication on a substantial subset, and limited detail on final label quality for directed vs. self vs. structural stigma. This creates uncertainty about noise in downstream analyses and training/evaluation splits.

606.human_review: The evaluation of the de-stigmatized content might not fully capture whether the rephrased messages maintain the original intent and emotional tone of the user.
606.llm_review: Evaluation depth is limited. Human assessment involves five reviewers and 110 posts, reporting win counts without statistical testing or inter-rater agreement; ablations isolating the contribution of stylistic components (emotion, syntax, MTLD, passive voice) are missing. Automatic evaluation relies on LIWC similarity and t-tests, but statistical reporting is underspecified (e.g., p-values, corrections) and LIWC may not capture semantic fidelity or harmfulness. There is no extrinsic or user-centric evaluation with affected communities, no safety/toxicity audits, and no robustness or adversarial tests to probe over-smoothing, content drift, or failure modes. The detection F1 (0.86) is also validated via GPT-4 rather than against an independent gold standard.

607.human_review: Interesting observations on how the LLM refusal behavior changes by decomposing the harmful prompts.
607.llm_review: The paper introduces a clear and modular attack framework (DrAttack) that defines a new decomposition-based category distinct from prefix/suffix/hybrid approaches. The model design cleanly separates decomposition, implicit reconstruction via ICL, and synonym search, making the approach black-box, broadly applicable to both closed- and open-source LLMs, and query-efficient. The conceptual insight—that fragmenting malicious intent reduces attention on rejection tokens—offers a coherent mechanistic explanation grounded in token-probability analysis on open models.

608.human_review: The proposed method that uses semantic parsing to decompose harmful prompts appears to be a more effective jailbreaking attack. The authors also build a useful pipeline to finally decompose the harmful prompt into instruction, structure, verb and noun components.
608.llm_review: Effectiveness: DrAttack achieves strong gains on powerful closed-source LLMs (e.g., human-evaluated ASR of 80% on GPT-4) and remains competitive on open-source models, while using fewer queries than iterative baselines. Method: The decomposition + implicit reconstruction via benign ICL exemplars is well-motivated and supported by ablations showing that semantically similar, affirmative, and structured exemplars raise ASR. Prompt: The templated rule/assignment/result format and automated benign exemplar generation make the method practical and reproducible across prompts, with synonym search providing a measurable performance boost.

609.human_review: Additionally, the authors find that in-context examples are needed to make the victim LLM fall for the latent intent in these deconstructed harmful prompts. Essentially, the fragments of the harmful prompts are spread across the input to the victim LLM in an obfuscated prompt template.
609.llm_review: The paper contributes a systematic prompt engineering scheme: parsing prompts into [instruction], [verb], [noun], and [structure] phrases; using a compact RULE with ASSIGNMENT and RESULT exemplars to implicitly reconstruct malicious intent; and automating exemplar creation and synonym replacement. The ICL template is simple, benign on its face, and demonstrably effective at guiding reassembly without overtly signaling harmful intent.

610.human_review: Relies on a strong model like GPT4 to craft the attack for several key steps, including semantic parsing, synonym generation, and harmless prompt creation.
610.llm_review: Model and Prompt: (1) The pipeline depends on accurate semantic parsing and category assignment (often via GPT-4), which may be brittle for noisy, multi-sentence, or non-English inputs; errors can cascade to reconstruction. (2) The fixed phrase taxonomy ([instruction]/[verb]/[noun]/[structure]) assumes relatively clean syntax and may struggle with figurative language, ellipsis, or multi-turn contexts. (3) The implicit reconstruction step still presumes the model will follow the RULE; safety-tuned systems might increasingly learn to detect this pattern. (4) The synonym search and optional word-game steps add complexity and reliance on external embeddings and APIs, which may hinder reproducibility and robustness.

611.human_review: Is cosine similarity always sufficient to maintain faithfulness with the original intent, does the human evaluation take this into account when measuring success.-
611.llm_review: Evaluation: (1) Heavy reliance on AdvBench and limited-sized subsets of other datasets constrains coverage; some results are based on the first 100 items only. (2) Automated evaluation uses GPT judges, which can be biased, and human evaluation counts an attack as successful if any annotator flags harm—both choices may inflate ASR. (3) Many comparisons are single-run due to cost, with no statistical significance testing or variance reporting. (4) Query efficiency is analyzed in detail primarily on Vicuna-7b; broader efficiency analyses on closed-source models would strengthen claims. (5) Faithfulness is measured via cosine similarity of embeddings, which is a coarse proxy and may conflate harmful specificity with superficial lexical overlap.

612.human_review:
It is not clear if a stronger defense that looks at the prompt structure [1] instead of generic moderation classifiers will reduce the effectiveness. 


[1] The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13208
612.llm_review: Effectiveness, Prompt, and Related Work: (1) The claimed novelty of a decomposition-based category would benefit from a more thorough positioning against recent and concurrent attacks (e.g., newer 2024 methods for automated red teaming, multi-turn or decomposition-like hybrids), as well as stronger baselines beyond those reproduced in EasyJailbreak. (2) Some defense results are limited; stronger or adaptive defenses (e.g., multi-stage input sanitization, explicit segmentation detectors, or reconstruction-aware filters) may reduce effectiveness. (3) Generalization beyond English and to more diverse prompt forms (long, multi-sentence, dialogue) is not convincingly demonstrated, yet central to the method’s premise. (4) The very high ASR on GPT-4 warrants more rigorous third-party replication and sensitivity analyses (e.g., temperature, system prompts, model updates).

613.human_review: The paper studies the importance of fairness of LLMs in processing tabular data, which is of importance to society.
613.llm_review: Data, Importance, Model: The paper targets an important and underexplored question—how in-context demonstration selection affects fairness for tabular classification—on two widely used fairness-focused datasets (Adult, Credit). It demonstrates the practical relevance of the problem to high-stakes applications and evaluates multiple strong LLMs (text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, Claude-3 Haiku, Claude-3 Sonnet), showing the findings are not model-specific.

614.human_review: The paper is well-written and organized. The figures clearly present the framework.
614.llm_review: Figure, Framework, Presentation: The work presents a clear experimental framework linking demonstration composition (ry, rz) to fairness metrics, supported by intuitive figures (e.g., prompt template and performance plots) and a readable algorithmic description with pseudocode for FCG. The presentation of metrics (Rdp, Reo, 9dp, 9eo) and their interpretation is concise, making the fairness framework and experimental flow easy to follow.

615.human_review: The authors conducted extensive experiments on evaluating LLM fairness on different datasets under various settings. The findings reveal the crucial factors that affect LLM fairness under the ICL settings.
615.llm_review: Data, Experiment, Findings, Model: The experiments are systematic: multiple seeds for stability, multiple LLMs, zero- vs few-shot comparisons, and a perturbation study that isolates the roles of demographic and label distributions. The key empirical finding is consistent and actionable—prioritizing minority-group demonstrations improves fairness, often without sacrificing accuracy—and is strengthened by the proposed FCG selection method that further boosts both predictive and fairness metrics versus random selection, with ablations substantiating the benefit of each FCG stage.

616.human_review: The authors only consider two datsets, which may not be necessarily sufficient for the evaluation of the framework. As there are plentiful tabular datasets, the authors should consider using more datasets.
616.llm_review: Data, Framework: The empirical scope is limited to two datasets with binary labels and a single binary sensitive attribute, constraining claims about generalizability. The framework does not assess intersectional or multi-attribute fairness, nor multiclass tasks, and does not explore alternative fairness definitions (e.g., equal opportunity, calibration) that might change conclusions.

617.human_review: The authors use various LLMs for evaluation. However, the performance of the framework on smaller LMs, such as LLaMA, could also be important and necessitates investigations.
617.llm_review: Framework, Model: The FCG scoring blends accuracy and fairness with a fixed b1=0.5 without principled justification or sensitivity analysis, and the evolutionary selection is evaluated on a dev set, raising concerns about overfitting to that split. The study lacks comparisons to established fairness baselines (e.g., post-processing or pre-processing debiasing for tabular data) or to stronger demonstration-selection baselines beyond simple random and a brief reference to LENS, making it hard to situate the model-agnostic framework against existing methods.

618.human_review: The authors only focus on binary classification tasks. However, the fairness problems of LLMs may involve more classification tasks and even generation.
618.llm_review: Model, Task: Details of the tabular-to-text prompt serialization are deferred to the appendix, leaving unclear how feature scaling, missing values, and categorical encodings are handled—important for reproducibility and for model behavior on tabular tasks. The task scope is narrow (binary classification, temperature 0, fixed prompt structure), and the reliance on proprietary black-box LLMs for most results limits insights into model-internal mechanisms and may hinder replication across deployments.

619.human_review: The paper does a thorough analysis of the memory and time complexity providing insights into how the method scared with increasing datasets and label numbers
619.llm_review: Solid methodological and analytical contribution: the paper introduces a simple, distributed-friendly ensemble over tree-based linear models with label subsampling and overlapping subsets, and clearly identifies a key training detail—retaining empty-labeled instances—to preserve level-1 probability estimates. The time and space complexity analyses are explicit, contrasting OVR, tree-based, and the proposed method, and show how per-machine model size and training cost scale roughly linearly with the subsampling rate r. The model-size derivation (O(Kn + r m ñ)) and discussion of how sparsity reduces ñ in subtrees make the approach practical for extreme label spaces.

620.human_review: The papers conducts comprehensive experiments across datasets and baseline comparison.
620.llm_review: Thorough empirical comparisons across six real-world XML datasets, including large-scale benchmarks (amazon-3m, wiki-500k). The study contrasts OVR, a tree with all labels, and the proposed method, and includes ablations on distributed settings (random partitions vs. random label forests variants), demonstrating that ensembling and bypassing level-1 probability estimation are important design choices. Results consistently match or surpass tree-based baselines and approach OVR on multiple datasets.

621.human_review: The evaluation metrics and computational requirements clearly highlight the benefit of the proposed techniques
621.llm_review: Evaluation uses standard XML metrics (precision@1/3/5), reports repeated runs with mean±std on four datasets to mitigate K-means randomness, and correctly notes when P@1 is less informative (wiki10-31k). Including model-size measurements complements the accuracy metrics and substantiates the claimed memory savings.

622.human_review: Impact of sub-sampling and negative sampling is highlighted and considered during the formulation of random label forests
622.llm_review: Clear problem framing and practical focus: the method integrates smoothly with existing linear tree-based systems, is natively parallelizable, and comes with transparent discussion of limitations (e.g., hierarchical labels, resource needs), which helps practitioners assess applicability.

623.human_review: In the XML , the paper does not study or highlight the impact on long-tail distribution .
623.llm_review: Limited impact on datasets with strong hierarchical or correlated label structures: performance drops notably on wiki-500k, and the paper attributes this to uniform label subsampling breaking label relations. This suggests applicability may be constrained in settings like Wikipedia or taxonomy-heavy domains; additional experiments on hierarchical datasets or label-aware subsampling strategies would clarify generalizability.

624.human_review: The paper does not highlight any hyper-parameters and sensitivity of the algorithm towards the same. Details for experimental setup is not-adequate for a fair comparison
624.llm_review: Algorithmic sensitivity and experimental coverage: key parameters (subsampling rate r, number of submodels N, tree branching K, tree depth, K-means settings) lack a systematic sensitivity study or guidance for selection. The ablations are helpful but incomplete (e.g., fixed r=0.1), and OVR is omitted on the two largest datasets, leaving open whether the proposed method truly narrows the gap at the highest scales. More extensive sweeps and stability analyses would strengthen conclusions.

625.human_review: Table 6 highlights reduction in training time, but does not highlight number of distributed compute used and total compute used to train the proposed algorithm
625.llm_review: Training design trade-offs are under-quantified: retaining empty-labeled instances is argued to be crucial for probability estimation, but the cost–benefit is not empirically assessed (e.g., wall-clock and memory overhead with vs. without removal). Moreover, labels never sampled cannot be predicted—a limitation acknowledged but not mitigated (e.g., coverage guarantees, adaptive sampling). The need to run K-means per submodel also raises training cost without an exploration of alternatives.

626.human_review: The proposed method introduces complexity which is not clearly explained  in the distributed training and label sub-sampling techniques. With the release of the code, it would be hard for the paper to be re-produced.
626.llm_review: Complexity claims hinge on ample parallel resources and hide important constants: repeating K-means and tree training across N submodels multiplies computation, and the paper does not provide end-to-end wall-clock comparisons (time-to-accuracy) in the main text, nor discuss communication, orchestration overheads, or straggler effects. Total model footprint across all machines versus baselines is not analyzed, only per-machine size.

627.human_review: Paper lacks theoretical proofs/guarantees to support the correctness or covergence of random forest labels method.
627.llm_review: Limited theoretical grounding: the probability estimation relies on heuristic transforms and multiplicative/averaging combinations across subsampled trees without analysis of bias/variance, calibration, or consistency. There are no guarantees on coverage for tail labels or on approximation error versus OVR, leaving the methodological claims largely empirical.

628.human_review: The paper offers a valuable critique of the current research trajectory in AES, encouraging the community to reconsider the emphasis on performance metrics.
628.llm_review: The paper provides a clear, technically accurate discussion of the dominant AES evaluation metric (QWK) and convincingly argues that reporting aggregate QWK alone obscures model behavior. It outlines concrete performance-analysis practices—per-prompt and per-genre breakdowns, minority-class accuracy, and trait-level diagnostics—that would make claims about improvements more meaningful. This reframing of performance from a single score to a richer diagnostic suite is valuable for the community.

629.human_review: By advocating for a broader outlook, the authors promote a more sustainable and impactful direction for AES research, which could lead to more robust and generalizable solutions.
629.llm_review: The manuscript foregrounds generalization as a first-class goal, especially cross-prompt AES, and articulates why prompt/rubric information and essay-type alignment are necessary for transfer. By proposing trait-based, prompt-independent representations and LLM-assisted knowledge/trait extraction, as well as broader multi-corpus evaluation and corpus development, it points to a roadmap that could materially broaden the impact of AES beyond leaderboard gains on ASAP.

630.human_review: The writing level is relatively clear and the writing quality is good.
630.llm_review: Presentation is clear and well-structured: the paper situates corpora, metrics, and system families before distilling seven actionable recommendations, and it includes explicit limitations and ethics statements. The narrative is readable and accessible to a general NLP audience while remaining useful to AES specialists.

631.human_review: I think some of the methods you mentioned in your article, such as heuristic or ML baseline , have already been mentioned in the previous work. You don't have to spend a lot of space describing this part. You need to describe more emphatically the evaluation and optimization methods of AES in the era of pre-trained models or even LLM.
631.llm_review: Despite extensive discussion, the paper does not specify concrete baselines, methods, or training protocols to instantiate its proposals (e.g., trait-only holistic models, LLM-based trait scoring, or cross-prompt models that consume prompts/rubrics). Without algorithmic descriptions, data splits, or training details, readers cannot reproduce or test the suggested approaches, and critiques of prior cross-prompt setups are not accompanied by alternative experimental baselines.

632.human_review: As a review article, the way the paper is written is too subjective (such as Line 523-559 and Line571-580), contains a lot of speculation, and does not give enough papers and evidence to support it. In addition, the descriptions of existing papers are too brief, which does not allow readers to fully understand the existing work (such as line 561-569).
632.llm_review: Several central claims are asserted without direct empirical evidence or systematic analysis, such as ASAP overfitting risks, the magnitude of length confounding, and the efficiency benefits of LLM-assisted corpus creation/annotation. The paper would be stronger with concrete case studies, meta-analytic statistics, or small pilot experiments to substantiate these points; as written, much of the support is anecdotal or inferential.

633.human_review: This paper tackles a novel and important problem of prompt optimization in multi-step tasks.
633.llm_review: Novelty/Prompt/Task: The paper tackles a largely unexplored problem—automatic prompt optimization for multi-step agent tasks—where prompts are long, structured, and must guide long-horizon decisions. PROMST is novel in combining human-designed feedback rules with LLM-driven prompt generation and a learned heuristic to navigate the large discrete prompt space. The work is tightly aligned with prompt engineering needs in complex, multi-step environments and demonstrates clear task relevance across 11 diverse agent settings.

634.human_review: The proposed method, PROMST, is well-motivated by important problems of multi-step prompt optimization, such as the difficulty of prompt engineering and automatic reasoning over errors.
634.llm_review: Method/Prompt: The framework is methodologically well-motivated and modular. It separates roles for TaskLLM and PromptLLM, introduces a Summarizer (SumLLM) to distill diverse error feedback into concise guidance, and uses a Generator (GenLLM) to propose new prompt candidates. The learned score prediction model (fine-tuned Longformer) provides an explicit, conservative filtering criterion (variance- and error-aware thresholding) to balance exploration and evaluation cost. The prompt optimization is conducted offline across trials, and the method remains orthogonal to online dynamic approaches (e.g., Reflexion), which underscores its flexibility and composability. The design choices are coherent with the unique constraints of long, multi-component prompts.

635.human_review: The experimental results are satisfactory in quality and quantity, as the authors provide results on multiple tasks and LLMs compared to a sufficient number of baseline methods.
635.llm_review: Experiment/Model/Result: The experimental evaluation is broad and generally strong. The authors test across 11 multi-step tasks and five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Mixtral-8x7B, Mixtral-Large), compare against six representative baselines, and consider two TaskLLM/PromptLLM configurations. PROMST typically achieves the best scores, with notable average gains over strong baselines (e.g., 0.69 vs 0.61 using GPT-4/ GPT-4; 0.32 vs 0.27 using GPT-3.5/GPT-4). Ablations show the score model improves efficiency and convergence, SumLLM adds measurable gains, and human-feedback templates are robust to paraphrasing. Additional studies cover cross-LLM transfer and combination with Reflexion, reinforcing the empirical claims.

636.human_review: The formatting for both the text and the visualizations has room for improvement. I have described a few of them in the suggestions, and I would suggest carefully reviewing the paper to fix them.
636.llm_review: Figure: Several figures would benefit from clearer quantitative presentation. For instance, in Figure 4a the binning/definition of distribution/ratio of prompt scores is not fully specified, and Figure 4c lacks detailed axis annotations and uncertainty visualization beyond a color legend. Figure 5a could include error bars or confidence intervals to contextualize the difference between GPT-4 few-shot and the fine-tuned model. Figure 2s feedback templates are illustrative but small and hard to parse; adding a structured legend or zoomed examples per error type would aid readability. Overall, clearer axis labels, units, and consistent plotting conventions would improve interpretability.

637.human_review: It seems that some descriptions and experimental results solely rely on the Appendix, which may confuse the readers of this paper.
637.llm_review: Description/Experiment/Result: Important experimental and reporting details are under-specified. The main text provides limited description of the human-designed feedback rules per task (delegated to the appendix), making it difficult to assess generality and ease of transfer. The scoring function R and the sub-goal vs. completion trade-offs are discussed but not systematically quantified (e.g., how sensitive are rankings to metric choice across all tasks?). The compute budget and evaluation cost (number of API calls per task/iteration, wall-clock time) are not explicitly reported, hindering reproducibility and fairness comparisons. Some hyperparameters (e.g., the generation s_d when the score model activates) are referenced but not fully detailed. Statistical significance and variance across trials are not consistently presented, and the decision to give baselines random feedback instances (without human rules) may disadvantage methods designed around learned/self feedback. Results on some tasks show small margins, making stronger significance or confidence reporting important.

638.human_review: Some explanations on tasks that PROMPST underperforms baseline methods would be helpful.
638.llm_review: Explanation/Performance/Task: While the paper offers some exploratory analyses (e.g., longer prompts tend to perform better), the explanatory depth remains limited. Performance variations across tasks are not fully accounted for, and in a few cases PROMST underperforms strong baselines (e.g., ScienceWorld with GPT-3.5/GPT-4, GridWorld2 with GPT-3.5), without a thorough task-specific diagnosis (e.g., which error types or prompt components fail). The reliance on human-crafted scoring functions and feedback rules raises questions about bias and generality; claims of preference alignment via score function changes are suggestive but would benefit from user studies or broader task families. The observed correlation between prompt length and performance may be confounded by content density or component structure; more controlled studies would clarify causal factors.

639.human_review: Introduction of the PrideMM dataset fills a critical gap in multimodal meme analysis, particularly for LGBTQ+ related content.
639.llm_review: The paper provides thorough dataset analysis, including clear label distributions, substantial inter-annotator agreement with improvements across the staged annotation process, and qualitative misclassification discussion; combined with transparent collection, OCR, filtering, and deduplication procedures, this analytical depth strengthens the credibility and usefulness of the PrideMM data.

640.human_review: The dataset is well-annotated for multiple aspects, including hate speech, targets, stance, and humor, offering a holistic approach to meme classification.
640.llm_review: PrideMM fills a notable gap by curating 5,063 LGBTQ+-related memes annotated across four aspects (hate, target, stance, humor), spanning multiple platforms and recent years, with multi-phase guidelines and predefined splits, offering a valuable multimodal, multi-aspect resource for the community.

641.human_review: Effective use of the pre-trained CLIP model helps in preserving valuable knowledge and improving classification performance.
641.llm_review: MemeCLIP offers a pragmatic training recipe that freezes CLIP encoders and adds lightweight projections, dual feature adapters, and a cosine classifier with semantic-aware initialization, achieving consistent gains across tasks and datasets while enabling efficient single-stage end-to-end training and improved robustness to class imbalance.

642.human_review: MemeCLIP is designed to be robust against imbalanced data, a common issue in real-world datasets, through the use of feature adapters and a cosine classifier.
642.llm_review: The dataset’s natural class imbalance in target categories provides a realistic robustness testbed, and MemeCLIP demonstrates resilience under this condition, delivering strong AUC and Macro-F1 on the four-way target task despite fewer samples, with additional cross-dataset validation on HarMeme supporting robustness claims.

643.human_review: Extensive benchmarking against unimodal and multimodal baselines establishes strong performance standards for future research.
643.llm_review: The paper establishes comprehensive benchmarks with both unimodal and multimodal baselines, prior SOTA frameworks, and ablations isolating each component’s contribution, reporting multiple metrics (Accuracy, AUROC, Macro-F1) to create clear performance reference points for future work.

644.human_review: Although the PrideMM dataset is novel, its size (5,063 images) might still be insufficient for training highly complex models without risk of overfitting.
644.llm_review: Methodological novelty is incremental: projections, adapters, cosine classifier, and semantic-aware initialization are adapted from prior work, and the fusion is simple element-wise multiplication; on the data side, dependence on OCR without explicit noise-robust training and the constrained topical scope limit broader novelty and training rigor.

645.human_review: The focus on LGBTQ+ related content may limit the generalizability of the findings to other domains or types of memes.
645.llm_review: Generalization is assessed only within meme domains (PrideMM and HarMeme) without out-of-distribution tests across platforms, time periods, OCR quality variations, or adversarial edits; there is no evaluation of zero-shot transfer, few-shot adaptation, or robustness beyond the considered datasets.

646.human_review: While qualitative analysis of misclassified samples is provided, a more detailed quantitative analysis could offer deeper insights into the model’s performance.
646.llm_review: The analysis of failure cases is brief and primarily qualitative, lacking per-class confusions, calibration, or statistical significance testing; on stance classification, the model trails a baseline in accuracy, yet the paper does not provide deeper diagnostics or targeted architectural changes to address this performance gap.

647.human_review: The heavy reliance on CLIP might limit the exploration of other potentially effective multimodal representations and frameworks.
647.llm_review: The framework omits explicit cross-modal attention and joint multi-task learning that could capture dependencies among hate, target, stance, and humor; freezing CLIP may limit modeling of nuanced irony, and sensitivity analyses for key choices (e.g., the residual ratio) are limited.

648.human_review: Comparison with similar existing dataset is missing.
648.llm_review: Comparisons exclude strong contemporary VLMs (e.g., BLIP-2, LLaVA, Florence-like models) and broader datasets beyond HarMeme; the limited GPT-4 comparison (100 samples, hate-only) offers narrow evidence relative to the multi-aspect dataset and does not fully contextualize results.

649.llm_review: The GPT-4 prompting is overly restrictive and safety-biased, using a binary, single-task instruction; the study lacks prompt engineering, few-shot exemplars, temperature control, and multi-aspect prompts, making the comparison with prompted VLMs less informative.

650.human_review: The paper introduces a unique method of globally explaining neural relevance models by constructing a "relevance thesaurus," which is innovative and addresses limitations of local explanations.
650.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear and novel method–model combination for global explanations in IR: PaRM, a two-stage Partial Relevance Model distilled from a cross-encoder to infer term–term relevance without explicit alignments. The first stage trains on attention-guided partial query–document views to learn coarse alignments; the second stage calibrates word-pair scores to [0,1] for direct use as a thesaurus. This design targets text-pair relevance directly (rather than single-text classification), avoids perturbation pitfalls, and scales to very large candidate spaces, yielding a principled pathway to interpretable global explanations.

651.human_review: The proposed method is practically implemented by integrating the relevance thesaurus into BM25 scoring functions to enhance ranking effectiveness and fidelity.
651.llm_review: Effectiveness is convincingly demonstrated and the implementation is well specified. BM25T (PaRM) achieves statistically significant gains over BM25 on MS MARCO Dev/DL’19/DL’20 and improves on 7/12 BEIR datasets, with consistent fidelity improvements to several neural rankers (cross-encoder, SPLADE, TAS-B, Contriever(+M)). The method is practical: it integrates seamlessly with BM25/QL via a simple replacement/translation logic, uses public models (MiniLM cross-encoder, BERT-base-uncased), specifies key settings (sequence lengths, Lucene+Krovetz tokenization, candidate vocabularies, thresholding), and keeps implied matches bounded under exact term matches to preserve interpretability and stability.

652.human_review: The proposed method identifies and demonstrates the existence of biases (e.g., brand name bias, temporal bias, encoding errors) in ranking models.
652.llm_review: The explanation logic and model are well aligned: a global thesaurus of query–document term pairs is integrated into BM25 and QL to approximate neural ranker behavior while remaining transparent. Evaluating fidelity against diverse neural architectures shows the model captures behavior shared beyond the teacher cross-encoder. Importantly, the thesaurus enables actionable global insights (e.g., brand-name, temporal, and encoding biases), illustrating the method’s capacity to surface systematic behaviors that local explanations often miss.

653.human_review: The paper concludes that the relevance thesaurus is effective for models trained on similar data. However, this suggests the method may not perform as well across different domains or datasets, potentially limiting its generalization ability and practical applicability.
653.llm_review: Application and generalization remain limited. The thesaurus is distilled from MS MARCO and restricted to frequent terms (top-10k queries, top-100k documents), leaving long-tail vocabulary, multiword expressions, and phrase-level semantics undercovered. Zero-shot BEIR gains are mixed, with notable degradations on some datasets, suggesting domain sensitivity. The approach relies on English-centric preprocessing choices (Lucene+Krovetz) and is only demonstrated for passage retrieval; there is no evidence for transfer to document-level retrieval, multilingual or morphologically rich languages, or real user-facing applications, so practical generalizability is uncertain.

654.human_review: Although the paper identifies various biases, it lacks a detailed analysis of the real-world impact of these biases on retrieval performance.
654.llm_review: Analysis and performance could be strengthened. The bias findings, while compelling, are primarily qualitative and limited in scope; a systematic, controlled study of ranking impact across contexts and mitigation strategies is missing. Performance-wise, a sizable gap to the cross-encoder remains; QLT is underexplored (not tuned to the thesaurus), and comparisons to stronger translation-model baselines are sparse. Key ablations (e.g., attention-based masking vs. alternatives, candidate vocabulary sizes, score thresholding, two-stage necessity, calibration choices) are absent, making it difficult to attribute gains and assess robustness and sensitivity.

655.human_review: The paper introduces a detailed benchmark for evaluating the resilience of language models against subtle and complex shortcuts. This framework categorizes shortcuts into three main types: occurrence, style, and concept.
655.llm_review: The paper introduces a well-scoped shortcut framework (occurrence, style, concept) with seven concrete types and operationalizes it into a reusable benchmark spanning Yelp, GoEmotions, and Beer. The benchmark design includes anti-test sets that invert correlations and a lambda parameter to control shortcut strength, enabling controlled robustness stress testing. Evaluations cover multiple model families (BERT, several Llama variants, and SOTA robust methods), revealing differentiated robustness profiles and practical insights about where models fail.

656.human_review: The paper provides a well-organized review of related literature, positioning the current study within the broader context of research on spurious correlations and model robustness.
656.llm_review: The study situates itself clearly against prior work that focused on trivial, explicit triggers, and instead targets subtler and more realistic shortcuts. By comparing small LMs, LLMs, and robust learning models, it provides model-level insights such as model size not guaranteeing robustness and robust methods sometimes outperforming LLMs under specific shortcuts, which refines the community's understanding of robustness across model classes.

657.human_review: The study evaluates a wide range of models, including traditional small LMs, LLMs, and state-of-the-art robust models.
657.llm_review: The evaluation is systematic: multiple datasets, multiple seeds with averaged results, both accuracy and macro-F1, significance testing, and a principled normal vs anti-test protocol. The inclusion of varying shortcut strengths via lambda and comparisons across several model types supports consistent conclusions about robustness trends.

658.human_review: The benchmark and experiments are focused solely on text classification tasks, specifically sentiment analysis and emotion prediction. This limits the generalizability of the findings to other NLP tasks, such as machine translation or question answering.
658.llm_review: The benchmark and experiments are confined to sentiment and emotion classification, with style shortcuts generated by LLM paraphrasing and occurrence/category shortcuts added via fixed templates. This raises concerns about generalization to other tasks (e.g., NLI, QA, information extraction) and to naturally occurring shortcuts. Without broader task coverage and human or quantitative validation of style fidelity and label preservation, the benchmark’s external validity remains limited.

659.human_review: The use of LLMs to rewrite text for creating style shortcuts may introduce noise or alter the original meaning of the text.
659.llm_review: Model coverage is narrow: among encoders only BERT-base is evaluated (no RoBERTa/DeBERTa), and among LLMs only Llama 2/3 small-to-mid variants are considered, without instruction-tuned models or alternative decoder families (e.g., Mistral, GPT-J). This limits conclusions about whether the observed robustness patterns hold across stronger or differently trained architectures.

660.human_review: The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of the quality of the modified datasets. Although manual checks were performed, a systematic quantitative evaluation would strengthen the validity of the conclusions.
660.llm_review: The analysis is shallow relative to the data interventions: SHAP-based interpretation is limited to occurrence shortcuts on a subset, there is no systematic, quantitative validation of rewritten style fidelity or label stability, and no data quality audit beyond spot checks. Evaluation relies primarily on anti-test drops, without complementary OOD datasets or per-group breakdowns, making it hard to disentangle shortcut reliance from potential artifacts introduced during data construction.

661.key_points: Weakness: Evaluation, Method, Model, Novelty, Robustness
661.human_review: While the paper evaluates existing robust models, it does not propose new methods to improve robustness against the identified shortcuts. Introducing novel techniques or strategies would add significant value to the study.
661.llm_review: Methodologically, several shortcuts still rely on detectable templates or highly stylized authors, which weakens the claim of subtlety and limits novelty beyond prior work that used synthetic triggers. The anti-test construction can exaggerate performance gaps and may not reflect real OOD shifts. Absent comparisons to stronger causal/IRL/invariance baselines or data augmentation strategies, the conclusion that no method is universally robust is expected and less informative about what methods work best under realistic constraints.

662.human_review: The study could explore the impact of different hyperparameter settings on model robustness.
662.llm_review: Robustness claims depend on hyperparameters that are under-specified in their rationale. The choice and range of lambda values, fine-tuning regimes, and early-stopping criteria differ across models and may affect robustness conclusions. A more thorough sensitivity analysis across seeds, lambda, learning rates, and training budgets, matched across model families, is needed to ensure that observed robustness differences are not artifacts of parameter choices.

663.human_review: This paper provides a method to balance two critical aspects (quality & diversity) of dataset curation, which is crucial for improving the robustness of language models in following instructions.
663.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear, data-driven method (QDIT) that jointly optimizes instruction-response quality and instruction diversity by combining a facility-location diversity term over instruction embeddings with a quality score via a tunable alpha. Methodologically, this gives principled control over the quality–diversity trade-off while remaining practical through greedy selection and standard accelerations. On the robustness front, the study carefully targets worst-case behavior (bottom 10% by reward or win rate) and shows that increasing data diversity substantially improves worst-case performance without harming best-case, e.g., aggregated gains of +5.2% in worst-case HH score and +6.26% in worst-case winning score over quality-only selection.

664.human_review: This paper offers detailed experiments on how quality and diversity inference the instruction tuning process. It's beneficial for potential researchers in data selection areas.
664.llm_review: The experimental design leverages multiple and diverse data sources (Ultrachat 1.3M, LMSYS-Chat 1M, a Mixed 270K set, and smaller Alpaca 52K and Dolly 15K), with consistent subset sizes (e.g., 10K for large sources, ~5% for small) to isolate selection effects. Evaluations span five instruction-following suites via LLM-based pairwise comparison and a reward model (HH score), and report average, worst-case (bottom 10%), and best-case (top 10%) metrics. The authors further probe evaluator sensitivity (Claude-2/2.1, GPT-3.5/4), perform ablations (alpha sweep, data size, selection variants), and report statistical significance (paired t-test) and multiple seeds, yielding a credible, data-centric picture of the method’s impact.

665.human_review: The authors conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets and models to validate QDIT's effectiveness and versatility. These experiments clearly demonstrate QDIT's superior performance in various scenarios, particularly in improving the worst-case instruction-following capability.
665.llm_review: Effectiveness is demonstrated across experiments and models: compared to quality-only selection, QDIT consistently improves worst-case metrics and often improves average metrics (e.g., Ultrachat 10K shows worst 10% HH 3.497 vs. 3.405; LMSYS 10K shows worst 10% HH 3.551 vs. 3.391), while leaving best-case largely unchanged. The method transfers across base models (LLaMA-1 7B and Llama-2-13B) and even shows gains on several general benchmarks (MMLU/BBH/ARC/DROP/LAMBADA/SCIQ), with higher average scores in most settings. Use of multiple evaluators and a human check strengthens the validation that improvements are not artifacts of a single judge.

666.human_review: This paper only compares QDIT with random, quality, and QDIT variant settings, lacking comparisons with other instruction data selection methods such as CaR and DEITA.
666.llm_review: Comparisons are limited primarily to random and quality-only selection, plus two in-house diversity variants (thresholding and clustering). The study does not compare against well-known alternative subset selection methods for diversity/coverage (e.g., determinantal point processes, k-center/coreset selection, other submodular objectives), nor does it probe alternative similarity backbones (beyond sentence-transformer cosine) or non-linear quality–diversity combinations. This narrows the methodological and data-selection comparison space and leaves open how QDIT stacks up against other established coverage/diversity techniques.

667.human_review: The experiments presented were primarily conducted on LLaMA-7B, leaving the effectiveness of QDIT on larger models (e.g., 13B) and more advanced versions (e.g., LLaMA2/3 7B) uncertain.
667.llm_review: Experimental scope is model-limited: most results center on LLaMA-1 7B with a light check on Llama-2-13B, and only supervised finetuning is considered. The evaluation relies heavily on LLM judges (Claude, GPT-3.5/4), with a small author-conducted human study; potential evaluator biases, calibration drift, or overlap effects are not deeply analyzed. Some ablations (e.g., varying data size) change training compute in ways that can confound interpretation, and details on how alpha is tuned per dataset/model are brief, making it hard to assess model-selection robustness.

668.human_review: As shown in Table 3, QDIT does not consistently outperform across various benchmarks; the improvement margins are quite limited, and in some cases, such as the Alpaca-3K benchmark, QDIT performs worse than the random baseline.
668.llm_review: On standard benchmarks, improvements are modest and sometimes inconsistent. For example, in Table 3 some tasks show negligible gains or even small drops (e.g., LAMBADA marginal decreases in certain settings; Dolly 1K average slightly lower for QDIT than quality-only). While the core claim targets instruction-following robustness, the broader performance story is mixed, and effect sizes on these benchmarks are small, which may limit perceived impact beyond the targeted robustness gains.

669.key_points: Weakness: Baseline, Experiment, Method, Model, Technique
669.human_review: The experiments in the paper are predominantly based on supervised fine-tuning. It is not yet clear if QDIT is equally effective for more complex alignment techniques, such as RLHF methods like PPO and DPO. I suggest that the authors conduct RLHF experiments using QDIT-SFT models and other baselines to demonstrate that models fine-tuned with QDIT can maintain performance superiority during the RLHF stage.
669.llm_review: Baseline and technique coverage leave gaps: there is no RLHF/DPO stage to test whether diversity-driven gains persist under more advanced alignment pipelines; no sensitivity study on the choice of embedding model or reward model for scoring; and scalability claims (starting from an O(|V|^3K) selection cost mitigated by heuristics) lack detailed wall-clock comparisons to strong baselines. The proposed thresholding and clustering variants are relatively weak baselines; stronger, widely used techniques from active learning/coreset selection or DPP-based diversity would provide a more convincing methodological baseline suite.

670.human_review: This work addresses the very important issue of assessing a model's performance in a generative setting, where token-level evaluation metrics fall short. While I am skeptical of training a model to evaluate another model, the increase in performance of using the reward model is positively correlated with an increase in the traditional automatic evaluations.
670.llm_review: Evaluation/Metric/Model/Performance: The paper proposes a trained evaluator (DeBERTa-Valid) that substantially improves alignment with human judgments over standard automatic metrics. Reported agreement with human evaluation reaches about 94% on FCR and transfers well to other datasets, while Pearson correlations also exceed those of ROUGE/BLEU/BERTScore. Integrating this evaluator as a reward model within PPO leads to consistent gains of roughly 2–4 points in the human-proximal metric across FCR, FinCausal, and SCITE, with modest improvements in exact-match/F1 as well. The approach directly addresses semantic boundary ambiguity in causal event spans and yields robust, reproducible performance improvements for FLAN-T5 over strong baselines.

671.human_review: The experimental design is robust and there is a significant amount of baseline exploration as well as ablation analysis to understand the degree of usefulness of each individual feature of this work
671.llm_review: Ablation/Analysis/Experiment: The study includes informative ablations comparing different reward surrogates (entailment-based NLI and SentenceTransformer similarity) and shows the proposed evaluator is more tolerant to wording variation and better captures semantic validity. The transferability experiment (training an evaluator on FCR and applying it to FinCausal and SCITE) demonstrates strong cross-dataset agreement with human labels. The "w/o EM" analysis highlights that the evaluator recovers semantically correct outputs missed by exact-match metrics. Weak-supervision experiments with 30/50/80% subsets, plus confidence-based filtering, show that a 50% subset yields an RL model comparable to the full-reward setup, supporting the data-efficiency claim.

672.human_review: The authors tested for domain transferability bay using different datasets and cross-evaluating models
672.llm_review: Data/Evaluation/Model: A dedicated human-feedback collection platform is used to curate binary validity labels for cause-effect extractions produced by GPT-3.5 and FLAN-T5, with detailed annotator instructions that specifically target wording variation and hallucination. Inter-annotator agreement (Cohens ba) is reported across datasets, indicating reliable supervision. The evaluator ingests source text, gold extraction, and model output, empirically showing each components importance. The model side is well-scoped: a supervised FLAN-T5 extractor is aligned via PPO using the evaluator as reward and a KL term to stabilize formatting, leading to consistent improvements while reducing reliance on brittle overlap metrics.

673.human_review: Using weak supervision for generative causal relation extraction appears to be a promising avenue
673.llm_review: The paper addresses an important pain point in causal event extractionevaluation under boundary ambiguityand demonstrates a practical and general strategy: learn a human-aligned evaluator and use it both for scoring and as an RL reward. The contributions are conceptually clear, empirically supported across multiple datasets, and show promising generalization and data-efficiency, making the work relevant to information extraction with generative models.

674.human_review: I would like to see more analysis on the discrepancies between human annotators and the trained reward model. The authors mention two main culprits: Hallucinations and word mismatches. A more detailed analysis with statistics beyond what is shown in __Pitfalls of Existing Evaluation Schema__ could bring more insight into this.
674.llm_review: Analysis/Model: (1) There is a potential evaluation circularity: the same learned evaluator is used as both the training signal (reward) and the primary test metric (human-prox). Without a final human evaluation on RL-trained outputs, it is hard to rule out reward over-optimization or evaluator-specific artifacts.
