(2) Limited error analysis is provided for failure cases (e.g., borderline spans, numeric mismatches, and hallucinations) post-RL; qualitative analyses or fine-grained breakdowns would help clarify what the model actually improves. (3) Some reported numbers appear inconsistent (e.g., a case where F1 exceeds both precision and recall), raising concerns about metric computation and the reliability of the comparative analysis.

675.human_review: It is unclear on how the initial model extractions to train the reward function where obtained. Did you use FLAN-T5 without fine tuning to generate the data for human feedback?
675.llm_review: Data/Model/Training: (1) The evaluator relies on gold references as inputs; this limits applicability in blind or low-resource settings where references are unavailable and introduces a dependency on reference quality the paper itself notes can be imperfect. (2) Dataset coverage focuses on span-based cause/effect; the approach does not extend to trigger-based or open-text settings, narrowing impact. (3) Training details for PPO and the reward pipeline (e.g., KL coefficient, reward scaling, rollout details, calibration of classifier confidence thresholds) are insufficient for full reproducibility. (4) Baseline prompt settings for GPT-3.5/4 might be under-optimized; stronger prompting or few-shot design and human evaluation for those baselines would provide a fairer comparison.

676.human_review: The paper presents a good framework for empirically experimenting with LLMs hidden states in the context of comparing ICL and IT. I appreciate the authors performing multiple experiments to reduce the variance of their estimates and performing significance testing when required to highlight experimental results.
676.llm_review: Comparison, Experiment, Framework, Model: The paper unifies ICL, IT, and zero-shot (anchor) in a single controlled framework that enables apples-to-apples comparisons using identical instructions/demonstrations/inference inputs while varying only the learning paradigm. The experiments are carefully constructed (30 randomized runs; controlled few-shot vs. epoch balancing; layer-wise analyses; attention-based sanity checks) and systematically probe multiple manipulations (demo count, semantic similarity, label correctness, task mismatch). The study spans multiple models in the same family (LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Base and Chat) with a consistent and transparent LoRA setup, increasing confidence that the observed convergence is not a one-off artifact.

677.human_review: The authors perform a well ablated analysis of the relationship between in context learning and instruction tuning and present various empirical findings on how they compare by varying a) semantic similarity between demonstration and inference examples , b) number of provided demonstrations, c) demonstrating with wrong labels, d) demonstration with different tasks. These findings are also relevant for actual practical uses, such as using ICL for identifying redundant data in instruction tuning.
677.llm_review: Analysis, Data, Findings: The methodology is clear and replicable: define h_anchor, h_ICL, h_IT and quantify s_anchor–ICL, s_anchor–IT, s_ICL–IT via cosine similarity. Across SST-2, WMT16 EN–CS, and XSum, the authors repeatedly find high ICL–IT similarity while both diverge from the anchor. The analyses capture key phenomena—ICL–IT convergence grows with demo–inference semantic similarity and number of shots; a U-shaped layerwise pattern; modest sensitivity to wrong labels; minimal impact from cross-task demonstrations—and include a per-token loss analysis showing larger loss reductions for example tokens after IT. The findings are novel, interpretable, and suggest practical implications for IT data selection and efficient prompting.

678.human_review: Although I appreciate the author's attention to detail and being rigorous in their experiments, I am a bit concerned about the generalizability of these findings on LLMs. In the paper, results on the Llama2 13B model show that the similarity between ICL-IT, Anchor-IT and Anchor-ICL all seem to converge, compared to the baseline Llama2 7B model. This fact alone seems to point that IT/ICL do not have a “significant” impact on the model performance compared to the anchor. However, we’ve seen in literature that Instruction Tuning LLMs does improve instruction following abilities quite a lot (ChatGPT, Llama-2), so this experimental setup seems a bit counter intuitive in this scenario.
678.llm_review: Experiment, Findings, Generalization, Model: (1) The central evidence relies on cosine similarity of the last-token hidden state; alternative representation views (e.g., sequence-wide metrics, trajectory distances, mutual information, probing) are not explored, leaving potential confounds from prompt position and token identity. (2) The link from representation convergence to downstream utility is only partially established: correlations between s_ICL–IT and task performance are not systematically quantified across conditions, and the wrong-labels study shows small, non-significant performance changes despite representation shifts. (3) Model coverage is limited to the LLaMA-2 family; generalization to other architectures/tokenizers (e.g., Mistral/MoE/T5-like enc-dec, RLHF-heavy models) remains untested. (4) The tuning configuration is narrow (LoRA on Q/V with fixed hyperparameters); full fine-tuning, other adapters, or varying target modules are only briefly touched, so the robustness of convergence to tuning strategy is unclear. (5) Task breadth is modest for the broader claims: while translation and summarization are included, reasoning/coding/multi-step tasks are absent, yet some implications for alignment and data selection are asserted. (6) Statistical reporting is uneven: main similarity results lack effect sizes and confidence intervals; 30 seeds may be underpowered for generative tasks and prompt variability; sensitivity to prompt format is relegated to appendices. (7) The measure of demo–inference similarity uses SBERT, which may not reflect the target model’s internal geometry; prompt-format effects could drive similarities without reflecting true task-level convergence.

679.human_review: This paper focuses on the zero-shot relation extraction task, which is significant for real-world relation extraction. The proposed method could have a high potential to solve relation extraction in low-resources.
679.llm_review: Introduces a clear and practical definition-only zero-shot RE setting and a coherent REPAL framework that leverages LLMs for seed generation and an SLM for efficient extraction, yielding large improvements over strong zero-shot baselines across two benchmarks.

680.human_review: The proposed method overall makes sense to me. Simply leveraging the LLMs for relation extraction could lead to low-quality RE results so the authors change the role of LLMs to produce some seed data. Further iterative improvement and fine-tuning are conducted to ensure the quality of the SLM-based RE model.
680.llm_review: Data/Method/Model: The paper thoughtfully constructs evaluation data by pairing Wikidata-derived definitions with FewRel and Wiki-ZSL and assembling an unlabeled corpus. Methodologically, REPAL combines definition-conditioned LLM synthesis (with diverse prompt templates), an NLI-style SLM for relation-specific binary classification, and a feedback loop that uses SLM inferences and synthesis history to expand pattern coverage and mitigate bias, including the generation of negative definitions and near-miss negatives. The design is validated via ablations showing the contribution of initial seeds, positive/negative feedback stages, and prompt choices, demonstrating a well-integrated LLM–SLM synergy.

681.human_review: Overall, this paper is well-written and easy to follow.
681.llm_review: Clarity/Presentation: The problem setup and assumptions are explicitly stated, with a formal task definition and a clear end-to-end pipeline diagram. Prompts and implementation details are documented in appendices, and the paper provides ablations, analyses of prompt effects, and discussions of limitations that help readers understand design choices and boundary conditions.

682.human_review: I have concerns about the sensitivity of the proposed method. Due to the wide applications of LLMs in the proposed method, it is applied to generate positive instances and improve the predicted inferences. The performance may rely heavily on the designed prompt and the generation quality of LLMs. I suggest the authors include a section discussing the generalization of different LLMs as backbones for the proposed method.
682.llm_review: Application/Method/Model/Prompt: External validity and robustness are under-explored. The binary-per-relation evaluation does not fully reflect multi-relation extraction scenarios, and negative sampling from an unlabeled corpus assumes low prevalence and may introduce false negatives without quantifying their rate. The approach depends heavily on GPT-3.5/4 with hand-crafted, multi-turn prompts, yet prompt sensitivity, cost, and LLM choice robustness are not systematically analyzed. The SLM backbone is restricted to a RoBERTa-NLI formulation without comparisons to alternative architectures or calibration strategies. Potential data contamination (LLMs memorizing Wikipedia-like content) and distribution shift between synthetic and real data are not investigated, raising concerns about overfitting to generated patterns and fairness of comparisons.

683.human_review: The authors could show more about the potential usage of REPAL on low-resource relation extraction to strengthen its significance.
683.llm_review: Significance: While the definition-only setting is interesting, the core technique—LLM-driven data synthesis with iterative feedback—resembles existing self-training/active-learning paradigms, making the conceptual novelty moderate. Impact is constrained by evaluation on a constructed setting and by continued gaps to fully supervised performance. The multi-way results rely on training a classifier on synthetic instances, leaving unclear how gains translate to standard zero-shot RE setups or to real-world end-to-end extraction where relation inventories and negatives are not controlled.

684.human_review: The introduction of the McMarket dataset provides a valuable resource for research in multilingual and cross-market product-based question answering. This dataset covers a wide range of languages and marketplaces, significantly enhancing the scope of research in this area.
684.llm_review: Data: McMarket is a large-scale, multilingual, cross-market resource that aggregates over 2M product questions and 7.7M reviews across 13 marketplaces in 8 languages, with both original-language content and English translations. The dataset includes both reviews and QA pairs, enabling multiple supervision signals for PQA. Two LLM-annotated subsets (for review-grounded answer generation and question ranking) are provided and quality-checked by human annotators, increasing the dataset’s practical utility for training and evaluation.

685.human_review: The paper provides in-depth analysis of the dataset and the performance of different models. It includes human evaluation of LLM-generated data, which adds credibility to the quality of the annotations and the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
685.llm_review: Analysis, Data, Evaluation, Performance: The paper offers thorough benchmarking across single- and cross-market settings on two subtasks (answer generation and question ranking), spanning lexical, encoder, and LLM-based methods. Results consistently show cross-market signals improve performance, especially in low-resource markets, and that LLMs outperform traditional baselines. The authors connect data characteristics to outcomes via temporal analysis, K-retrieval sensitivity, and multilingual comparisons (translated vs non-translated), and complement automatic evaluation with targeted human assessments, yielding a well-rounded empirical picture.

686.human_review: While human assessments are used to evaluate the quality of annotations, there is a lack of direct user feedback on the actual usefulness and relevance of the generated answers in practical e-commerce settings.
686.llm_review: Annotation, Evaluation: The auto-labeling relies on GPT-4 operating on English translations, which can introduce translation and annotator-model biases. Human verification covers only a relatively small sample and lacks a detailed error taxonomy, making it hard to characterize residual errors. Using GPT-4 outputs as ground truth for evaluation (on McMarket_r and McMarket_q) risks circularity and alignment bias when assessing LLM baselines. For answer generation, BLEU/ROUGE may not reflect factual faithfulness to the cited reviews; no faithfulness or hallucination checks are reported.

687.human_review: The paper mentions the use of professional translation tools and LLMs for data annotation, but there is a risk of inconsistency and quality issues in the translated and annotated data, which could impact the overall performance of the models.
687.llm_review: Annotation, Data: The criteria and reliability for aligning or retrieving ‘same’ versus ‘similar’ products across marketplaces are not fully specified, raising concerns about noise in cross-market supervision. Translation quality is summarized but primarily deferred to the appendix, and mixing DeepL (QA) with NLLB (reviews) may introduce systematic inconsistencies. Coverage is incomplete (some marketplaces left untranslated), and the LLM-annotated subsets are small relative to the full corpus, which may introduce sampling bias and limit supervised training breadth.

688.human_review: The use of large, complex models like LLMs might lead to overfitting, especially given the size and specificity of the dataset. The paper could benefit from a discussion on strategies to prevent overfitting and ensure robust performance.
688.llm_review: Data, Model: The dataset focuses on Electronics and primarily leverages the US market as the auxiliary source, which may constrain generalizability to other domains or auxiliary choices. Model baselines omit strong cross-lingual dense retrievers and retrieval-augmented generation approaches (e.g., multilingual dual encoders, mContriever, LaBSE, or more recent multilingual instruction-tuned RAG pipelines), limiting conclusions about the state of the art. There is limited ablation on product matching versus similar-product retrieval, and no error or robustness analyses (e.g., hallucination, sensitivity to noisy reviews), which would clarify where the data and models succeed or fail.

689.human_review: The design of the hybrid framework is comprehensive and meticulous, and it adopts an innovative proxy method of symbolic reasoning to elevate the quality of explanation. The utilization of Isabelle/HOL theorem prover and Neo-Davidsonian event semantics deserves acknowledgment, which enhances the entire process.
689.llm_review: Explanation and Framework: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated neuro-symbolic framework (Explanation-Refiner) that couples LLMs with Isabelle/HOL to verify and refine natural language explanations. The pipeline is explicitly decomposed into autoformalisation with Neo-Davidsonian event semantics, a syntax refiner, rough inference to identify relevant facts, proof construction, and iterative verification/refinement driven by theorem-prover feedback. The roles of each component and their interactions are well-explained, making the approach reproducible and highlighting why the external prover can provide objective feedback on logical validity and non-redundancy.

690.human_review: The authors have conducted a series of experiments to show that the proposed method can effectively improve the logic validity of existing annotated explanations. Ablation studies are also presented to discuss the impact of autoformalisation on performance.
690.llm_review: Ablation, Experiment, Validation: The empirical study is broad and informative: five LLMs across three datasets (e-SNLI, QASC, WorldTree) with varying explanation complexity; detailed tracking of initial vs. final provability; iteration-wise refinement curves; and syntax-error reduction statistics. The ablation that swaps in GPT-4 only for autoformalisation cleanly isolates the contribution of the formalisation component and shows large gains for weaker models. Human validation of factuality and triviality (on GPT-3.5/4) strengthens claims that refined explanations are generally factually correct and not mere paraphrases. Headline results (e.g., GPT-4 improving provable explanations to 84%, 55%, and 37% on the three datasets; syntax-error reductions up to ~69%) substantiate the framework’s effectiveness.

691.human_review: It should be stated clearly what language generation metrics are used in previous studies, why they could be flawed for this task, and how they would be correlated with the proposed metrics.
691.llm_review: Metric: The core metric operationalizes explanation quality as the percentage of hypotheses provable in Isabelle from LLM-generated axioms and proof steps. This can conflate formalization fluency with explanatory faithfulness and may be sensitive to the chosen encoding (Neo-Davidsonian FOL), proof tactics (e.g., blast), and timeout settings. It does not quantify explanation completeness/compactness beyond provability, nor does it report statistical uncertainty or robustness to prompt variations. The human evaluation of factuality/triviality is helpful but limited (sample size not reported) and does not measure faithfulness to human rationales or causal sufficiency.

692.human_review: This paper is missing some baseline experiments. As stated in the paper, existing work possesses inherent issues, and the paper appears to be deficient in certain effect comparisons. The most straightforward notion is to conduct a comparison with the baseline of directly employing LLM for refinement and additionally using the feedback based on the metrics used in previous studies.
692.llm_review: Baseline, Comparison, Experiment, Metric: The experimental comparisons lack strong baselines for automatic verification/refinement, such as LLM self-critique without a theorem prover, differentiable/abductive reasoners, or alternative provers/frameworks. The study covers only 300 samples, raising concerns about statistical power and generalizability, and it does not report runtime/efficiency or resource costs per iteration. There is no analysis of downstream task accuracy improvements attributable to refinement, no significance testing, and no comparison to standard explanation metrics (e.g., sufficiency/necessity, compactness). These gaps make it hard to gauge how much the proposed system advances the state of the art beyond the specific setting and encoding choices.

693.human_review: The introduction of the Structure Guided Prompt is innovative, providing a systematic approach to improve LLMs’ multi-step reasoning.
693.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear, three-stage structure-guided prompting approach (concept-map construction, task-specific planning, and execution) that turns unstructured text into an explicit graph and then instructs the model to navigate it. This design leverages LLMs as both graph constructors and reasoners, separates planning from execution, works in a zero-shot setting without external KGs, and yields interpretable, step-by-step reasoning traces driven by the prompt.

694.human_review: The framework is tested on diverse datasets (CLUTRR, BBH, HotpotQA, and Entailment Bank), demonstrating its robustness and versatility.
694.llm_review: The framework is exercised across diverse datasets (CLUTRR, multiple BIG-bench hard tasks, HotpotQA bridging questions, EntailmentBank), spanning relation prediction, dynamic KG tracking, graph sorting/query, and logical inference. Results are reported for both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and the framework shows reduced degradation with increased path length or number of objects, suggesting robustness across data regimes and model backbones.

695.human_review: The experimental results show substantial performance gains in various reasoning tasks compared to baseline methods.
695.llm_review: Experiments consistently show gains over zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, with especially large improvements on CLUTRR and BBH tracking shuffled objects (e.g., the reported ~146% relative improvement over GPT-4 w/ 0-CoT on dynamic tracking). The results are coherent with task difficulty and indicate that structuring the context into graphs yields tangible performance benefits.

696.human_review: The three-stage prompting framework is well-explained, making it easy to understand.
696.llm_review: The framework provides a unified prompting template complemented by task-specific planning strategies, yielding a modular and extensible prompting recipe. The explicit prompts guide graph construction and traversal, improving controllability and interpretability of multi-step reasoning compared to generic CoT prompts.

697.human_review: The main paper lacks detailed descriptions of the experimental settings with GPTs and the specific prompts used in the reasoning tasks, which are crucial for reproducibility and understanding the methodology.
697.llm_review: Method and experimental description lack important details for reproducibility and fair comparison: (1) the graph construction procedure is under-specified (entity/relation schema, coreference resolution, disambiguation, handling directionality/negation); (2) no ablations isolating the contribution of each stage (graph vs. plan vs. execution) or sensitivity to alternative prompt wordings; (3) baseline coverage omits strong structured reasoning prompts (e.g., Least-to-Most, self-consistency, Tree/Graph-of-Thoughts) and tool-augmented methods; (4) no analysis of prompt robustness or error propagation from noisy graph extraction; (5) missing cost/latency/token-usage comparisons despite multi-stage prompting overhead.

698.human_review: Appendix Length: The appendix is more than double the length of the main content of the paper, indicating that a significant portion of important details may/can not be included in the main sections of the paper.
698.llm_review: Key implementation and reporting details are missing or relegated to the appendix: exact prompt templates per task, dataset splits and sample counts per setting, evaluation metrics and judging protocols for open-ended answers, randomization/seeding and run-to-run variability, and comprehensive error analysis in the main text. These omissions hinder reproducibility and assessment of result reliability.

699.human_review: Complexity in Real-World Scenarios: Constructing and maintaining Knowledge Graphs can be complex and expensive, which may limit the practical applicability of the proposed framework.
699.llm_review: Applicability to real-world, long-context scenarios is unclear. Most evaluations use synthetic or simplified tasks; performance gains shrink on longer, noisier contexts (HotpotQA) and more brittle logical inference (EntailmentBank). The multi-stage prompting increases complexity, latency, and token cost, and the framework requires hand-crafted planning strategies per task, which may limit scalability and practical deployment.

700.human_review: The framework struggles with tasks requiring precise, logical order and distinguishing between premises and conclusions.
700.llm_review: The claimed task-agnostic framework relies on task-specific planning prompts, which weakens generality. Using the same LLM to construct and traverse the graph risks unverified assumptions and error cascades. The framework lacks mechanisms for enforcing logical consistency (e.g., rule directionality, constraint checking) or verifying edges, leading to fragility in settings that demand strict inference order.

701.human_review: The methodology and dataset used for different contributions need to be presented in a better manner.
701.llm_review: The contribution appears incremental relative to prior structured reasoning prompts (e.g., Tree/Graph-of-Thoughts, MindMap-like KG guidance). Without comparisons to these stronger baselines or demonstrations on open-source models to disentangle method vs. model effects, it is hard to gauge methodological novelty. The data choices, while varied, do not convincingly establish broad impact beyond curated reasoning benchmarks.

702.human_review: The authors introduce LoRAN, a simple and straightforward way of adding non-linearity to LoRA based adapter methods which enhance the adapter’s ability to model the underlying finetuning function without introducing extra parameters.
702.llm_review: Method: The paper proposes a simple yet principled modification to LoRA by inserting a non-linear transformation f(·) after the low-rank product, aiming to approximate high-rank weight updates with no additional trainable parameters. The custom Sinter function (f(x) = A*sin(ωx) ⊙ x + x) is designed to behave as a near-identity mapping with controlled, input-scaled interference, which is well-motivated for stabilizing optimization while increasing expressivity. The approach is generic, easy to implement, and compatible with existing LoRA/QLoRA setups, providing a clear methodological contribution for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

703.human_review: To highlight the effectiveness of their method, the authors also introduce an example for a nonlinearity which can be used for LoRAN - $\mathbb{S}inter$ - and show that their method leads to improvements on top of the QLoRA baseline on summarization and classification tasks.
703.llm_review: Baseline, Effectiveness, Improvement, Method: The method is evaluated against a strong and widely-used baseline (QLoRA) across multiple LLM families (Flan-T5-Large, Falcon-7B, Llama-2-7B/13B) and two tasks (SAMSum summarization and 20 Newsgroups classification), showing consistent gains. On SAMSum, LoRAN improves ROUGE scores across most model configurations (e.g., Llama-2-7B: +0.55 R1, +0.62 R2, +0.60 RL; Falcon-7B: +0.51 R1, +0.38 R2, +0.76 RL). On 20 Newsgroups, LoRAN yields accuracy improvements for all models, with a notable +1.22 for Llama-2-7B. The benefits are amplified under tighter parameter budgets (r=8), with +0.62/+0.41/+0.53 ROUGE and +1.95 accuracy on Llama-2-7B, indicating that the proposed method improves effectiveness particularly in low-rank regimes. An ablation over the non-linearity shows Sinter outperforms Identity and Swish variants, supporting the method’s design choice.

704.human_review: In experimental section 3.1, the authors mention using $A = 5e-5$ and $\omega = 1e-4$. However, it is not clear from the paper how these hyperparameters were chosen. Specifying how the parameters were swept, or how different values influence performance would be very useful for users of LoRAN.
704.llm_review: Experiment, Parameter, Performance: The experimental exploration of the non-linear transformation’s hyperparameters is limited—A and ω are fixed without a sensitivity study, making it unclear how robust performance is to these choices. Only two ranks (r=64 and r=8) are tested, and other adapter design factors (e.g., where to insert adapters, α, dropout) are not systematically analyzed. Several reported gains are modest and may fall within run-to-run variance; there are no statistical significance tests or multiple seeds. Performance is not universally improved (e.g., ROUGE-L drops by 0.05 for Flan-T5-Large on SAMSum), suggesting that benefits can be configuration-dependent. Overall, the parameter/performance trade-offs need more thorough experimental coverage to substantiate the claimed generality.

705.human_review: In experimental section 3.2, the authors mention that LoRAN enhances the performance of downstream tasks significantly. However, it is not clear how the significance of these improvements has been calculated. It would be great if the authors could use different seeds for the QLoRA experiments to estimate the variance of downstream metrics and estimate the statistical significance of these improvements.
705.llm_review: Experiment, Performance: The empirical scope is narrow—only two datasets (one summarization, one classification), with no evaluation on larger or more diverse benchmarks, limiting conclusions about generalization. Comparisons are restricted to QLoRA; there are no head-to-head results against stronger PEFT baselines that target expressivity under tight budgets (e.g., parameter budgeting or improved decompositions cited in the paper), leaving the relative performance unclear. Claims about matching full-rank capacity are not supported by direct experiments (e.g., parity with full fine-tuning on any task). Finally, while the paper mentions a small time overhead, there is no quantitative profiling of inference latency or memory usage, which is important for performance claims in PEFT contexts.

706.human_review: This paper proposes a new self-jailbreaking method called IRIS, which enables a single language model to act as both the attacker and the target. The iterative refinement and self-explanation steps are distinctive compared to previous jailbreaking methods.
706.llm_review: IRIS presents a simple yet novel two-stage method that uses a single black-box LLM as both attacker and target. The iterative self-explanation step is a pragmatic mechanism to refine prompts without adversarial suffixes, keeping the attack interpretable and conversational. The subsequent rate-and-enhance step leverages the models own internal assessment to systematically increase harmfulness, yielding a clear, modular pipeline that is easy to implement and reason about. The approach is query-efficient and avoids white-box assumptions, aligning well with real-world threat models.

707.human_review: IRIS achieves near-perfect jailbreak success rates (98% on GPT-4, 92% on GPT-4 Turbo) with significantly fewer queries (under 7 on average) compared to state-of-the-art methods like TAP and PAIR. The experiments comprehensively validate the effectiveness of IRIS.
707.llm_review: The experimental evaluation is comprehensive for a black-box setting: results on GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo show large gains in ASR and substantial query savings over PAIR and TAP; human evaluation (instead of an automated judge) is used to decide success; ablations isolate the contribution of the rate-and-enhance step; and transfer tests to Claude 3 (Opus/Sonnet) probe generalization. Reporting both single-run and two-run (IRIS-2x) results, along with query counts, strengthens the empirical validation.

708.human_review: The paper is well-organized and clearly written. The figures, such as the diagram of the IRIS method in Figure 1, effectively illustrate the proposed approach. Notations and formulations are properly defined, enhancing the readability of the paper.
708.llm_review: The paper provides a clear, stepwise exposition supported by an intuitive pipeline diagram and concise pseudo-code. The figure effectively communicates the control flow from iterative refinement to rating and enhancement, and Algorithm 1 mirrors that flow, making the method easy to follow and reproduce from the description.

709.human_review: While IRIS introduces a new self-jailbreaking method, the paper does not provide a clear justification for why and how the proposed modifications, such as the iterative refinement and self-explanation steps, effectively address the limitations of existing jailbreaking methods.
709.llm_review: Key claims would benefit from stronger justification. The central premise that self-explanation suppresses safety refusals is asserted but not mechanistically explained or probed (e.g., via prompt ablations or behavioral analysis). The 15 harmfulness rating is assumed to be meaningful and self-consistent across models, yet its validity is not justified beyond observed performance. The JAILBROKEN detection during refinement relies on a >20-word heuristic that is weakly tied to harmfulness, while the headline successes emphasize near-perfect jailbreak rates. Together, these choices leave a gap between the procedural criteria and the claimed causal explanation (latent knowledge, self-jailbreaking efficacy).

710.human_review: The experiments in this paper only compare IRIS with TAP and PAIR. More recent and stronger baselines need to be added to reflect the comprehensiveness of the experiments. The authors should also provide a more detailed discussion about the intended incremental contributions of IRIS above and beyond existing research.
710.llm_review: Baselines and comparisons are limited relative to the scope of the claims. Only PAIR and TAP are included; other competitive black-box attacks (e.g., instruction-attack variants, fine-tuned prompt generators like PAP, recent search-based red-teaming, or safety-filter evasion techniques) are excluded or dismissed without empirical comparison. The experimental design rests on 50 AdvBench prompts and a single in-house annotator for success labels, with no inter-annotator study beyond a brief tutorial, and no statistical testing or confidence intervals. As a result, the contributionwhile practically impactfulreads as an incremental variant of iterative prompt refinement (self-explain + self-rate) without sufficient breadth of baselines or robustness checks (e.g., across newer API checkpoints, additional model families, or larger/more diverse datasets) to firmly establish superiority.

711.human_review: The paper shows that the models enhanced with DEFT show improved alignment capabilities and generalization abilities compared to previous methods. This suggests that DEFT can effectively maintain or improve a model’s performance while better adhering to desired human values.
711.llm_review: Generalization, Model, Performance: The framework preserves or improves generalization while aligning preferences. On MT-Bench with GPT-4 judging, DEFT notably boosts DPO (e.g., aggregate average rises from ~5.55 to ~7.53 with consistent gains across Writing, Roleplay, Coding, STEM, and Humanity), indicating that distribution-level guidance can strengthen instruction-following without sacrificing model breadth. The approach integrates cleanly with Llama3-8B-based PRO/DPO pipelines and yields stable improvements on multiple axes rather than narrow, task-specific gains.

712.human_review: One significant advantage noted is the reduction in training time when using DEFT. This can make the process more efficient
712.llm_review: Efficiency, Training: DEFT achieves efficiency through two mechanisms: (i) pre-computed distribution rewards select a small high-quality subset (top 5%) that outperforms training on the full dataset, and (ii) adding the reward term to the loss accelerates alignment by steering updates toward preference-relevant tokens. The ablation and data-volume study show that 5% of the data is near-optimal for the compute–performance trade-off, reducing training steps and time while improving scores, which is attractive for practical fine-tuning regimes.

713.human_review: Data filtering is quite important and this paper proposes new method on automatic filtering instead of labor intense human filtering
713.llm_review: Data, Method: The discrepancy distribution (token-frequency difference between chosen vs. rejected responses) combined with the model’s averaged log-prob distribution defines a simple, model-agnostic distribution reward. This dual use—for data filtering and as an auxiliary training signal—provides an elegant, easily pluggable method that augments existing alignment algorithms (PRO/DPO) without architectural changes or RL infrastructure, and it is supported by ablations isolating each component’s contribution.

714.human_review: How are the positive and negative distributions, Q_{+} and Q_{-}, derived? Are these distributions based on word frequencies from the data? Can you provide a more detailed explanation?
714.llm_review: Data, Detail, Explanation: Important implementation details are under-specified. It is unclear how tokenization, stopword handling, and normalization affect the discrepancy distribution; how thresholds are set when mapping ranked responses to positive/negative bins; how the ω coefficient is tuned; and how negative values in Qdiff are stabilized during training. The data curation process (e.g., ChatGPT-augmented D3, filtering percent selection criteria) and human evaluation protocol (annotator guidelines, inter-annotator agreement) need more explicit description.

715.human_review: It would be beneficial to elaborate on how word frequency effectively addresses distributional rewards. Considering that the context in which words are used may be more critical than the words themselves, do you have any insights or statistical evidence to support this approach?
715.llm_review: Evidence: Claims of efficiency and stability would benefit from stronger evidence. The paper lacks wall-clock time, GPU-hours, and convergence speed comparisons across runs, and does not report variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance for automatic metrics, MT-Bench, or human evaluations. Heavy reliance on proxy reward models and GPT-4-as-judge introduces evaluator bias risks without robustness checks (e.g., alternative judges/reward models).

716.human_review: I wonder if the proposed framework is more effective when applied to reinforcement learning-based alignment methods such as PPO, beyond just comparing it with DPO or PRO.
716.llm_review: Comparison, Effectiveness, Framework: The empirical comparison is limited to integrating DEFT with PRO and DPO on a single base model and dataset family. It omits strong RL-free/alignment baselines and data-selection approaches (e.g., RRHF, ORPO/IPO/KTO/SimPO, inference-time methods), making it hard to assess framework-level superiority. Cross-model generality (other base LLMs) and cross-domain datasets are absent, which weakens claims of broad effectiveness.

717.human_review: As mentioned in Appendix A, the inference length is set to 128. Were the MT Bench results also based on this length? It seems that a length of 128 might be insufficient for obtaining good score in the MT Bench evaluation.
717.llm_review: Benchmark, Evaluation, Result: BLEU and BARTScore are not ideal for preference alignment quality; modifying references with ChatGPT can bias evaluation and blur comparability. The reward metric relies on a single external reward model, raising reward hacking concerns. MT-Bench results use GPT-4 judging without reporting prompt/judging configurations or agreement checks. Stronger, standardized alignment/safety benchmarks (e.g., Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval, safety stress tests) and significance analyses would make results more convincing.

718.human_review: Have you considered using larger or more advanced reward models? If so, is there any notable difference in performance?
718.llm_review: Model, Performance: Improvements are sometimes modest and uneven across subsets. For instance, in D3 the harmlessness reward for DEFT-DPO drops relative to DPO, and DEFT-PRO shows category-specific regressions versus SFT/PRO in MT-Bench. The mixed per-category outcomes and small absolute gains in some settings temper the performance claims and suggest the method’s benefits may be sensitive to task composition and metric choice.

719.human_review: The difficulty of evaluation NFQA lies in the lack of clear borderline of correctness. Putting too many criteria or constitutions in the evaluation prompts would hinder LLMs from upvoting the better answers due to commonly known problems such as recency bias and limitations in prompts lengths. **LINKAGE tackles this by transferring these onerous meta-instructions into multi-grade ground truths or synthetic reference answers, which forms a clear spectrum for LLMs to rank the candidate answers.**
719.llm_review: Evaluation and Prompt: The paper designs a clear, task-aligned listwise judging prompt that asks the LLM to place a candidate answer within a descending-quality reference list, which matches the evaluation objective and reduces ambiguities inherent in absolute scoring. The authors systematically explore zero-shot vs. few-shot prompting and show that few-shot exemplars consistently improve correlations, indicating the prompt effectively communicates evaluation criteria. They also present the prompt setup for constructing varied-quality references and, in the single/no-GT settings, explicitly generate all references via LLMs to reduce human–machine style mismatch. The evaluation uses multiple rank-correlation metrics (Kendall’s tau, Spearman’s rho, Pearson’s r) and includes bias-aware measures in baselines (e.g., randomizing order in pairwise), demonstrating attention to prompt and evaluation design details.

720.human_review: Comprehensive experiments, ablation study and case study could to some degree support their claims.
720.llm_review: Ablation and Experiment: The experiments span three NFQA datasets and three supervision regimes (multi-grade, single-grade, and no ground truth), consistently showing higher correlation with human judgments than automatic metrics and pointwise/pairwise LLM evaluators. The ablations on reference-list composition (length and grade distribution) are informative—uniform sampling across grades works best, and the optimal list length depends on dataset quality/noise. Robustness to reference sampling randomness is quantified with small standard deviations across runs. Few-shot vs. zero-shot analyses demonstrate the benefit of in-context examples. The WebGLM study additionally measures accuracy at selecting best/worst answers, further validating the approach across task variants.

721.human_review: The proposed method is a LLM-based evaluation method. LLM-as-Judge is biased in evaluating predictions from different LLMs. Analysis should be added with different (open-weight) models, **which could be more appreciated by the open-source community**.
721.llm_review: Analysis, Evaluation, Method, Model: (1) LLM-as-judge biases are not fully analyzed for the listwise setting: while pairwise baselines randomize positions, the listwise prompt relies on an ordered reference list labeled Best/Good/Average/Poor, which can induce anchoring or position bias; permutation tests of the reference order and alternative label phrasings would strengthen claims. (2) Cost/scalability is underexplored: listwise evaluation requires long contexts and per-question reference construction (sometimes with GPT-4), yet no token/latency/cost analysis is provided to substantiate the claimed efficiency over pairwise. (3) The human-evaluation footprint is relatively small (e.g., 55 TREC-DL-NF questions; 50 WebGLM cases with three answers), and there are no formal significance tests across randomizations, limiting statistical confidence. (4) Hyperparameter sensitivity is not studied (e.g., temperature fixed at 0.8 for evaluation), nor are context-length limits or truncation effects analyzed—important for long-form NFQA. (5) Model coverage is narrow: results rely on Mistral-7B and GPT-3.5 as judges; evaluating stronger/different families (e.g., GPT-4, Claude, larger Llama) would better assess generality and mitigate potential style bias when the judge is related to reference generators. (6) Methodological clarity could be improved on how ranks are mapped to numeric scores for correlation and how per-question outputs are aggregated, as calibration to human scales is only briefly illustrated.

722.human_review: The proposed method is, to some degree, **lack of novelty**. From the first point of the strength part, this could be perceived as a choice of engineering method in evaluation question answering with more subjectiveness, which is believed to be mentioned in prior works. Besides, I do not see the essential difference between LINKAGE and the pointwise approach with references as they are both input with sorted lists of references.
722.llm_review: Method, Novelty, Related Work: The core idea—moving from pointwise/pairwise to listwise ranking for evaluation—largely adapts classic learning-to-rank concepts to LLM judging without substantial new algorithmic elements or theoretical analysis, so the novelty is incremental. The related work could better situate LINKAGE among recent LLM evaluation frameworks and preference aggregation/calibration methods (e.g., Bradley–Terry/Plackett–Luce models, tournament-style aggregation, reward-model-based judges like PairRM, G-Eval, MT-Bench/Arena-style calibration, or debiasing approaches). A direct empirical comparison or discussion of why listwise with fixed references is preferable to these alternatives would clarify the distinctive contribution.

723.human_review: This paper introduces the first pitch-based similarity representation, a novel and innovative approach that will significantly facilitate tone research.
723.llm_review: Novelty: The paper introduces Tone2Vec, a representation that maps five-scale tone transcriptions to smooth pitch curves and measures similarity via area-between-curves, alongside a pitch-based loss for training. Coupled with a simple linearity-based rule for variable-length inference, this constitutes a novel, domain-appropriate approach that enables the first reported end-to-end pipeline for cross-dialect tone transcription and clustering, with promising empirical gains on dialect clustering and automatic transcription.

724.human_review: The authors have collected data from Jianghuai Mandarin, thereby extending the toolkit to achieve better dialectal coverage.
724.llm_review: Data: The work assembles two complementary resources focused on Jianghuai Mandarin: 2,238 expert-labeled recordings across 11 dialects (with age/sex stratification) for modeling, and 31,000 five-scale transcriptions across 31 dialect regions for analysis. Despite modest size, the datasets capture cross-regional variation and provide a practical low-resource testbed for tone transcription and dialect clustering/variance studies where open data are scarce.

725.human_review: The authors present a lightweight framework for practical use, making it highly beneficial to a group of researchers.
725.llm_review: Framework: The study delivers a coherent, end-to-end framework spanning representation (Tone2Vec), modeling (automatic transcription with variable-length inference), and unsupervised categorization (clustering on learned embeddings), integrated into an accessible toolkit (ToneLab) with APIs for documentation and analysis. The modular design supports pretrained or user-trained models and facilitates cross-regional, cross-lexical analyses, enhancing practical utility.

726.human_review: The authors placed most of the implementation and design details of Tone2Vec into the appendix. While I understand the constraints of page limits, this makes it challenging to grasp the complete picture when reading the main text. I suggest including more details in the camera-ready version.
726.llm_review: Detail, Implementation: Important implementation specifics are missing or insufficiently documented, hindering reproducibility: MFCC configuration (window, hop, coefficients), model hyperparameters and training schedules, the method for choosing the linearity threshold b2, and DBSCAN parameter selection are only briefly stated. The evaluation protocol for transcription "accuracy" under relative pitch equivalence and the formal definition of the Variance metric need fuller specification. There are minor equation inconsistencies (e.g., loss sign and duplicated length-three cases), and results lack confidence intervals and ablations.

727.human_review: I personally feel that some of the design choices require additional justification. For the tone transcription task, the authors employed ResNet, VGG, and DenseNet. Why were these models specifically chosen? A common factor is that all three models are CNN-based. What role does convolution play in this context? These aspects might need further clarification.
727.llm_review: Justification, Model: Several modeling choices are weakly justified. Constraining the decoder to three outputs and inferring sequence length via a linearity threshold may be brittle; the MAE surrogate for area-based distance is asserted but not rigorously validated against alternatives. The choice of MFCC-based CNNs is not compared to stronger speech representations (e.g., wav2vec 2.0) or sequence objectives (e.g., CTC variants). DBSCAN is adopted without comparison to other clustering approaches. The dialect-clustering baseline (exact-match vs non-match) is weak, leaving uncertainty about gains versus stronger baselines (e.g., Levenshtein-based or learned embeddings) and about generalization beyond the limited held-out regions.

728.human_review: The problem of alignment is very relevant right now and the extension of preference optimization to more languages is therefore a timely and important contribution.
728.llm_review: The paper makes a clear and substantive contribution by systematically extending preference optimization to a multilingual setting across 23 languages. It disentangles key factors for multilingual alignment—data sources and coverage, online vs. offline optimization, and cross-lingual transfer—and demonstrates that standard RLHF techniques (notably RLOO) can yield strong cross-lingual gains. The work advances the state of practice by showing that multilingual preference training is not only feasible but materially improves over English-only alignment and prior multilingual RLHF efforts.

729.human_review: In an increasingly multilingual setting, it is not obvious that the existing preference optimization techniques would be as effective. This papers shows that these techniques can still be effective and propose a new method to more reliably generate multilingual feedback data based on translation.
729.llm_review: Data: The paper introduces a scalable multilingual preference dataset construction pipeline that blends in-language generations (Command R+) with translated outputs (Command) to increase response diversity and steer away from translationese. It explores multiple mixtures (EN-1, ML-5, ML-23 with fixed and expanded budgets) and reports high RM–GPT-4-Turbo agreement across languages, lending credibility to labels. Effectiveness: The data leads to consistent gains in win-rates over the base model and competitive open-weight baselines, with clear evidence that broader language coverage improves multilingual performance and cross-lingual transfer. Method: The study carefully controls for data size and language coverage and ties them to outcomes under both DPO and RLOO, yielding actionable guidance on dataset design.

730.human_review: The results are clear and useful for practitioners.
730.llm_review: Clarity: The claims are clearly stated and supported by well-structured figures/tables, explicit training details (e.g., KL penalties, learning rates, epochs, sampling temperatures), and a transparent evaluation protocol with randomized output order and judge prompts. Result: Results are reported comprehensively: average and language-specific win-rates, cross-lingual transfer to unseen languages, ablations on data mixtures, and a discussion of reward over-optimization. The findings (e.g., RLOO outperforming DPO and multilingual data benefiting English) are presented with interpretable metrics and caveats.

731.human_review: The paper is well written and easy to follow  and the methodology seems sound.
731.llm_review: Method: The experimental design is thoughtful—benchmarking DPO vs. an online RL method (RLOO), controlling the number of training languages under a fixed budget, and expanding to a larger budget to probe scaling. Using a separate multilingual RM from the LLM-as-a-judge reduces evaluation bias, and hyperparameter sweeps improve methodological robustness. Presentation: The narrative ties design choices to outcomes (e.g., contrastive nature of RLOO aiding transfer), includes negative findings (reward model over-optimization), and contextualizes results with relevant literature, making the methodology and its implications easy to follow.

732.human_review: The approach still relies on translated prompts meaning that differences in the types of preferences based on culture are not accounted for.
732.llm_review: Approach, Prompt: The prompting and data-generation pipeline leans heavily on machine-translated ShareGPT prompts and translated completions, which may encode translationese and Western-centric topical biases. Although the method attempts to steer away from translation artifacts via in-language generations and ranking, the approach may still conflate translation quality with preference quality, especially in lower-resource languages. The reliance on synthetic preferences and closed models (Command/Command R+) for generations and a closed-source RM for ranking limits auditability of prompt distributions and could underrepresent culturally specific or safety-critical prompts.

733.human_review: I can imagine that randomly selecting another 5 languages will lead to different results compared to using all 23 languages. I would be more convinced if different subsets of 5 languages where tested also and then the average result was compared to using all 23 languages, for instance.
733.llm_review: Comparison, Result: The primary comparisons hinge on judge-based win-rates (GPT-4-Turbo) without sufficiently extensive human evaluation or statistical significance testing across languages. While the paper compares against popular 7–8B instruction-tuned models, it omits stronger multilingual baselines trained explicitly with preference optimization in comparable settings, and provides limited per-language error analysis. Using the same RM family for data creation and RLOO optimization raises potential fairness concerns (even though a separate LLM judge is used), and the results do not quantify sensitivity to the RM choice. Broader metrics (safety, toxicity, robustness) are also not reported, which narrows the interpretability of the claimed gains.

734.human_review: a new dataset on coping strategies that involved generating controversial scenarios about abortion, immigration, racism, LGBTQ, and drugs using GPT4 and two crowdsourcing tasks
734.llm_review: The paper contributes a new, well-structured dataset (COPING) targeting a rarely available signal: coping strategies linked to emotions. The corpus is balanced across four strategies and five sensitive topics with multiple scenarios per topic, and it contains multiple aligned views per instance (verbal reply, non-verbal behavior, and Likert ratings for 16 emotions). Useful metadata such as topic and power relation are included, enabling controlled analyses. The resource is released with code and an ethics statement, increasing its utility for the community.

735.llm_review: The paper offers thoughtful analyses tied to annotation quality. It quantifies alignment between strategy and emotion ratings (Cram�e9r's V), distinguishes character vs. self-reported emotions with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and conducts an in-house inter-annotator agreement study (Fleiss' ba) on strategy recognition from text. The token-level distributional analysis (via Jensen-Shannon divergence) helps interpret which strategies exhibit clearer linguistic markers. These steps provide transparent, data-driven insight into what is and is not reliably annotated.

736.human_review: example analyses using several models, including both non-generative and generative LLM methods
736.llm_review: Methodologically, the study scopes the task carefully and benchmarks both fine-tuned SLMs (BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa) and zero-shot LLMs (phi-2, mistral-2, dolphin-2, nous-hermes) with consistent inputs (answers, behaviors, concatenation). Analyses break down performance by input type, topic, and label, revealing that non-verbal behavior descriptions can be more predictive than replies and that contact is easier than reject. The modeling setup and reporting are systematic and help clarify where signal resides.

737.human_review: there is an experimental test of Roseman's theory that relates coping strategies to emotions
737.llm_review: Experiments are directly driven by psychological theory (Roseman), and the role-playing design operationalizes theoretical constructs into observable linguistic behavior. The RQs are clearly posed, and the empirical tests probe whether coping strategies manifest in text and whether models can detect them. The partial alignment found between theory-driven emotion groupings and observed ratings provides a concrete bridge from theory to experiment.

738.human_review: the annotator agreement was fairly low.  I think that there is still benefit in results publishing that are not always positive, but I do think this warrants a bit more discussion. E.g., maybe Roseman's strategies are not the best way to classify coping, maybe strategies are non-exclusive, maybe annotators should have an "unsure" flag, etc.
738.llm_review: Despite careful design, results are modest: best F1 scores remain below ~0.55 and inter-annotator agreement on strategy recognition is only fair overall, with some labels near chance. The discussion could better contextualize these outcomes by offering a deeper error analysis, examining confounds (e.g., politeness/toxicity proxies for contact/attack), and clarifying what practical inferences are warranted at this performance level. Additional analyses of generalization (e.g., across topics or to naturally occurring data) would strengthen the implications of the results.

739.human_review: the appendix mentions that the coping annotation changed from round to round. I think this should have been mentioned in the text body.
739.llm_review: Gold labels for strategy are induced by role prompts rather than established through independent consensus annotation, and the external annotation study is small (100 texts) with low agreement, especially for reject. Earlier description-validation rounds also showed difficulty (e.g., only ~52% recognition for reject), suggesting construct clarity remains an issue. Priming effects from character descriptions and scenario wording (LLM-generated) may bias annotators, and there is limited evidence of adjudication or annotator training to stabilize the label space.

740.human_review: This paper presents a simple idea of incorporating both direct answers and contextual information when retrieving documents for LFQA. The combination of direct answers and contextual information documents improves the recall of relevant documents, QA performance, and the groundness of the answer.
740.llm_review: Method and improvement: The paper proposes a simple yet effective weak-supervision scheme (SILVER) that combines long-form answers (LFAs) and direct answers (DAs) to select silver passages for training a cross-encoder re-ranker. This method explicitly targets both direct answer evidence and broader contextual information in one shot, which is well-aligned with the needs of LFQA. Empirically, it yields consistent end-to-end gains over a DPR baseline on ASQA (DR 35.5 vs. 34.3; ROUGE-L 43.4 vs. 42.5; D-F1 29.0 vs. 27.7) and improves contextual recall (Wikipage recall 0.516 vs. 0.450). It also substantially boosts groundedness (0.858 vs. 0.763 on ASQA; 0.839 vs. 0.726 on CONVMIX) and improves follow-up answer recall on CONVMIX (0.306 vs. 0.260), indicating the method’s utility for anticipating conversational follow-ups. The approach reaches state-of-the-art DR on ASQA with Vicuna-13B while remaining computationally light due to effective lexical matching.

741.human_review: The paper is well-written and easy to follow, with additional experiment details in the Appendix.
741.llm_review: Clarity, experiments, and presentation: The problem is clearly motivated (standard retrievers miss context needed for LFQA), and the methodology is described with sufficient detail to reproduce the pipeline (candidate retrieval, silver passage selection, BERT re-ranking, Vicuna-13B generation). The experimental setup is easy to follow, with well-chosen metrics for both answer quality (ROUGE-L, D-F1, DR) and grounding, plus retrieval recalls tailored to direct and contextual evidence. The paper includes ablations across multiple weak-supervision strategies (DA-only, LFA lexical, LFA semantic, LFA perplexity, and the combined SILVER), clear tables for both ASQA and CONVMIX, and qualitative examples that concretely illustrate reduced hallucinations and better grounding. The analysis (e.g., per-turn recall plot) and limitations section improve readability and transparency.

742.human_review: The generalization of the proposed method might be limited. The proposed method is only based on the ASQA dataset with annotated long-form answers (LFAs) and direct answers (DA). When annotated long-form answers are not available, it is still a fundamental challenge to obtain the training data for the retriever.
742.llm_review: Data, generalization, and training: The approach is validated on two Wikipedia-centric datasets (ASQA and CONVMIX), leaving open questions about generalization to other domains, corpora, or information needs (e.g., ELI5, QAMPARI, non-Wikipedia sources). The training signal requires access to LFAs to construct silver passages, which may limit applicability where long-form annotations are scarce. Because silver labels are derived via lexical overlap with LFAs (and DAs), the retriever may be biased toward lexically similar content, potentially inflating metrics that rely on lexical matching (e.g., groundedness, ROUGE-L). The study fine-tunes a single LLM (Vicuna-13B) and relies on DPR for first-stage retrieval, so it remains unclear how robust the training recipe is across different backbone LLMs or retrieval stacks, or whether gains persist under domain shift.

743.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Effectiveness, Experiment, Improvement, Method
743.human_review: The improvement of the proposed method is marginal, with about 1-2% improvement. In addition, the experiments do not compare with other reranker models, making the effectiveness of the proposed method under-measured.
743.llm_review: Comparison, effectiveness, experiments, improvement, method: While the paper compares several weak-supervision variants for re-ranking, comparisons to stronger modern retrieval/reranking baselines are limited. The first-stage retriever is DPR; there is no evaluation against contemporary dense or hybrid retrievers (e.g., Contriever, GTR/T5-based retrievers, SPLADE, ColBERTv2/hybrids) or stronger cross-encoders (e.g., monoT5, E5 rerankers) and LLM-based rerankers. The reported end-to-end gains on ASQA, though consistent, are modest (e.g., +1.2 DR absolute vs. DPR), and there is no statistical significance analysis or sensitivity study (e.g., top-k retrieved, number of silver passages k, negatives, or effect of first-stage choice). The method itself is straightforward and largely heuristic (lexical matching proves strongest), so additional experiments that isolate where the improvement comes from (beyond ablations already shown), test human judgments of long-form quality, and probe robustness across architectures and corpora would strengthen the claims about effectiveness.

744.human_review: The paper introduces PsyGUARD, an automated system for suicide detection and risk assessment in psychological counseling, showcasing advancements in fine-grained taxonomy development, dataset creation, and benchmark establishment.
744.llm_review: Strong combination of Benchmark and Data: The paper contributes PsyGUARD, a large-scale Chinese dataset (14.8k utterances) with 11 fine-grained, action/thought-aware classes and limited multi-labeling, aggregated from multiple sources (Weibo, Zhihu, Yixinli, and open-source counseling dialogues). The annotation pipeline is carefully designed (initial training, iterative labeling, adjudication, quality control) with substantial agreement in large batches (Fleiss’ kappa > 0.7). Alongside, the authors provide comprehensive benchmarks spanning zero/few-shot LLMs and fine-tuned encoder models, enabling reproducible comparisons and establishing a solid baseline for counseling-oriented suicide risk detection.

745.human_review: Empirical results provide valuable insights into the performance of automated systems in detecting suicide risk, contributing to understanding the capabilities and limitations of such technologies in personalized risk assessment.
745.llm_review: Performance and Result are clearly reported and compelling: Fine-tuned models substantially outperform prompting. ChatGLM2-6B with LoRA reaches about 92% accuracy (best ~91.99%), and RoBERTa-large achieves ~91.7%, while the best prompting baseline (GPT-4 zero-shot) attains ~75%. Results include micro and macro metrics plus an error analysis (e.g., sensitivity to suicide-related terms, confusion between exploration and intent), providing a transparent picture of strengths and failure modes.

746.key_points: Strength: Benchmark, Data, Framework, Method, Related Work
746.human_review: The paper's clear organization, including sections on related works, taxonomy construction, data collection processes, benchmarks, and risk assessment frameworks, aids technical readers in comprehending the research context and methodology.
746.llm_review: Coherent integration across Benchmark, Data, Framework, Method, and Related Work: The paper is well-situated in prior taxonomies (e.g., C-SSRS, 4-level, binary), articulates why counseling-specific, fine-grained labels are needed, and proposes a theory-informed 11-class taxonomy. It delivers the PsyGUARD dataset, methodologically diverse baselines (prompting, full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning), and a practical risk assessment framework for triage. Together, these elements form a clear, end-to-end research pipeline that advances the area and is useful to both practitioners and researchers.

747.human_review: Limited dataset diversity may hinder the generalizability of the proposed system, impacting its scalability and effectiveness across different demographics and cultural backgrounds.
747.llm_review: Data, Effectiveness, and Generalization limitations: A large portion of the corpus derives from Chinese social media and open-source counseling dialogues, which may not fully reflect real, diverse counseling sessions. The work does not evaluate end-to-end effectiveness (e.g., counselor outcomes, response time, safety events), and there is no assessment of cross-demographic, cross-lingual, or cross-platform generalization, limiting confidence in real-world impact.

748.human_review: Absence of tailored models for fine-grained suicide prevention in counseling services poses a challenge, potentially limiting the system's precision and adaptability in real-world scenarios.
748.llm_review: Adaptation and Model gaps: Although the target is counseling, the core modeling is largely single-utterance classification without conversation-level context, personalization, or clinician-validated calibration. The risk assessment component is presented as a rule-guided/LLM prompting template rather than a trained, integrated module, making adaptation to varied counseling workflows and sustained supervision less convincing.

749.human_review: Issues with data format and biases in existing datasets raise concerns about the dataset's robustness and representativeness, affecting the reliability and reproducibility of the study's results.
749.llm_review: Data and Robustness concerns: The dataset is highly imbalanced (e.g., very few ‘Suicidal Preparatory Act’ cases), yet the training regime does not explicitly address imbalance, and per-class results are not reported. Robustness to figurative language, sarcasm, typos, code-switching, or adversarial phrasing is not tested, leaving uncertainty about stability under noisy, real counseling inputs.

750.human_review: Lack of a holistic risk assessment framework for diverse suicide categories may restrict the system's predictive accuracy and practical utility in counseling interventions.
750.llm_review: Accuracy and Framework risks for safety-critical use: While micro-level metrics are high, macro F1 is notably lower (around 70% for the best fine-tuned models), and the analysis does not quantify false negatives in the most critical classes. There is no calibration analysis, precision–recall trade-off study, or thresholding strategy. The proposed risk assessment framework lacks empirical validation of escalation criteria, alert latency, and operator burden—key requirements for safe deployment.

751.human_review: While insightful, the study's perceived impact within computational linguistics and mental health support systems may be constrained, potentially affecting its visibility and significance among the readers.
751.llm_review: Significance is moderate: The taxonomy extends known schemes, the benchmarks use standard models, and the resource is limited to the Chinese setting. Without stronger clinical validation, deployment studies, or cross-lingual extensions, the impact is more incremental than transformative for the broader *ACL community.

752.human_review: Innovative Approach: The paper's proposal of an iterative selection mechanism that integrates zero-shot CoT reasoning represents a significant advancement in the area of in-context learning.
752.llm_review: Approach and novelty: The paper introduces a simple, training-free retrieval scheme that selects in-context demonstrations by matching training examples to the model’s zero-shot chain-of-thought (reasoning path) for the test query, rather than to the raw input. This reasoning-aligned retrieval is an original angle that operationalizes the long-discussed trade-off between similarity and diversity: the CoT-driven similarity anchors demos to the test case, while iterative updates to the reasoning path naturally inject diversity across iterations. The method is model- and parameter-agnostic (no logits or gradients), requires only a lightweight embedding model for KNN, and integrates seamlessly with standard prompting and majority voting, making it broadly applicable.

753.human_review: Empirical Validation: The method has been robustly tested across multiple tasks, showing that it not only improves accuracy but also effectively balances diversity and similarity in the selection process.
753.llm_review: Accuracy, method, and validation: IDS consistently outperforms strong baselines across six benchmarks (BoolQ, GSM8K, MATH, CommonsenseQA, LogiQA, AGNews), with an average accuracy of 69.8% vs. 68.1% for the best baseline (Top-k-Consistency), and notably larger gains on reasoning-heavy datasets (e.g., GSM8K 78.5 vs. 76.1; MATH 37.5 vs. 35.6). The evaluation is careful: five seeds to reduce randomness, matched numbers of iterations/decoding paths across baselines, and comparisons against both classical and recent selection methods (e.g., Vote-k, MMR, G-fair-Prompting, Skill-KNN). Robustness is shown across model families and scales (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama-2-chat 7B/13B/70B), indicating the method’s reliability beyond a single API.

754.human_review: Detailed Quantitative Analysis: The inclusion of detailed quantitative analyses, such as the comparison of average similarity scores between selected demonstrations and test samples, provides a strong empirical basis for the claimed improvements.
754.llm_review: Analysis: The paper provides clear diagnostics on why the approach works. It first motivates the task-specific nature of the diversity vs. similarity trade-off with pilot results, then shows IDS achieves a middle ground in similarity scores between random and top-k methods. Additional analyses explore iteration count effects (q=1,5,7), model robustness (GPT-4, open-source Llama-2), and qualitative case studies illustrating how iterative selection avoids misleading similar demos and corrects earlier mistakes. Appendices further examine the number of shots, embedding models, and Zero-shot-CoT triggers, painting a well-rounded picture of behavior and robustness.

755.human_review: Need for Ablation Studies: Despite detailed analyses, the paper could be strengthened by including comprehensive ablation studies that delineate the contribution of each component of the IDS methodology to the overall performance. This would offer deeper insights into the essential elements of the approach and validate the necessity of each iterative step.
755.llm_review: Ablation, method, and validation: While the paper includes several analyses, it lacks targeted ablations to isolate the contribution of each component. In particular: (1) a direct comparison of selecting demos via the reasoning path vs. via the original query under identical decoding and voting would clarify the source of gains; (2) an ablation of iteration mechanics (one-time selection with multiple samples vs. reselecting every round) would quantify the value of iterative re-retrieval; (3) removing majority voting or reasoning generation during inference would show their marginal contributions; (4) a study of alternative rationale strategies (e.g., manual-CoT, shorter rationales, or no-CoT selection) would test dependence on rationale quality. From a validation standpoint, results rely on subsampled test sets due to cost; adding statistical significance tests and a cost/latency breakdown (API calls, context length growth, retrieval time) would strengthen claims about efficiency and practical reliability.

756.human_review: Generalization Concerns: The paper primarily focuses on a single model architecture (GPT-3.5), and while it hints at broader applicability, demonstrations of effectiveness across a range of models or further validation on open-source models could enhance the paper's impact and generalization claims.
756.llm_review: Application, architecture, generalization, and model: Practical deployment may be hindered by iterative reasoning generation, which increases API calls and latency and could stress context windows when demonstrations and rationales are long. The approach assumes models produce useful zero-shot CoT; weaker or non-CoT-friendly models, multilingual settings, or domains with noisy rationales may degrade selection quality. The retrieval backbone uses general-purpose SBERT embeddings and a single KNN strategy; domain shift, long-document inputs, or structured generation tasks are not evaluated. Although results span multiple LLMs, applications beyond English short-form QA/classification and arithmetic/logic reasoning remain untested, and no guidance is provided for adapting the method to long-context or non-text tasks where memory and retrieval strategies might need architectural adjustments.

757.human_review: The proposed reverse instructions generation process, though a simple idea, seems to  be empirically effective for long text generation task.
757.llm_review: Effectiveness: The approach delivers strong empirical gains on long-form generation. LongForm models consistently outperform prior instruction-tuned baselines (e.g., FLAN-T5, T0++, Tk-Instruct) and even surpass a 10x larger untuned model (OPT-30B) across in-domain and out-of-domain settings, with large relative METEOR improvements (reported ~63% in-domain and ~35% OOD).

758.human_review: Authors addressed the previous concerns raised by reviewers by including the ablation study demonstrating the effectiveness of reverse instructions.
758.llm_review: Ablation and Effectiveness: The subset ablations (NLP vs. NLP+SC vs. NLP+RI vs. all) clearly attribute the majority of the NLG gains to the Reverse Instructions subset. Including RI yields the best NLG scores and slightly improves or maintains NLU (MMLU), supporting the claim that reverse-instruction data is the key driver of effectiveness.

759.human_review: The paper is overall well written and well organized.1. Though ablation study shows that RI helps, but it only helps in NLG but not NLU. This raises the question on effectiveness of the RI generation process specifically for the NLU task.
759.llm_review: Ablation, Effectiveness, Presentation: The paper presents ablations and cross-dataset evaluations in a clear, easy-to-interpret manner (separate tables for in-domain, OOD, and FLAN vs. LongForm comparisons). This presentation makes the effectiveness claims traceable to specific dataset components and helps readers understand where the gains come from.

760.human_review: With the recent updates in LLMs generation capabilities, I am skeptical whether the proposed  reverse instructions is still needed and its overall effectiveness. It would be nice to try out on newer versions of similar sized LLMs such as Llama2.
760.llm_review: Effectiveness and Model: The method works across multiple backbones (encoder-decoder T5-3B and decoder-only OPT-6.7B/LLaMA-7B), showing parameter-efficient improvements and consistent benefits. Small architectural details (e.g., [EOI] token for autoregressive models) and straightforward finetuning yield large effectiveness gains without scaling model size.

761.human_review: Though ablation study shows that RI helps, but it only helps in NLG but not NLU. This raises the question on effectiveness of the RI generation process specifically for the NLU task.
761.llm_review: Ablation, Effectiveness, Task: While the subset ablations are informative, they do not isolate key design choices within Reverse Instructions (e.g., instruction style templates, length-control prompts) or quantify their individual contributions. Task-wise, effectiveness is demonstrated mainly on three OOD long-form generation datasets with automatic metrics; there is no comprehensive human evaluation of generated outputs (coherence, factuality, planning), limiting the strength of the effectiveness claims for long-text quality.

762.human_review: With the recent updates in LLMs generation capabilities, I am skeptical whether the proposed  reverse instructions is still needed and its overall effectiveness. It would be nice to try out on newer versions of similar sized LLMs such as Llama2.
762.llm_review: Effectiveness, Model: Some comparisons risk confounds due to heterogeneous pretraining and tuning pipelines across models (e.g., Alpaca reimplementation, untuned OPT-30B). More controlled model-level studies—holding the base model constant and varying only the instruction data across multiple backbones (not just LLaMA-7B)—would better substantiate the parameter-efficiency and effectiveness claims.

763.human_review: The question examined is an important one, as more modern automatic speech recognition systems are applied in language documentation of endangered languages (which are frequently morphologically complex).
763.llm_review: Timely and well-motivated study that addresses an underexplored but important question for endangered-language ASR: whether modern multilingual architectures generalize to polysynthetic morphology. The paper frames the problem clearly, situates it in relevant literature, and executes a cross-architecture comparison that will interest the *ACL community working on low-resource speech.

764.human_review: The authors explore several combinations of indicators of morphological complexity and performance metrics in trying to tease out the underlying cause.
