764.llm_review: Thoughtful operationalization of morphological complexity and evaluation metrics: the study triangulates surface proxies (average word length, type–token ratio) with unsupervised segmentation-derived measures (morphemes/word, morpheme length), then relates them to WER, CER, and an OOV-robustness metric under controlled OOV stress tests. The link between higher type–token ratio and greater WER/CER degradation, replicated across two architectures (and largely consistent barring identified outliers), makes the performance–complexity connection concrete and testable.

765.human_review: In doing so, they come up with ingenious ways of comparing ASR performance between languages in spite of the complex landscape of varied morphologies, amounts of data, quality of recordings, and contents diversity.
765.llm_review: Data coverage spans 10 languages across the isolating–polysynthetic spectrum, including multiple polysynthetic languages rarely represented in ASR work, with explicit attention to permissions and field conditions. Evaluating two strong multilingual ASR models (Whisper medium, XLSR-53) under consistent fine-tuning protocols reveals performance gaps that are practically informative for documentation pipelines (e.g., larger WER degradation for morphologically complex languages, higher CER for isolating ones).

766.human_review: In the end the authors succeed at least in establishing an impact of morphological complexity on the performance of modern ASR systems, but without being able to identify a precise cause or mechanism.
766.llm_review: The complexity–performance conclusions are weakened by confounds and instability: (i) complexity is partly proxied by Morfessor-based segmentation quality that may vary by language and orthographic conventions; (ii) data size, domain, speaker diversity, and audio quality differ substantially (e.g., single-speaker Hupa; Bible readings for Cree/Yupik), all of which can drive WER/CER irrespective of morphology; (iii) several key findings hinge on excluding outliers or show opposite trends across architectures (e.g., CER vs OOV evolution), and OOV-robustness shows no significant relationships with complexity. Together, these factors make the claim of reduced robustness for polysynthetic languages suggestive rather than definitive.

767.human_review: It turns out that type-to-token ratio comes out as the main factor that influences degradation of WER and CER for morphologically complex languages, however properly estimating type-to-token ratio is not trivial and the method used  is not presented in enough details given its importance in the conclusion.
767.llm_review: Methodological choices limit rigor and interpretability: no development set or model selection (last checkpoint used), a small sample size (n=10) with Pearson tests but no correction for multiple comparisons, ad hoc outlier handling, and a trigram LM trained on the same training text used for decoding. The OOV manipulation (700 utterance swaps) is under-specified in constraints and may alter other distributions; OOV is defined at surface type level without normalizing tokenization/orthography across languages. These issues reduce confidence in causal interpretations and the reproducibility of the reported correlations.

768.key_points: Strength: Data, Experiment, Model, Result, Robustness, Task
768.human_review: The paper provides thorough experimental results across multiple datasets, demonstrating the robustness and effectiveness of CasCoD on both IND and OOD tasks. The authors also conduct the ablation study on model and data sizes to validate the scalability and adaptability of this method. Overall, this is a sound and solid work.
768.llm_review: Data/Task: The paper evaluates on a well-chosen in-domain task (BBH with a clear 4:1 train/test split) and multiple out-of-domain multiple-choice reasoning suites (BB-sub, AGIEval, ARC-E/C), providing a diverse set of reasoning tasks. Experiment: The study compares against strong and relevant baselines (Std-CoT, MT-CoT, Step-by-step, SCOTT, Answer-SFT) and includes thorough ablations on model size (1.1B/7B/13B), training data size (12.5%–100%), loss weighting, and a single-step variant, as well as a faithfulness analysis (LAS). Model: A practical teacher–student framework (ChatGPT → LLaMA2 with LoRA) and a simple, reproducible cascading objective (q→r, q⊕r→a) that aligns training and inference. Result: CasCoD improves accuracy over distillation baselines on both IND and OOD settings and reaches a substantial fraction of teacher performance; it is competitive with Answer-SFT on OOD while retaining the ability to generate CoTs. Robustness: Gains persist across model sizes and with substantially less training data, and OOD performance is relatively insensitive to loss-weight α. Task: The approach directly targets reasoning with CoTs and demonstrably increases generalization across unseen multiple-choice reasoning tasks.

769.human_review: The paper is well-formulated, with a clear structure that is easy to follow. The flow of writing and thinking is logical and coherent.
769.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is clearly structured with a motivating example, an intuitive figure contrasting standard and cascading distillation, and precise training objectives with equations. The training–inference alignment is well explained, datasets and setups are described in sufficient detail, and ablations are easy to follow. Limitations and ethical considerations are explicitly acknowledged, which improves readability and transparency.

770.human_review: The novelty and contribution of this work are a little incremental and limited. The paper builds on existing CoT distillation methods by introducing a two-step process, which, although effective, may not be seen as a large progress from current techniques.
770.llm_review: Novelty: While the cascaded conditioning (q→r followed by q⊕r→a) is a neat reorganization, the core idea overlaps with prior work that separates rationale and answer objectives (e.g., Step-by-step, MT-CoT). The incremental difference—conditioning answer prediction on the generated rationale and training both steps jointly—may be perceived as a modest extension rather than a fundamentally new distillation paradigm.

771.key_points: Weakness: Analysis, Effectiveness, Explanation, Generalization, Method
771.human_review: The analysis of the method primarily focuses on generalizability. A deeper exploration of the effectiveness and explanation of the method would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the advantages of the methods.
771.llm_review: Analysis/Effectiveness/Explanation/Generalization/Method: (1) The central claim that spurious question–answer correlations drive poor OOD generalization is plausible but not directly tested; there are no controlled diagnostics (e.g., counterfactuals, answer shuffling, correlation probes) to establish causality beyond aggregate performance gaps. (2) Effectiveness versus the simplest baseline (Answer-SFT) is mixed on some OOD sets (e.g., AGIEval and ARC-E/C), tempering the claim of broadly superior generalization. (3) Methodologically, delimiter-based rationale–answer splitting can be brittle across tasks/teachers, and the two-pass training introduces exposure bias (answer is trained on gold rationales, but inference uses generated ones) without mitigation (e.g., scheduled sampling or self-refinement). (4) Generalization is evaluated primarily on multiple-choice tasks that are still close to BB/BIG-Bench distributions; broader domains (open-ended reasoning, math/code with free-form answers) are not assessed. (5) The study would benefit from deeper analyses to isolate components (e.g., masking out answer tokens in single-step training as a control; sensitivity to noisy/incorrect rationales; error propagation from r to a) and statistical significance reporting.

772.human_review: Logical Design. This paper analyzes the complex issue of clickbait and designs a multimodal model based on the causal representation framework. The model extracts a wide range of multimodal information and makes predictions based on the invariant and causal factors.
772.llm_review: Analysis, Framework, Model: The paper offers a clear analysis of spurious correlations arising from disguised multimodal clickbait and proposes a principled causal framework to address them. The model disentangles three latent factors—invariant, scenario-specific causal, and non-causal noise—grounded in a stated causal structure. It operationalizes this with an IRM-driven invariance mask, iterative scenario estimation, and a contrastive mechanism (via Gumbel-Softmax masking) to separate causal from non-causal variant features. This combination of invariance learning and contrastive dissociation is a thoughtful modeling contribution tailored to the problem.

773.human_review: Sufficient Experiments. Experimental evaluations have been conducted on multiple datasets of varying scales, demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed algorithms.
773.llm_review: Data, Efficiency, Evaluation, Experiment: The study evaluates on three established datasets (CLDInst, Clickbait17, FakeNewsNet) with consistent gains over strong multimodal and causal baselines. The experimental protocol includes 20-run averages, class-imbalance handling, significance tests (p < 0.005), PR curves, ablations isolating all major components, and t-SNE case studies. The proposed social-metadata-based augmentation meaningfully improves label efficiency by leveraging historical signals, reducing annotation burden while maintaining content-based inference at test time.

774.human_review: The model diagram is not sufficiently appropriate. It is stated that five types of features across multiple modalities are extracted, however, Figure 2 only illustrates the extraction of four features, omitting the interaction between textual and visual features, which may lead to confusion.
774.llm_review: Figure, Model: The causal graph in Fig. 3 and the end-to-end pipeline in Fig. 2 do not fully clarify modeling assumptions or variable roles, which weakens the theoretical grounding. For example, the semantics of C and S, how backdoor paths are concretely blocked, and what is observed vs. latent are not rigorously specified in the figure. The iterative dependence where scenarios are estimated from variant features that themselves depend on the learned mask m risks circularity, but this is not depicted or discussed in the figures. Similarly, the Gumbel-Softmax mask and the choice of k_d are central to the model but are not visually or mathematically tied to the causal story in the figures, making it difficult to assess identifiability and stability from the visual model specification.

775.human_review: Lack of technical details introduction. The meaning of the dashed lines in Figure 3 should be explained in detail to facilitate the reader's understanding.
775.llm_review: Detail, Figure: Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or hard to locate (e.g., values or search ranges for α, β, k_d, number of scenarios |S|, stopping criteria for the scenario–mask alternation, convergence checks, and exact data augmentation rules). Figure readability could be improved: PR curves are crowded and lack clear legends/fonts; the t-SNE plots use many colors/markers without a detailed legend, and axes or scaling are not described; Fig. 2’s module boundaries and data flow are dense and could benefit from clearer labeling of inputs/outputs and training vs. inference paths.

776.human_review: The task are well defined, though there are no previous benchmarks they have worked on.
776.llm_review: Benchmark and Task: The paper defines a clear cross-task benchmark for conversational task-switching, spanning five heterogeneous tasks (summarization, MCQ reasoning, QA, sentiment) and 15+ switch pairs. The setup cleanly separates the conversation-history task (CH task) from the target task, includes zero-shot baselines, and reports a full switch matrix per model, which makes the benchmark useful for reproducing and extending analyses of task interference in multi-turn chat.

777.human_review: A good message to practioners as well as LLM creators. They should be careful about the context they condition on. In fact, those creating apps should probably weight the context in attention based on the task classification.
777.llm_review: Attention and Task: The study explicitly ties task-switch behavior to the autoregressive attention over the full conversational history and formalizes the ideal conditional-independence condition r ⟂ h | u for distinct tasks. By varying the number of history turns, it probes how attention to prior task exemplars affects the new task, offering task-aware insights into when history should be ignored versus leveraged.

778.human_review: The performance problem seems to be across model sizes as per certain tables provided. Hence, it is an important problem.
778.llm_review: Importance, Model, Performance: The work highlights an important reliability issue for conversational agents: prior-task interference can degrade downstream performance, and this is shown across both small (7B) and large (GPT-4) models. Documenting that even top models can be affected elevates the practical importance, and the performance analyses identify concrete vulnerability patterns that model and system designers must consider.

779.human_review: There is a lot of work to be done in this area. This work takes the first step. It would have been great if the work was a bit more comprehensive. 4 tasks with 4 switches is a simple work, and possibly needs extension to become a major benchmark. Having said that, the work in the current form is good.
779.llm_review: Benchmark: Beyond the main results, the paper contributes a practical evaluation suite: prompt templates per task, ablations over conversation length, multiple seeds, and confusion-matrix style summaries of all task-switch pairs. This breadth, plus inclusion of both open and closed models, makes the benchmark broadly applicable despite the limitations of log-prob access for closed models.

780.human_review: Some of these points are known. But it is good to see numbers behind claims like multi-turn with wrong context degrades performance.
780.llm_review: Performance: The results clearly show the contrasting regimes of in-context gains within-task versus potential losses after task-switch, and they quantify both accuracy/metric deltas and a sensitivity score. Additional analyses (e.g., format-failure rates, variance across seeds) help interpret performance movements and separate confidence shifts from formatting artifacts.

781.human_review: A paper like this should be a dataset paper. They should release their dataset and provide the initial benchmark for others to improve on.
781.llm_review: Benchmark, Data, Improvement: The benchmark’s task coverage, while diverse, is still narrow (five datasets, small MMLU subsets, and synthetic teacher-forced histories) and lacks real conversational logs with naturally occurring task switches. Expanding to more domains, multilingual settings, longer histories, and real-world multi-intent dialogues would strengthen ecological validity and benchmark utility.

782.human_review: The experiments show mixed results. So I find an improvement in performance in some cases and a decrease in performance in other cases. In fact all of this might be within error bars. Therefore it would be *very* helpful to know the standard deviation of some of the metrics reported.
782.llm_review: Experiment, Metric, Performance, Result: The proposed sensitivity metric depends on the zero-shot response as the reference and cannot be computed for closed models, limiting cross-model comparability. Format-extraction errors in generative classification further confound performance results, and there is little statistical testing to substantiate claims of significant degradation. Incorporating alternative metrics (e.g., reference-likelihood variants, calibrated confidence), significance tests, and controlled prompt formats would make the experimental results more robust.

783.human_review: What do we know about noisy multi-turn conversations? What if we filled the context with noise? Does it degrade performance? Can the authors divide the sections into classes of tasks, and for each class what is the correlation of performance improvement or degradation?
783.llm_review: Performance: Some observed degradations are modest (often within a few percentage points) and vary by model and switch direction, which makes it hard to gauge practical impact in deployment. The paper stops short of quantifying end-user effect sizes or proposing/validating mitigations, leaving performance implications somewhat preliminary.

784.human_review: Figure 2 shows a fluctuation with performance for different number of turns. Does this suggest that there is a lot of noise with little signal? I couldn't really interpret the results for GPT4.
784.llm_review: Figure, Interpretation, Performance, Result: Several figures use clipped axes and minimal uncertainty visualization, making it difficult to interpret effect sizes and variability. The relationship between accuracy change and sensitivity is not always aligned, yet the interpretation is mostly qualitative. Clearer axis ranges, consistent scales across models, confidence intervals, and tighter linkage between figures and claims would improve interpretability of the performance results.

785.human_review: The ASC method represents a significant contribution to the field of information retrieval by enhancing the efficiency of sparse document retrieval.
785.llm_review: Contribution, Efficiency, Method: The paper introduces ASC, a two-parameter (mu, eta) thresholding scheme with segmented cluster-level maximum term weights that tightens cluster bounds and enables adaptive, probabilistically safe pruning at both cluster and document levels. This methodological refinement directly translates into substantial efficiency gains on CPUs (e.g., multi-x speedups with <=0.1% MRR@10 loss) while incurring modest memory overhead (~9%), making it a practical contribution for high-throughput sparse retrieval.

786.human_review: The paper validates the efficacy of the ASC method using established benchmarks such as MS MARCO and BEIR. These comprehensive experiments not only confirm the method’s capability in improving relevance scores and reducing latency but also offer a thorough comparison with existing methods, thereby solidifying the practical advantages of ASC.
786.llm_review: Benchmark, Comparison, Experiment, Validation: The empirical evaluation is broad and careful: MS MARCO Dev and TREC DL’19/20 with SPLADE, plus zero-shot BEIR, and additional models (uniCOIL, LexMAE). ASC is compared against strong DAAT/SAAT baselines (MaxScore, Anytime Ranking, IOQP), reports both mean and P99 latencies, includes recall along with MRR/nDCG, uses significance testing, and presents ablations (mu sweeps, segmentation strategy random vs. k-means). Results consistently show that ASC attains comparable or better effectiveness with sizable speedups, validating the approach under diverse settings.

787.human_review: A formal analysis providing a probabilistic guarantee on rank-safeness is a strong point of the paper. This rigorous mathematical backing is essential, as it substantiates the reliability and effectiveness of the new retrieval method under various operational conditions.
787.llm_review: Analysis, Method: The paper provides formal analysis for the method: (i) segmentation tightens cluster bounds (Theorem 1); (ii) an adaptive pruning rule using MaxSBound and AvgSBound regulates aggressiveness based on bound tightness (Theorem 2); (iii) rank-competitiveness within a factor mu without time budget (Theorem 3); and (iv) a probabilistic safeness guarantee within factor eta under random segmentation (Theorem 4). The empirical correlation between AvgSBound/MaxSBound and bound tightness supports the theoretical design.

788.human_review: The paper is well-written, presenting complex ideas in a structured and accessible manner, which makes it easy for readers to understand and follow the proposed method and its implications.
788.llm_review: Method, Presentation: The method is presented with clear formulas and a step-by-step flow (two-level pruning conditions, cluster traversal order, document-level bounds), a worked example, and practical guidance (default hyperparameters, cluster/segment choices, quantization, space overhead). The limitations section is candid and situates ASC relative to block-based pruning frameworks and potential integrations, improving readability and practical uptake.

789.human_review: The paper could improve the accessibility and clarity of its data presentations. Tables and figures should ideally be placed at the top of the page using the ‘[t]’ placement specifier in LaTeX, rather than ‘[h]’, to ensure they appear at the beginning of pages. This would enhance readability and make it easier for readers to reference these visual aids as they navigate through the text.
789.llm_review: Clarity, Data, Presentation: (1) The definition of (mu, eta)-approximate retrieval is somewhat unconventional (average of top-k' rank scores and expected values), and the choice of k' is not emphasized, which may hinder interpretability for practitioners; the claim of being "probabilistically safe" depends critically on random segmentation and may feel stronger than warranted in non-ideal conditions. (2) While the dense retrieval comparison is discussed as out of scope, the absence of empirical dense baselines limits the data-driven perspective on end-to-end tradeoffs; sensitivity analyses on the number of clusters/segments and space-time trade-offs are only partially explored. (3) Presentation of some tables/figures is dense and occasionally hard to parse (shorthands like C%/Re, split equations/labels, minor typos), which can obscure key takeaways.

790.human_review: My other concerns in the last submission have been tackled. Please continue to improve the presentation of the paper as I have suggested.
790.llm_review: Presentation: Notational and formatting issues detract from clarity: mixed use of theta/mu/theta-eta thresholds without an algorithm box, figure/table layouts that blend examples and decisions, and scattered references to settings (e.g., mu choices across k=10 vs. k=1000) that require cross-referencing appendices. A concise pseudocode or algorithm listing, more consistent notation, and streamlined figure captions would significantly improve readability.

791.human_review: Confidence calibration with black-box techniques is an important area of research right now, so the author's method will likely help future works in this direction
791.llm_review: Method/Technique: The paper introduces a clear, modular decomposition of confidence into (i) question-level uncertainty, estimated via the entropy of sampled answer frequencies, and (ii) answer-level fidelity, elicited through a hierarchical "fidelity chain" built by iteratively replacing an option with "All other options are wrong." The plug-and-play formulation is black-box friendly (no logits required), uses a principled combination Conf = (1 - Uncertainty) * Fidelity, and includes an interpretable weighting scheme (controlled by c4). The methodology is thoughtfully stress-tested with ablations (showing Fidelity carries most of the signal) and temperature-scaling analyses, supporting the technical soundness of the technique.

792.human_review: I think the proposed technique, specifically decomposing confidence into two more specific aspects (fidelity and uncertainty) is an interesting way to think about confidence calibration
792.llm_review: Technique: The fidelity elicitation mechanism is simple yet inventive: by forcing the model to re-decide after replacing content with a canonical statement, it reveals preference strength among options and yields an interpretable fidelity chain. Weighting chain positions by c4 provides a tunable, transparent way to downweight fallback choices. Using greedy decoding makes the fidelity signal robust to sampling temperature, and the practical call budget (few extra queries per question) is reasonable for many black-box LMs.

793.human_review: The method performs well across LLMs and datasets in multiple-choice tasks
793.llm_review: Data/Method/Model/Performance: The evaluation spans four MCQA datasets (ARC-Challenge, MMLU, CommonSenseQA, TruthfulQA) and six RLHF LMs (GPT-3.5/4, Baichuan2-13B-Chat, LLaMA2-Chat at 7B/13B/70B), demonstrating broad applicability. Across models and datasets, the method consistently improves calibration metrics (ECE, IPR, CE) while maintaining accuracy, and analyses cover temperature robustness, parameter scaling, and ablations. The introduction of IPR (monotonicity) and CE (confidence distribution evenness) provides complementary views beyond ECE, and reliability diagrams further substantiate the reported gains.

794.human_review: There is still a missing discussion on why "All of the other options are incorrect" is a valid approach for quantifying fidelity. Many MCQA questions have answers that depend just on the remaining answers (e.g. "which of these animals is the largest?")
794.llm_review: Discussion: The treatment of "Truly Well-Calibrated Confidence" is suggestive but not fully grounded in established calibration theory. IPR and CE are only lightly motivated; CE reduces to normalized entropy over bin densities, and both IPR/CE depend on binning choices without sensitivity analysis. The paper does not connect its metrics to proper scoring rules, resolution vs. reliability trade-offs, or sharpness, and omits statistical significance testing and failure-mode analysis. As a result, the normative claim about balancing ECE, IPR, and CE feels under-argued, and the broader conceptual discussion would benefit from deeper theoretical framing and empirical validation.

795.human_review: This approach also can only be used on multiple-choice settings and not long-form generation, where confidence calibration is often more important. The authors should qualify the scope of their claims to note that this approach has only shown to work for multiple choice tasks. This is brought up in the limitations but should be clearly explained in the main paper as well
795.llm_review: Approach/Task: The method is restricted to closed-set tasks (MCQA, classification) and relies on a specific prompt transformation ("All other options are wrong") that can induce distribution shift, be sensitive to option ordering, and confound fidelity with process-of-elimination behavior. The reliance on greedy decoding and a small sampling budget (e.g., K=10) may make uncertainty estimates brittle; cost/latency can be high due to multiple calls per question. Comparisons omit stronger calibration baselines (e.g., temperature scaling tuned on validation, isotonic/Dirichlet/beta calibration on logits where available, self-consistency ensembles), and sensitivity to label permutation/paraphrasing is not studied. The applicability to open-ended generation is acknowledged as a limitation but remains unexplored.

796.human_review: The proposed method operates as a post-processing step, which means it does not require retraining the individual models. This can be advantageous in practical applications where retraining can be computationally expensive.
796.llm_review: Training: The framework is entirely post-hoc and training-free, enabling practitioners to fuse heterogeneous multimodal language models without any additional finetuning or architectural alignment. This makes the approach resource-efficient, easy to adopt, and particularly attractive for settings where retraining is infeasible. The study further shows that weaker models benefit substantially from self-composition, highlighting practical utility under constrained training budgets.

797.key_points: Strength: Clarity, Contribution, Method, Related Work
797.human_review: The paper is well-organized and clearly written, with a logical flow that makes the proposed method easy to understand. The related work section is thorough and positions the contributions in the context of existing research.
797.llm_review: Clarity, Contribution, Method, Related Work: The paper articulates a clear, unified framework for likelihood composition that organizes prior ideas into self-composition (debias, highlight), mutual-composition (ensemble, majority vote), and their mix. The methods are simple, well-defined with explicit formulas, and easy to implement. The narrative situates the work within related literature on ensembling, contrastive decoding, and logit-based composition, while delineating the contribution as a unification plus useful mixed variants validated across multiple VQA datasets and model families.

798.human_review: The ensemble methods used, such as debiasing, highlighting, majority-vote, and traditional ensemble strategies, are well-known and commonly used in the field. The paper does not introduce fundamentally new techniques or methodologies in model ensemble.
798.llm_review: Method, Model, Novelty, Technique: The technical novelty appears incremental. Debias resembles subtracting a no-image baseline, highlight mirrors contrastive/negative prompting, and mix-composition is a straightforward linear combination of per-option likelihoods. The approach does not address cross-model calibration or tokenization differences in a principled way (softmax per model may not suffice), and the reported use of option-letter likelihoods raises concerns about unintended biases. Stronger fusion baselines (e.g., temperature calibration, stacking/meta-learning, Bayesian model combination) are missing, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed techniques rather than generic ensembling effects.

799.key_points: Weakness: Analysis, Framework, Method, Result, Theory
799.human_review: The paper lacks a deep theoretical analysis explaining why the proposed combination of common ensemble methods yields better results. Incorporating a more rigorous theoretical framework could strengthen the understanding of the method's advantages.
799.llm_review: Analysis, Framework, Method, Result, Theory: The framework lacks a theoretical justification for why subtractive debias or highlight should approximate the desired decision rule across heterogeneous models, and under what conditions it is guaranteed to help. The analysis provides useful heuristics (alpha sensitivity, inter-model heatmaps) but does not include significance testing, error typologies, or principled hyperparameter selection. Results are sometimes inconsistent (highlight often degrades performance), yet the paper does not probe failure modes or offer a rationale beyond empirical tuning. Claims of generality are not supported beyond multi-choice VQA.

800.key_points: Weakness: Benchmark, Data, Experiment, Method, Robustness, Validation
800.human_review: There is a concern that the method may be overly fine-tuned to specific benchmarks. It would be useful to include experiments on out-of-sample datasets or unseen tasks to validate the robustness of the approach.
800.llm_review: Benchmark, Data, Experiment, Method, Robustness, Validation: Evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice VQA, with no tests on open-ended generation or other multimodal tasks, limiting external validity. There is no discussion of training-data overlap or contamination for the base models, and robustness checks are missing (e.g., option-order shuffling, paraphrased prompts, negative/positive prompt variants). The study reports point improvements without variance, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to decoding settings. The computational overhead of multiple prompts and multiple models is not contextualized against single-model or budget-matched baselines, leaving robustness and practical deployment trade-offs underexplored.

801.human_review: The construction of a dataset of 472 moral scenarios based on Chinese moral words adds empirical depth and gives a robust evaluation of LLMs.
801.llm_review: Data, Evaluation, Model: The paper curates a sizeable Chinese dataset of 472 moral scenarios derived from a moral lexicon, with clear two-option choices and explicit links to moral principles, plus gender-augmented variants. The evaluation spans word-level polarity judgments and scenario-level decisions, enabling consistency checks across levels, prompts, and option orders. Comparing four widely used LLMs (two Chinese, two English) on the same Chinese inputs provides informative cross-model, cross-linguistic evidence, and the inclusion of firmness scores adds granularity to model behavior.

802.human_review: The paper introduces a unique three-module framework for evaluating the moral beliefs of LLMs
802.llm_review: Framework, Model: The three-module, pluralistic framework (moral choice, moral rank via BWS+ILSR, and moral debate) is a novel, coherent way to probe moral beliefs beyond binary correctness. It not only yields preference rankings over moral principles but also tests the stability of those preferences under adversarial pressure, enabling nuanced, model-level insights such as individualist vs. collectivist tendencies and alignment with human annotators.

803.human_review: The study employs rigorous methods, including moral ranking through Best-Worst Scaling and Iterative Luce Spectral Ranking, and robustness checks through repeated experiments and parallel experiments.
803.llm_review: Experiment, Method, Robustness: The study employs multiple robustness checks—two complementary prompts at the word level, option-order flipping, repeated runs, and post-debate reevaluation—alongside quantitative ranking (BWS+ILSR) and correlation analyses (e.g., SROCC). The addition of a human baseline (Chinese university students) strengthens external validity, while the debate module stress-tests the stability of choices, offering a richer methodological picture than single-shot evaluations.

804.human_review: The study deliberately provides minimal context in moral scenarios to avoid randomness, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world moral decision-making.
804.llm_review: Complexity: The pipeline introduces many moving parts (LLM-generated scenarios, manual filtering, principle assignment, BWS+ILSR, and multi-round debates), making causal attribution difficult and increasing the chance of compounding errors. The mapping from options to moral principles and then to developmental stages adds another abstraction layer that can obscure interpretability and magnify annotation or generation biases.

805.human_review: Assigning and evaluating "immoral" stances in debates may ethically charge the LLMs' training processes and output. The paper does not sufficiently address how these ethical risks are mitigated or the potential long-term effects on the models' behavior.
805.llm_review: Evaluation, Model, Training: Cultural claims are potentially confounded by running English LLMs entirely in Chinese, mixing effects of translation quality, safety policies, and RLHF with purported cultural differences. The human baseline is small (n=30) and homogeneous, limiting generalizability. Scenarios are LLM-generated from negative moral words, risking leakage of ChatGPT’s priors into the test set. Important evaluation details (e.g., statistical significance, effect sizes, firm control of temperature/seed across models, exact model versions) are under-specified, and the dataset/code are not yet publicly available, hindering reproducibility.

806.human_review: The construction of the moral scenarios and the binary choices presented may inherently bias the models' responses. The study does not adequately discuss how it ensures that these scenarios are balanced or how it handles the ambiguity inherent in moral decision-making.
806.llm_review: Model: The model set is limited (two Chinese vs. two English) and heterogeneous in size, capability, and safety tuning, which can drive differences unrelated to moral beliefs. There is no capability-matched control or ablation to disentangle scale and alignment effects, and debate pairings may advantage stronger models. The absence of additional open, similarly sized baselines or controlled variants weakens model-level conclusions.

807.human_review: The paper is clearly presented and easy to follow, and the inventory of 10 logical patterns is illustrated in a clear and concise manner.
807.llm_review: The paper is generally clear and well structured. The task is motivated convincingly, the template design criteria (comprehensive/expressive/simple) are articulated upfront, and the annotation workflow is described step by step (calibration, MACE filtering, expert verification), aiding readability and reproducibility. Releasing data and scripts further strengthens the presentation.

808.human_review: The author provides detailed examples in the body and appendix to illustrate the rationality of the 10 logical pattern designs. In particular, Figure 4 explains the possibility of multiple reasonable interpretations using different logical patterns for the same IA-CA pair.
808.llm_review: The figures effectively convey the core ideas: Figure 1 neatly illustrates the IA–CA interplay and the two subtasks (template selection and slot filling), and Figure 2 clarifies the model I/O format. Visual cues (e.g., red arrows indicating attack points) help readers grasp what is being challenged in each template. The visuals make the contribution accessible to both NLP and argumentation audiences.

809.human_review: In Table.1, Mig and Alt patterns are relatively easy to understand. However, examples are lacking to illustrate the distinction and necessity of MM1 and MM2 logical patterns. In MM1, x promotes z and z promotes y, which is used to explain that x does not suppress y. In MM2, it is explained that x promotes z and z suppresses y, which means x promotes y. I believe that x can also suppress y here. Is there a more reasonable explanation to illustrate this?
809.llm_review: Several important choices are under-explained, which hampers interpretability: the distinctions between closely related templates (e.g., Alternative vs. Another true cause, or the two Missing mechanism variants) could be clarified with more contrasting examples; the computation of coverage and how "Not Applicable" is decided need clearer criteria; the rationale for the RougeL threshold in slot evaluation and what constitutes acceptable overlap is not given; and the handling of sentences with multiple applicable templates (beyond the expert pass) would benefit from a more explicit description with edge cases.

810.human_review: The CA logical structure analysis task involves two sub-tasks: template selection and slot filling. When the template selection is ambiguous in the first sub-task (multiple logical pattern templates may be selected), there is a lack of further processing of slot-fillers in the second sub-task, which may also be due to conflicts in template understanding by LLMs (e.g., GPT-4), leading to poor performance.
810.llm_review: The experimental analysis is too shallow to illuminate the task’s difficulty beyond reporting low scores. Combining template selection and slot filling into a single generative setup likely depresses performance, yet there is no comparison to simpler or modular baselines (e.g., sentence-level multi-label classification, extraction via span tagging). Results lack per-template breakdowns, cross-topic generalization, and error categorization tied to task properties (implicit reasoning, attack point). The slot-filler metric appears so strict that precision collapses to near-zero, but no sensitivity analysis of thresholds or semantic matching is provided. Overall, the performance section falls short of diagnosing where models fail on this task.

811.human_review: Is the use of RougeL in the Precision score too strict? Slot-filler extraction may be paraphrased after LLM.
811.llm_review: Methodologically, the scope is narrow: templates are restricted to Argument from Consequences and data span only three topics, limiting generalizability. The single-template-first annotation design risks under-capturing multi-pattern sentences, and expert verification is applied only to a subset determined via MACE, which may bias which multi-template cases are recovered. The choice of MACE threshold (0.8), the decision to fine-tune/generate both subtasks jointly, and the reliance on lexical-overlap scoring for slots are reasonable but not validated against alternatives (e.g., multi-label training, span extraction models, semantic matching). A small per-template human upper bound or agreement breakdown would better ground method choices.

812.human_review: Novel methodology: The authors' use of causal mediation analysis in the context of VLMs is innovative. This approach allows them to identify both direct and indirect effects of interventions on model bias, providing a more nuanced understanding of bias propagation.
812.llm_review: The paper introduces a clear and novel methodological framework that adapts causal mediation analysis to vision-language models for object detection. The analysis is carefully structured around well-defined interventions (mask-gender, replace-gender, null) and decomposes effects into direct and indirect contributions at the level of specific model components and even attention layers. The per-module and per-layer mediation design, along with the examination of cross-modal alignment of bias, provides fine-grained, interpretable insights that go beyond prior work relying only on output probability shifts, making the methodological contribution both original and analytically compelling.

813.human_review: Quantitative findings: The paper presents concrete, quantitative results that support their claims. For example, they found that image features contribute significantly more to bias than text features, accounting for 32.57% and 12.63% of the bias in the MSCOCO and PASCAL-SENTENCE datasets, respectively. This level of specificity is valuable for understanding the relative importance of different model components in bias generation.
813.llm_review: Using MSCOCO and PASCAL-SENTENCE in a zero-shot GLIP setup, the paper operationalizes a concrete BIAS_VL metric and provides empirical findings that are easy to interpret. Results consistently show that image features drive more bias than text features (e.g., ~32.6% vs. ~15.5% reduction on MSCOCO; ~12.6% vs. ~5.6% on PASCAL-S), that deep-fusion contributes substantially, and that modality contributions are aligned rather than conflicting. The FPR analyses across object categories corroborate stereotype-like patterns (e.g., indoor objects with females, vehicles with males). The proposed image-encoder mitigation achieves notable bias reductions (22.03% on MSCOCO; 9.04% on PASCAL-S) with negligible AP loss, which strengthens the practical relevance of the findings.

814.human_review: Limited scope of bias: The study focuses primarily on gender bias, which is indeed important, but doesn't address other forms of bias such as racial, ethnic, or age-related biases. This narrow focus may limit the generalizability of the findings to other types of biases in VLMs.
814.llm_review: Generalization is limited by the scope: the study centers on a single architecture (GLIP) and task (object detection) with two datasets, relies on binary gender labels, and employs a face-centric mitigation that may not transfer to settings where gender cues are non-facial or occluded. The framework depends on white-box access to internal components, which restricts applicability to black-box VLMs common in practice. It remains unclear how well the metric and insights extend to other biases (e.g., race, age), broader VLM families (e.g., captioning, retrieval), and more diverse data regimes.

815.human_review: Computational complexity: The paper doesn't provide a detailed discussion of the computational resources required for their causal mediation analysis. Given the complexity of VLMs, this analysis could be computationally intensive, which might limit its practical applicability.
815.llm_review: The causal analysis hinges on strong assumptions (e.g., no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcomes) that are not explicitly justified, and the procedure for setting mediators to the "state of intervention" may introduce distribution shift. Statistical rigor is underdeveloped: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analyses for BIAS_VL or mediation quantities, and robustness to metric design choices (e.g., thresholds, aggregation over objects) is not examined. The intervention pipeline adds complexity (layer-wise mediator manipulations; MTCNN+MobileNet at inference; face replacement averaging) without thorough ablations on computational overhead, hyperparameters, or artifact effects, raising questions about reproducibility and the stability of conclusions.

816.human_review: The paper is clearly structured and includes figures that effectively clarify and illustrate the central concepts.
816.llm_review: Clarity and Figure: The paper is clearly written and benefits from well-chosen figures that make the method easy to follow. The flowchart (Fig. 1) concretely illustrates the HyQE pipeline, the prompt examples (Figs. 2, 6, 8, 10) make the query-generation setup reproducible, the causal diagrams (Fig. 3) help motivate the design choice, and the ICA visualizations (Fig. 5) provide an intuitive, visual contrast between cosine-similarity ranking and HyQE. Ablation plots (Figs. 4, 11) are legible and directly tied to the key hyperparameter and setting choices.

817.key_points: Strength: Effectiveness, Experiment, Improvement, Model, Performance, Result
817.human_review: Experimental results show that applying HyQE consistently improves the performance of most combinations of retrieval models, embedding models, and LLMs used for generating hypothetical questions, demonstrating its effectiveness in ranking retrieved contexts given input queries.
817.llm_review: Effectiveness, Experiment, Improvement, Model, Performance, Result: Across multiple datasets (DL19, DL20, COVID, NEWS, Touche) and a broad set of embedding backbones (Contriever, BGE, E5, nomic-embed, text-embedding-3-large), HyQE consistently improves NDCG@10 over baseline embedding-only ranking, often by several points, and does so with different hypothetical-query generators (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Mistral-7B). The results also show compatibility gains when combined with HyDE, further lifting performance. Ablations on λ and K, plus the comparison between the max-based (Eq. 2) and average-based (Eq. 5) scoring, substantiate the robustness of the improvements and provide practical guidance on model and hyperparameter choices.

818.human_review: The proposed method can reduce the computational overhead of generating hypothetical queries by generating them once and storing and reusing them when needed. This addresses the limitations of other baselines, which have to expand queries every time input queries are given.
818.llm_review: Baseline and Method: The method is simple, modular, and easy to integrate into existing retrieval stacks. It leverages off-the-shelf LLMs to generate hypothetical queries per context and uses standard embedding similarity for scoring, avoiding LLM fine-tuning. Baselines are reasonably comprehensive on the retrieval/ranking side—covering both sparse (SPLADE++) and multiple dense models—and the paper evaluates HyQE as a drop-in ranker atop these baselines, highlighting method generality and compatibility.

819.human_review: While the authors emphasize the need for their proposed methods in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems multiple times in the Abstract and Introduction, they only perform experiments in document retrieval tasks and skip the experiments in RAG. Including experiments in RAG would strengthen the authors' claims.
819.llm_review: Experiment and Method: Key design choices are under-specified or under-ablated. The number of hypothetical queries per context (M), selection/diversity controls, and de-duplication are not systematically studied, making it hard to assess stability and reproducibility. Hyperparameter selection (e.g., λ per backbone) lacks a clear validation protocol, and results may be sensitive to LLM prompting and sampling settings (temperature, n). The evaluation focuses on NDCG@10 re-ranking but does not measure end-to-end RAG quality (answer accuracy/faithfulness), leaving uncertainty about downstream impact.

820.human_review: Although they address their efficiency in theory compared to other query expansion methods, including a quantitative analysis of their superiority in complexity in practice would make the authors' claims even stronger.
820.llm_review: Analysis, Complexity, Efficiency: The complexity discussion is largely asymptotic and does not include empirical efficiency results (indexing time, latency, memory footprint of storing H(c), retrieval time over hypothetical-query indices). Claims of amortized cost and scalability would be stronger with wall-clock benchmarks and memory/throughput numbers, plus comparisons to alternative re-rankers. Practical aspects such as corpus updates (requiring regeneration of H(c)), storage growth with M, and serving-time ANN queries over H(c) are acknowledged but not quantified.

821.human_review: While the authors mention that their method can avoid hallucinations seen in the previous work HyDE (Gao et al., 2023), they do not perform a direct comparison with HyDE in the experiment table. Showing a direct comparison between HyQE and HyDE would strengthen the authors' claims further.
821.llm_review: Comparison and Experiment: While comparisons to several embedding backbones and HyDE are provided, the study omits strong supervised and cross-encoder re-rankers (e.g., monoT5, T5-based re-rankers, ColBERTv2) and recent LLM re-ranking baselines (e.g., RankGPT/RankZephyr, Cohere Rerank). Including these would better situate HyQE against state of the art and clarify the trade-off between effectiveness and computational cost relative to widely used re-ranking alternatives.

822.human_review: The proposed dataset effectively incorporates a range of media types, including text, images, videos, and audio, contributing to the advancement of multimodal fact-checking systems.
822.llm_review: Data: The paper contributes a sizable and novel benchmark (M3DC) specifically targeted at multimodal, multi-document, fine-grained claim verification. The dataset is large (≈414K claims across >10K topics), includes long, realistic claims, and provides node- and relation-level labels aligned with AMR structures, enabling granular supervision. The construction pipeline fuses text, images, video, and audio into cross-document KGs and uses a controlled claim synthesis/manipulation process with multiple quality filters (reward model, Mixtral label check, ClaimBuster). A small expert-annotated subset adds initial human validation and helps anchor the synthetic labels.

823.human_review: This paper offers detailed insights by labelling and predicting the logical relationship of each claim aspect, enhancing the utility and interpretability of fact-checking beyond binary true/false classification.
823.llm_review: Interpretation: The fine-grained outputs over AMR nodes/tuples and the fusion with cross-document, cross-modal evidence provide transparent, actionable interpretability. The model highlights exactly which sub-claims (entities, events, relations) are entailed, contradicted, or unknown, and the qualitative examples demonstrate the ability to pinpoint the specific contradictory component while maintaining semantic consistency across the graph—an interpretability advantage over sample-level or per-fragment-only methods.

824.human_review: Experimental results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on M3DC, indicating the efficacy of the approach in multimodal fact-checking tasks.
824.llm_review: Experiment, Improvement, Result: The method shows consistent gains over task-specific baselines (FGVE, MOCHEG) and competitive LVLMs on the proposed benchmark, particularly improving neutral detection and fine-grained F1. Results transfer reasonably to MOCHEG in fine-grained settings, despite domain/style differences, suggesting some robustness. Ablations are included and indicate the relative contribution of modalities and the centrality of text; importantly, performance trends on the small human-labeled subset track the synthetic-labeled set, supporting the utility of the synthetic benchmark for evaluation.

825.human_review: The process of dataset construction is not described clearly and the introduction of the fine-grained claim labeling is missing.
825.llm_review: Clarity, Data: The dataset description omits several critical details needed to gauge data quality and replicability: limited human evaluation (≈30 samples) without clear inter-annotator agreement, unclear train/dev/test splits and topic leakage controls, and sparse coverage statistics per modality. Because the pipeline uses model-generated labels (reward classifier, LVLM filtering), there is a risk of label bias/propagation that is not quantified. The ablation suggests text dominance, raising questions about how often audio/video actually provide decisive evidence and whether the dataset truly stresses multimodal reasoning as claimed.

826.human_review: The presentation of the methodology proposed in this paper is not very clear. For example, how to initialize the GCN? How to get and use the Joint Representation in Figure 3?
826.llm_review: Clarity, Method, Presentation: Methodological exposition has gaps that affect readability and reproducibility. The GCN update equations are underspecified (e.g., missing or unclear learnable transforms/activations), and the integration of multimodal embeddings with LongT5 pretraining (GSG) lacks precise training details (loss weighting, end-to-end fine-tuning, optimization hyperparameters). The multi-stage pipeline (AMR/grounding/reward RL/GCN) is complex, yet hyperparameters, model selection criteria, and training stability are not fully documented. Figures are dense and occasionally hard to parse, and there are minor typos and formatting artifacts that hinder clarity.

827.human_review: The method proposed in this paper does not perform well on the MOCHEG dataset. The gap with LLaVA and MiniGPT in sample-level prediction is relatively large.
827.llm_review: Data, Method, Performance: Empirically, the multimodal claim is weakened by ablations showing modest gains from images/audio/video beyond text. On MOCHEG, sample-level macro-F1 trails strong LVLM baselines, and neutral detection remains challenging. Heavy reliance on synthetic fine-grained labels (reward model + manipulator) risks overfitting to the labeling pipeline and potential leakage of modeling assumptions into the evaluation; robustness, significance testing, and out-of-domain or adversarial stress tests are not provided. The work also lacks a direct evaluation of evidence grounding accuracy and explanation faithfulness, which are central to fine-grained verification.

828.human_review: The paper is well-written, easy to read and understand.
828.llm_review: The recall–detect–predict framing is clearly articulated and grounded in an intuitive cognitive metaphor. The paper explains each phase with concise equations and consistent notation, and Figure 1 effectively orients the reader to the overall flow, improving readability and conceptual coherence.

829.human_review:
The final experimental results of the paper are very good and competitive.

The strengths of the paper in this cycle:
829.llm_review: Experiments show consistent gains across three benchmarks: on IEMOCAP the model reaches 76.15 Acc/76.01 W-F1/76.40 M-F1, on DailyDialog 75.55 Acc/70.20 Micro-F1, and on EmoryNLP 42.68 Acc/40.78 W-F1. The improvements over strong baselines (e.g., +4.24% vs EmoCaps on IEMOCAP) indicate meaningful progress in ERC performance.

830.human_review: The paper is well-written, easy to read and understand.
830.llm_review: The presentation of datasets, metrics, and training settings is clear and detailed (e.g., splits aligned with COSMIC, per-dataset hyperparameters, optimizer, early stopping), aiding reproducibility. Tables are well-labeled with clear notations for reproduced vs. reported results, and the narrative stays focused with minimal ambiguity.

831.human_review: The final experimental results of the paper are very good and competitive.
831.llm_review: The experimental design is comprehensive: comparisons include sequence-, graph-, and PLM-based baselines with both paper-reported and reproduced numbers, and an ablation study demonstrates that removing either the recall or detection phase degrades performance substantially, supporting the necessity of each component.

832.human_review: The paper includes new analytical experiments and provides some interpretable analysis through feature visualization, which is of certain value.
832.llm_review: Analysis is strengthened by a comparative case study and informative figures. The heatmaps from the detection phase and MLP layer provide interpretability into class-specific activations, and the discussion of emotional inertia ties qualitative observations to quantitative performance, offering insight beyond raw scores.

833.human_review:
The use of ablation analysis and case studies makes it difficult to prove that the capabilities claimed by the method are consistent with the actual capabilities of the model. The former can only show that the module contributes to the results, while the latter makes it hard to generalize the conclusions.

The  weaknesses of the paper in this cycle:
833.llm_review: The ablation and analysis could be deeper and broader: (1) no ablation is reported on DailyDialog; (2) component disentanglement is incomplete (e.g., no modality-wise ablations on IEMOCAP, no sensitivity to the number of transformer blocks, and limited clarity on the distinct impact of intra-context vs. recall GRUs); (3) statistical significance is not reported. From a generalization standpoint, the model relies on different input features across datasets (multimodal vs. RoBERTa-only), which complicates cross-domain conclusions, and there is no evaluation beyond the three English datasets.

834.human_review: The visual analysis is conducted on individual cases, which might result in conclusions that are not generalizable.
834.llm_review: While the cognitive framing is compelling, the analysis remains largely qualitative; there is no targeted test isolating the effect of the proposed cognitive reasoning beyond standard ablations. Generalization remains uncertain for short-turn or sarcasm/humor-heavy settings (as noted), multi-party conversations with many speakers, and low-resource or multilingual domains, and there are no robustness or distribution-shift evaluations.

835.human_review: The proposed SCA method is model-independent, plug-and-play, and does not require training or fine-tuning.
835.llm_review: Fine-tuning, Method, Model: The paper introduces a simple, training-free, plug-and-play KV-cache compression method (SCA) that operates at token level by selecting representative entries via a greedy redundancy-minimization criterion computed jointly over keys and values (with RoPE applied to keys). By avoiding fine-tuning and changing no model parameters, SCA is model-agnostic and can be dropped into standard Transformer LLMs, addressing long-context extension without retraining specialized long-context variants.

836.human_review: Preliminary experiments are conducted to provide a reasonable basis for removing redundant vectors to compress the KV cache.
836.llm_review: Experiment: The empirical study is broad and well-structured: short-text in-context tasks (IMDB, RACE, AG News, Cosmos QA) at fixed compression ratios; long-context language modeling on PG19 and ArXiv across 4k–64k with periodic compression; a stress-test via passkey retrieval at varying lengths; closed-ended long-context tasks from L-Eval; and ablations on selection sharing across layers. Baselines (StreamingLLM, Sparse, H2O) are included, and metrics (accuracy, perplexity) are appropriate for each setting.

837.human_review: The extensive experiment verifies the performance of SCA in modeling long text, while retaining the long context capabilities of the model better than other methods.
837.llm_review: Experiment, Model, Performance: Across multiple LLMs (Llama2-7B/13B-Chat, Vicuna1.5-7B), SCA maintains near-full-attention accuracy at 50% KV compression on short-text tasks, matches or beats alternatives in perplexity during long-text language modeling, and yields strong downstream gains on long-context evaluations. Notably, it sustains very high passkey retrieval accuracy even when extending context well beyond the native window, and on L-Eval closed-ended tasks it improves averages by roughly 2.8–4.2 points when extending to 16k, surpassing certain fine-tuned long-context baselines (e.g., Longchat1.5-7B-32k, Vicuna1.5-7B-16k).

838.human_review: SCA employs cosine similarity to identify redundant vectors and employs a greedy algorithm to select the most representative vectors for compressing the KV cache. While these measures aim to minimize information loss during compression, they may overlook subtle semantic differences that can impact the model's performance in nuanced tasks.
838.llm_review: Algorithm, Performance: The selection rule is driven solely by intra-K/V cosine similarity (via a greedy max-sim redundancy proxy), without considering queries or attention dynamics, which may discard tokens that are globally similar yet crucial for future predictions. Moreover, SCA requires building similarity matrices and computing per-step Add values, implying at least quadratic time/memory in the number of tokens per compression event; the paper does not report wall-clock throughput, latency overhead, or memory trade-offs versus baselines. In several settings, the empirical margins over strong baselines (e.g., H2O) are modest, making it hard to quantify the real efficiency–quality trade-off absent runtime benchmarks.

839.key_points: Weakness: Architecture, Evaluation, Generalization, Model, Validation
839.human_review: The evaluation of SCA was confined exclusively to the Llama2 and Vicuna model architectures. The generalizability of SCA's effectiveness remains unvalidated across a broader range of LLMs.
839.llm_review: Architecture, Evaluation, Generalization, Model, Validation: Evidence is limited to a small set of English Llama/Vicuna models (7B/13B) with RoPE; there is no validation on larger models or different attention variants (e.g., ALiBi, multi/grouped-query attention), nor analysis for architectures with different positional schemes or KV sharing. The evaluation excludes open-ended generation and multilingual scenarios and uses relatively small test samples in some settings. Important baselines for KV compression or token reduction (e.g., token merging, KV quantization/offloading hybrids, other eviction or clustering strategies) are missing. Finally, the method lacks theoretical guarantees or statistical analyses of information loss, and ablations omit key sensitivities (e.g., similarity metric choices, recent-token retention hyperparameters, compression schedules), limiting claims about generalization and robustness.

840.human_review: Customized Knowledge Base (MatSciKB): The creation of a high-quality, structured materials science knowledge base represents a substantial contribution to the field, providing a reliable and up-to-date resource for scientific inquiry.
840.llm_review: Clear and timely contribution: the paper introduces HoneyComb as, to my knowledge, the first end-to-end LLM-based agent system purpose-built for materials science. The system unifies a curated domain knowledge base (MatSciKB), a tool hub tailored to materials tasks, and an adaptive retriever, addressing a well-motivated gap where general-purpose LLMs struggle with domain-specific reasoning and up-to-date knowledge. The contribution is relevant to *ACL communities interested in domain-specialized LLM systems and practical scientific applications.

841.human_review: Sophisticated Tool Hub (ToolHub): The introduction of ToolHub, with its Inductive Tool Construction method, offers a new paradigm for enhancing LLMs with specialized computational capabilities, which is a significant methodological contribution.
841.llm_review: Contribution and method are well-aligned: beyond the high-level system, the paper proposes concrete mechanisms that are methodologically meaningful. The Inductive Tool Construction pipeline (LLM-generated functions, human verification, decomposition into reusable atomic tools) provides a practical recipe to grow a domain tool set. The hybrid retrieval (BM25 + Contriever) and the two-phase Assessor/Executor policy for tool selection are sensible design choices for precision and efficiency. Ablations indicate each component contributes, e.g., the full system improves GPT-4 accuracy on MaScQA over MatSciKB-only (+0.76%) and ToolHub-only (+5.84%), supporting the claim that the combination matters.

842.human_review: Broad Applicability: The adaptable framework of HoneyComb is showcased to have potential for extension to other scientific domains, suggesting broader impacts beyond the specific focus on materials science.
842.llm_review: Strong adaptation and application story: HoneyComb is plug-and-play across multiple base LLMs (GPT‑4, GPT‑3.5, LLaMA‑2/3, HoneyBee) and consistently improves performance on MaScQA and SciQA. Notable gains include +20.61 points for GPT‑4 and +16.76 points for HoneyBee on MaScQA, and a large jump for HoneyBee on SciQA. The per-topic analysis on MaScQA further illustrates where tool and knowledge augmentation help (e.g., Material Testing), underscoring practical utility for diverse material subdomains.

843.human_review: Interdisciplinary Relevance: The work bridges the gap between AI and materials science, appealing to an interdisciplinary audience and fostering collaboration across fields.
843.llm_review: Solid AI/agent framing: the work situates HoneyComb within agentic LLMs that mitigate hallucinations via retrieval and tool-use, adding an explicit decision protocol (Preliminary Tool Assessor and Strategic Tool Executor) to reduce information overload. The integration of a Python REPL for precise calculations and an adaptive retriever advances the broader AI goal of safer, more reliable scientific reasoning with LLMs, and the blueprint appears extensible to other scientific domains.

844.human_review: Lack of Comprehensive Analysis: The paper could provide more comprehensive comparative analysis with other state-of-the-art systems in the field to better position HoneyComb's contributions and performance.
844.llm_review: Analysis and performance interpretation could be deeper: the evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA, with little statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or significance testing), limited qualitative error analysis, and no human or expert baseline. The observed per-topic performance drops for GPT‑3.5 when integrated with HoneyComb are noted but not thoroughly probed (e.g., ablations targeted at the failure categories, tool-call traces, or retrieval diagnostics). There are no efficiency/latency metrics, tool-invocation success rates, or calibration analyses, making it hard to assess practical performance trade-offs and robustness.

845.human_review: Reliance on LLM Quality: The performance of HoneyComb is contingent on the quality and capabilities of the underlying LLMs used for knowledge base construction, tool development, and retrieval processes. This reliance may introduce limitations if the LLMs have inherent biases or knowledge gaps.
845.llm_review: Model and performance baselines are under-specified: the paper lacks comparisons to strong agent/RAG baselines (e.g., ReAct-style agents, standard RAG with fusion-in-decoder, or domain-adapted ChemCrow-like toolkits for materials). Important configuration details (prompting templates, decoding settings, top‑k, stopping criteria, maximum tool calls, and tool coverage/size) are missing, as are generalization tests beyond QA (e.g., open-ended reasoning or synthesis planning). The reliance on human-verified, inductively built tools is not accompanied by coverage metrics or generalization measurements, leaving uncertainty about performance consistency in the wild.

846.human_review: The article is clear and logical, making it easy to read.
846.llm_review: The paper is clearly written and easy to follow. The motivation for decomposing tool use into planner, caller, and summarizer is articulated up front, and the roles, inputs, and outputs of each component are precisely specified with both equations and informative figures. The GLPFT training pipeline is described step-by-step, including how data are reorganized for each subtask and how losses are applied. The evaluation setup (benchmarks, metrics, in-/out-of-domain split) is defined unambiguously, with references to appendices for prompts and dataset details, which aids reproducibility.

847.human_review: The proposed concept is valuable; if smaller models can replace larger ones, it will lower the implementation threshold for deploying large models in various business applications.
847.llm_review: From an application perspective, the modular multi-LLM framework is practical: it isolates planning, tool invocation, and summarization so each can be updated independently as tools or requirements evolve. The implementation choices (LLaMA-2-chat 7B/13B backbones, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, explicit prompting for each role) demonstrate a feasible path for deploying smaller open-source models in tool-use agents. The design supports plugging in lighter models per capability, making it attractive for resource-constrained settings where a monolithic larger model is impractical.

848.human_review: The authors demonstrate that using only three Llama2-7B or Llama2-13B models can achieve results comparable to GPT-4, which is quite impressive. They also analyze the characteristics of the α-Umi framework from various perspectives, providing valuable insights for industrial implementation.
848.llm_review: The paper provides strong empirical analysis backed by careful implementation. Results consistently show gains over single-LLM baselines on ToolBench across Plan ACC, Action EM, hallucination rate, and argument F1, with additional real-time RapidAPI evaluations. The ablations are thorough: multi-LLM one-stage vs GLPFT, single-LLM multi-task, LoRA vs full fine-tuning, instruction reuse vs non-reuse, and data scaling laws, plus training-loss tracking for different output spans. These analyses, enabled by a clear implementation, substantiate that decomposition and the GLPFT procedure drive the improvements.

849.human_review: The authors do not provide specific advantages of the α-Umi framework in terms of resource consumption for model training and deployment.
849.llm_review: Framework, model, and training-wise, the approach incurs nontrivial overhead: GLPFT first fine-tunes a backbone and then instantiates and fine-tunes three separate models, increasing compute, memory, and engineering complexity. Coordination is handled via a planners discrete Next: decisions and fixed prompts rather than a jointly optimized interface; there is no explicit learning signal to align modules or mitigate error propagation across plannercallersummarizer. The reliance on ToolBench-style traces for subtask data may also imprint dataset-specific biases on the trained components.

850.human_review: The article proposes a multi-LLM framework but does not adequately discuss the increased complexity of the models and how to manage this complexity.
850.llm_review: In terms of complexity, the framework multiplies inference cost and system orchestration: three models must be loaded and invoked iteratively, which likely increases latency and memory footprint relative to a single model. The paper does not report resource usage, throughput, or end-to-end latency, making it hard to assess the practical trade-off between higher accuracy and operational cost. Without these measurements, it is unclear when the added framework complexity is justified in production.

851.human_review: The authors do not clearly explain why they chose to define the split models as Planer, Caller, and Summarizer. What specific basis do they have for these definitions?
851.llm_review: Definitions around the central claim are under-specified. Small LLMs are weak tool learners is stated broadly, but small is effectively instantiated only as LLaMA-2-chat 7B/13B. The scope of tool learning is anchored primarily to ToolBench APIs, and the out-of-domain split is defined at the tool level; it is not clear how these definitions generalize to other tool ecosystems or more complex schemas. Clarifying these terms and their intended generality would strengthen the claim.

852.human_review: The paper presents a splitting method that has certain reference significance for the industry, as it allows for better and more cost-effective deployment. However, it inherently leads to error accumulation, similar to traditional pipelines. How to strike a balance is worth a more detailed discussion.
852.llm_review: Methodologically, several evaluation choices may introduce bias or limit interpretability: the stepwise offline metrics depend on ChatGPT-derived references, and the real-time evaluation uses ChatGPT as the judge, which can favor certain styles or plans. Comparisons do not normalize for total parameter budget at inference (three 7B models vs a single larger model), and there is no latency/cost analysis or statistical significance testing. The study would benefit from human evaluation of final answers, broader baselines (e.g., other structured function-calling SFT methods), and clearer fairness controls.

853.human_review: One issue of image generation models is generating images that accurately align with the given text input. In this paper, the authors evaluate image captions based on precision and recall metrics and analyze their impact on the text alignment of T2I models. This direction is interesting and should be explored further.
853.llm_review: Evaluation/Metric/Model: The paper sets up a coherent, multi-faceted evaluation for text-image alignment. It leverages T2I-CompBench with five sub-tasks (color, shape, texture, spatial, non-spatial) and uses established automatic evaluators (BLIP2 QA, detection, CLIP) to derive consistent, decomposed metrics. It also quantifies caption precision/recall via a modified FaithScore pipeline aligned to the compositional categories, enabling a direct link between caption properties and downstream performance. The study triangulates across models: PixArt-b (for long text with T5), and Stable Diffusion 2.1/XL, as well as multiple LVLM captioners (LLaVA, BLIP2, uform). The consistency of trends across these models strengthens the external validity of the findings.

854.human_review: The authors conducted an ablation study, demonstrating that utilizing LVLMs for caption generation can yield comparable results to captions written by human evaluators.
854.llm_review: Ablation/Evaluation: The precision-recall ablation is systematic and interpretable: precision is controlled by the proportion of positive sentences, while recall is controlled by the number of subcaptions (submasks). The grid over {0%,25%,50%,75%,100%} precision and {0,1,2,3} recall produces clear, monotonic patterns that support the main claim (precision > recall in impact, with recall helping most at low precision). The second set of experiments with synthetic captions serves as an external ablation that reproduces the same trend across different LVLMs, reinforcing the causal interpretation suggested by the evaluation results.

855.human_review: The analysis demonstrates that the precision of the caption is more critical than the recall when training T2I. One of its primary use cases is to establish a methodology for enhancing the text-image alignment of T2I based on these findings. It would be beneficial to present some experiments in this direction.
855.llm_review: Analysis/Experiment/Method: The way precision and recall are manipulated may introduce confounds. Precision is lowered by inserting LLaMA2-generated negative sentences that are still often partially correct, which may not reflect real misalignment distributions encountered in web-scale T2I training. Recall is operationalized by adding subcaptions, but this also increases token length and effective supervision per image, potentially conflating recall with training signal volume. The choice to ignore subimages while reusing subcaptions to describe the full image could introduce content irrelevant to the global scene. Experimental controls (e.g., matching total token budgets or examples per epoch across conditions, multiple random seeds, variance estimates) are not reported, making it hard to separate the effects of precision/recall from dataset size and training stability.

856.human_review: The measurement of text alignment for ‘Attribute binding’ and ‘Object relationship’ was conducted using various methods. It would be good to demonstrate that it aligns with human evaluation, even on a small portion of the samples.
856.llm_review: Evaluation/Method: The study relies heavily on automatic evaluators (BLIP2 QA, object detection, CLIP) known to have biases and to correlate imperfectly with human judgments; no human evaluation or significance testing is provided. The modified FaithScore uses GPT-3.5 to extract entities and LLaVA-13B to judge correctness, but LLaVA is also one of the captioners being evaluated, introducing evaluator-as-author bias. The FaithScore probe covers only 1,000 captions and lacks uncertainty estimates, and the mapping between the decomposition categories and T2I-CompBench tasks may not be fully aligned. Overall, the evaluation could be strengthened by using multiple independent judges (e.g., ensemble of VLMs, GPT-4V), human verification on a subset, confidence intervals, and tests of statistical significance.

857.human_review: The paper identifies an important problem called "speech anchor bias" that arises when directly fine-tuning LLMs with speech instructional data. This is a valuable contribution to understanding the limitations of current approaches.
857.llm_review: Contribution and Data: The paper makes a clear and useful contribution by diagnosing speech anchor bias—the tendency of speech-text models to over-attend to the speech stream and ignore textual instructions—backed by layer-wise attention-flow analysis. On the data side, it leverages abundant ASR corpora to synthesize multi-task instruction data without needing costly multimodal collections, and commits to releasing the augmentation dataset, which can have practical value for the community.

858.human_review: The proposed self-powered data augmentation method is an innovative solution to address the speech anchor bias. Generating and using the model's own instructional data is a clever way to better align the speech and text modalities.
